Md Nazrul Islam Talukder, Deputy Attorney-General ------For the Government-respondents (in all cases).
parties:
Jahid Faisal ----- Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh & others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: As common question of facts and law are involved in these Rules they were heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment.

2. In all these Rules the respondents were called upon to show cause as to why section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2006 putting an embargo in filing of appeal against the order of conviction and sentence under sub-section (1) of section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act unless an amount of money not less than 50% of the dishonoured cheque amount is deposited in the Court shall not be declared to be void as it conflicts with the right of appeal as enshrined in section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

3. Writ Petition No. 4425 of 2008 is from judgment and order dated 27-11-2007 passed by the respondent No. 3, Joint Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Metro. Sessions Case No. 320 of 2007 arising out of CR Case No. 3115 of 2006 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1(one) year and to pay a fine of Taka 12,00,000.

4. Writ Petition No. 3854 of 2008 is from the judgment and order dated 31-10-2007 passed by the respondent No. 3, Joint Metro Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Metropolitan Sessions Case No. 339 of 2007 arising out of CR Case No. 3547 of 2006 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for a period of 1(one) year and to pay a fine of Taka 12,88,97,229.62.

5. Writ Petition No. 8506 of 2008 is from judgment and order dated 9-9-2008 passed by the respondent No. 3, Joint Metro Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Metro Session Case No. 1391 of 2007 arising out of CR Case No. 2476 of 2006 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1(one) year with a fine of Taka 69,03,360.

6. Writ Petition No. 196 of 2007 is from judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 25-7-2006 passed by the respondent No. 2, Joint Metro Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Metro Sessions Case No. 802 of 2006 arising out of CR Case No. 4799 of 2004 convicting the petitioners under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instrument Act and sentencing them thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 2(two) months and to pay a fine of Taka 2,12,000.

7. Writ Petition No. 9454 of 2008 is from judgment and order dated 23-10-2008 passed by the respondent No. 2, Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Chittagong in Sessions Case No. 380 of 2008 arising out of CR Case No. 322 of 2007 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 6(six) months and to pay a fine of Taka 58,00,000.

8. Writ Petition No. 9318 of 2008 is from judgment and order dated 4-11-2008 passed by the respondent No. 2, Joint Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Sessions Case No. 1017 of 2006 arising out of Petition Case No. 1854 of 2005 (CMM Court, Dhaka) convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1(one) year and to pay a fine of Taka 15,29,504.

9. The learned Advocates on behalf of the petitioners after placing their respective cases asserted the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act (as amended on 9-2-2006) mainly on 3(three) counts.

Firstly, that the statutory law must be comprehensive in its nature and should provide adequate provision in respect of trial and appeal but the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act (hereinafter referred to as "the Act) is harsh, unreasonable, oppressive and arbitrary.

Secondly, that the petitioners were tried by the Sessions Judge/Additional Sessions Judge/Joint Metro Sessions Judge under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provided appeal against judgment and order of conviction as a matter of right but section 138A of the Act provides a restriction in filing of appeal in case of any order of conviction and sentence under section 138(1) of the Act unless an amount of money not less than 50% of the cheque amount is deposited in the Court which awarded the sentence which is not only unconstitutional and also curtailment of the statutory right of appeal of the petitioners and it causes hardship to the petitioners and, as such, the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2006 is liable to be declared null and void.

Thirdly, that the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act was promulgated on 9-2-2006 and the same cannot be applicable retrospectively as those cases were filed prior to the said law came into force.

10. Mr Nazmul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the complainant-respondent No. 4 in Writ Petition No. 8506 of 2008 and Writ Petition No. 3854 of 2008 submits that the provision of section 138A of the Act is not ultra vires to the Constitution or contrary to Articles 27, 31, 40 and 42 of the Constitution, inasmuch as the right to file appeal is not a fundamental right but it is a statutory right and therefore, it cannot be said that the petitioner's right has been curtailed by provision of section 138A of the Act. He further submits that the respondent No. 3, Joint Metro. Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka on consideration of the entire materials on record rightly convicted the petitioners under section 138(1) of the Act. He finally adds that by now it has been well settled specially in Artho Rin Adalat Ain that the provision for depositing 50% of the decretal amount at the time of preferring appeal is well maintained and it cannot be said that the defaulters have lost their fundamental right as guaranteed by the Constitution. The learned Advocate in support of his submission has relied on the decisions reported in 2 BLC (AD) 87, 2006 BLD (AD) 172, 13 BLC 686.

11. In order to appreciate the legal aspects involved in this case it would be useful; if we trace the scheme and purpose of the amendment of Negotiable Instruments Act on 9-2-2006. Section 138 of the Act provides for special forum for realisation of dishonoured/ unpaid cheque money from the drawer by special method. The law is by now well settled that the appeal is a continuation of the suit/case and there is no dispute that in the society a class of borrowers or drawers in taking shelter of this principle of law deliberately used to drag the appeal for an indefinite period in order to hang the process of realisation of loan money or unpaid cheque's money for an indefinite period in which the payee or the holder of the cheque not only suffers a lot also the process of realisation of cheque amount or loan money falls into dark. Keeping the said view in mind the legislature in applying their wisdom made amendment in section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act providing to deposit not less than 50% of the dishonoured cheque at the time of filing an appeal in the Court which awarded the sentence.

13. We have in this connection gone through the section 138A of the Negotiable Instrument (amendment) Act, 2006 which runs as follows:

138A. Restriction in respect of appeal—Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, no appeal against any order of sentence under sub-section (1) of section 138 shall lie, unless an amount of not less than fifty percent of the amount of the dishoriourd cheque is deposited before filing the appeal in the Court which awarded the sentence.

14. A similar precondition has been provided in Artha Rin Adalat Ain. The Legislature in applying their wisdom put similar type of restriction in section 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and later on in section 41(2) of the new Ain namely, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

15. Section 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 1990 is reproduced herein below:

(৩) অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের কোন রায় বা ডিক্রির বিরুদ্ধে কোন বিবাদী আপীল দায়ের করিতে ইচ্ছুক হইলে এবং তিনি উক্ত রায় বা ডিক্রির বিরুদ্ধে-

(অ) ধারা ৬(২) এর দরখাস্ত এবং উপ-ধারা (২)(ক)এর অধীন আপীল করিয়া থাকিলে,উক্ত-ধারা ৬(২)এবং উপ-ধারা (২)(ক)এর অধীন জমাকৃত অর্থ বাদ দিয়া মূল মামলায় ডিক্রিকৃত অবশিষ্ট অর্থের অন্ততঃ অর্ধেক অর্থ-

ডিক্রি প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা করিয়া উপধারা(১)এ নির্ধারিত সময়ের মধ্যে হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে আপীল দায়ের করিতে পারিবেন।

(৪)কোন বিবাদী উপ-ধারা (২)এবং এ নির্ধারিত অর্থ ডিক্রি প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা না করিলে বিবাদীর আপীল গ্রহণযোগ্য হইবে না।

16. Section 41(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is reproduced herein below:

আপীলকারী,ডিক্রীকৃত টাকার পরিমাণের ৫০% এর সমপরিমাণ টাকা বাদীর দাবীর আংশিক স্বীকৃতিস্বরুপ নগদ ডিক্রীদার আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানে,অথবা বাদীর দাবী স্বীকার না করিলে, জমানতস্বরুপ ডিক্রী প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা করিয়া উক্তরুপ জমার প্রমান দরখাস্ত বা আপীলের মেমোর সহিত আদালতে দাখিল না করিলে, উপ-ধারা (১)এর অধীন কোন আপীল কার্যার্থে গৃহীত হইবে না।

17. The provisions of those sections were challenged upto the Appellate Division unsuccessfully

18. In the case of Md Nur Islam vs Agrani Bank reported in 1 MLR (AD) 373, it has been decided that deposit of 50% decretal amount as a pre-condition is mandatory both in the case of an appeal or an application for setting aside an ex parte decree.

19. In the case of Anisur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 12 BLC 22, it has been held as follows: "We are of the view that the provision of section 41(2) of the Ain or any part of the same is not violative of Article 27, 31, 40 or 42 of the Constitution. Similar view has been taken in the case of Chandpur Jute Supplier reported in 2 BLC 49 and in other cases decided by this Court."

20. In the case of AHN Kabir vs Bangladesh reported in 13 BLC 686, it has been held as follows:

"Therefore, depositing 50% of the face value of the dishonoured cheque cannot be said to be illegal in case of a pending case ended up in conviction and sentence."

21. In the case of AJM Helal vs Bangladesh along with 8 other cases (unreported judgment dated 9-2-2009 passed in Writ Petitions No. 3058 of 2008 along with 8 other writ petitions), it has been held that the provision of section 138A of the Act is not violative of the Articles 27, 31, 40 and 42 of the Constitution.

22. Negotiable Instruments Act is a special law. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provided certain pre-condition for bringing prosecution against the drawer of the unpaid cheque. Under section 138(c) of the Act, 30 days' time is given for payment of the amount due under the cheque from the date of receipt of notice regarding dishonour of the cheque issued by the payee. The payee has to wait for 30 days anticipating payment of the amount by the drawer. After the expiry of 30 days, if the drawer does not pay the amount, the cause of action starts from 31st day onwards. The limitation to file a complaint as prescribed under section 142(b) of the Act is one month. On trial, both the parties are entitled to adduce evidence both oral and documentary. The trial Judge in deciding the case under the Act has to consider first whether the cheque in question was dishonoured and whether after fulfilling the legal requirement of section 138(b) and (c) of the Negotiable Instruments Act the case was filed or not. In that view of the matter, there is little chance of success in the appeal on the part of the drawer of the unpaid cheque, although, the appeal takes much more time for disposal. We have already noticed that the convict-appellant on various pretext used to take adjournment in order to hang the process of realisation of cheque amount. In order to meet such situation the legislature in applying their wisdom inserted section 138A providing the provision for depositing not less than 50% of the unpaid cheque amount as pre-condition in the case of an appeal.

23. On the face of the foregoing facts and circumstances vis-a-vis the above quoted decisions, Mr MA Samad finds it difficult to submit that the provisions of section 138A of the Act is ultra vires to the Constitution rather he concedes this patent position of law.

24. Mr Abu Bakar Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 9318 of 2008, however, argued that the requirement of 50% deposit of cheque amount prior to filing an appeal in the Court as laid down in section 138A of the Act is contrary to the petitioner's substantive right to prefer appeal against any such order of conviction under section 138(1) of the Act and it causes hardship to the petitioner. There is, however, the other side of the coin. Admittedly, the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 9318 of 2008 gave 4 post-dated cheque amounting to Taka 6,50,000, Taka 21,252, Taka 72,000 and Taka 21,500 in favour of the complainant respondent No. 3. Subsequently, on presentation those cheques were dishonoured lastly on 28-8-2005. In such background after fulfilling the legal requirements of section 138(b) and (c) of the Act the complainant-respondent No. 3 filed the petition of complaint in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka against the petitioner. Eventually, the petitioner was put on trial in the Court of Joint Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka to answer a charge under section 138(1) of the Act. The learned trial Judge on consideration of the evidence and materials on record by judgment and order dated 28-9-2008 convicted the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Act and sentenced him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1 (one) year and also to pay a fine of Taka 15,29,504. Moreover, on going through the materials on record it seems to us that the complainant-respondent No. 3 in order to recover his earned money has been running after the petitioner more than 5 years and in such view of the matter, we do not find any logic to say the petitioner's right is taken away by the provision of section 138A of the Act. It is not right that the strong should be allowed to push the weak to the wall. Therefore, we are unable to see eye to eye to such submission of the learned Advocate Mr Abu Bakar Siddique.

<u>25. So, our considered view is that, the requirement of 50% deposit of cheque amount at the time of filing an appeal in the Court under the provisions of section 138A of the Act is not unconstitutional or violative to the provisions of the Constitution.</u>

26. Let us, now, consider another aspect of law. At the fag end of the hearing Mr Md Zafarullah Chowdhury, the learned Advocate relying on a Single Bench decision namely, in the case of Akhter Hossain vs Hasmat Ali reported in 60 DLR 368, submitted that the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act was promulgated on 9-2-2006 and the same cannot be applicable retrospectively in those cases which were filed prior to the said law that came into force.

27. In reply Mr Deputy Attorney-General relying on the decisions reported in 2 BLC (AD) 87, 8 MLR 404 = 56 DLR 31 and 13 BLC 686 has submitted that the Negotiable Instruments Act is a special law, the amendment in question is procedural in nature and by now it is well settled that a procedural law always would apply retrospectively even to pending proceedings.

<u>28. On perusal of section 138A of the Act as amended on 9-2-2006 and on consideration of the whole enactment, it appears to us that the Negotiable Instruments Act being a procedural law, there is no bar in giving its effect retrospectively and moreso, by the Act there is no difference in awarding sentence, if any, upon the accused. Furthermore, the right of appeal accrues on the date of pronouncement of judgment.</u>

29. Similar question arose while the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 came into force. In the case of Md Mofiz Mia vs Artho Rin Adalat reported in 16 BLT 476 and so many other cases, it has been consistently held that all cases relating to recovery of loan including execution cases pending in those Adalats established under Artho Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 stood transferred by operation of law to the Artho Rin Adalats established under section 4 of the Artho Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and the trial of those cases shall be resumed from its previous position as far as practicable.

30. It is the established principle of law that "Special Law always prevails over the general law".

<u>31. On consideration of the matter vis-a-vis the cited decisions, we find no possible reason to hold that the provisions of section 138A of the Act will not apply in those cases which were filed before the said section came into force.</u>

32. Be that as it may, it has been a long standing practice of this Court that where there is a conflict between the decisions of Single Bench and Division Bench of this Court the decision of the Division Bench shall prevail. So, on this score also we are led to hold that there is no legal bar in giving its effect retrospectively in respect of all cases filed prior to section 138A of the Act came into force.

33. Mr Md Zafarullah Chowdhury, the learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 4425 of 2008, Writ Petition No. 3854 of 2008 and. Writ Petition 8506 of 2008, also submitted that it is the petitioner's statutory right to prefer an appeal against the judgment and order of conviction but the embargo to prefer appeal as laid down in section 138A of the Act has, in fact, taken away the vested right of the petitioner to prefer appeal.

<u>34. We have already indicated that the pre-condition of depositing 50% of decretal amount at the time of preferring appeal was first introduced in Artho Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 which has also been challenged in various writ petitions unsuccessfully. The proposition of law is clear, that if the appellant succeeds in the appeal he will get back his entire deposited amount and in that view of the matter, we find no merit in such argument that deposit of 50% cheque amount at the time of preferring appeal after losing the case is one kind of punishment or taken away the statutory right of the convict-petitioner to prefer appeal as canvassed by Mr Zafarullah Chowdhury. Moreover, the provision of section 138A of the Act does not debar the petitioners to file appeal under section 410, CrPC. Hence, question of violation of the right as guaranteed under Articles 27, 31, 40 and 42 of the Constitution does not arise at all.</u>

35. Mr Abu Bakar Siddique, the learned Advocate has also submitted that due to certain embargo as laid down in section 138A of the Act the poor petitioner could not prefer appeal against the impugned judgment and order of conviction under section 138A of the Act although the petitioner has every chance for success in appeal. However, it is to be observed that a convict may invoke the inherent jurisdiction of the Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure if he can make out a case of coram non judice of the trial Court or that the facts alleged do not constitute any offence or that the conviction has been based on no legal evidence or otherwise for securing the ends of justice. Hence, this bunch of arguments also fails.

36. Mere allegation of violation of provisions of law cannot give rise to any cause of action for filing a writ petition when there is forum for seeking remedy against the impugned order/judgment.

37. Besides, another striking feature of this case is that the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 4425 of 2008, Writ Petition No. 3854 of 2008, writ petition 8506 of 2008 and Writ Petition No. 196 of 2007 are fugitive from law inasmuch as the petitioners after conviction in their respective cases did not surrender in the Court. The law is well settled that a fugitive has no right to seek any kind of redress as against his grievance, if any, against the judgment and order of a Court convicting him to imprisonment.

38. Mr MA Samad, however, referring to the decision reported in 56 DLR 239 tried to impress us that non-appearance in a criminal case, if any, shall not debar a person from seeking justice in this forum under Article 102 of the Constitution. Taking into account the material facts, our straightforward answer is, after having been convicted without surrendering in the Court this argument on behalf of the convict bears no merit. The decision cited is distinguishable on facts.

39. In view of the above provisions of law and our discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs vis-a-vis the decisions as cited above, we have no hesitation to hold that the provisions of section 138A of the Act is not violative of the Articles 27, 31, 40 and 42 of the Constitution.

40. No other points urged, all the points having failed, we find no substance in these Rules.

In the result, all these Rules are discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated. The petitioners in Writ Petition No. 9454 of 2008 and Writ Petition No. 9318 of 2008 are directed to surrender to their respective bail bonds within one month from date.

End.

lawyer:
Md Ramzan Ali Sikder with Shamim Hossain, Advocates — For the Petitioner. 
Nahid Mahtab, Assistant Attorney-General — For the Respondents.
parties:
Sheikh Ahmed ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Commissioner of Customs and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Abdus Salam Mamun J: This Rule Nisi was issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 3-8-1996 (Annexure K) as contained in the file notes of the respondents refusing to assess customs duties on the goods imported by the petitioner on the basis of the CRF value pursuant to SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994 (Annexure A) and the impugned notification dated 17-6-1996 (Annexure E) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect and as to why the respondents should not be directed to levy customs duty and other taxes in respect of the said goods, cigarette paper, on the basis of invoice value.

2. The petitioner's case, in short, is that the petitioner opened Letter of Credit No. 16-123-96 dated 5-6-1996 relying upon the SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1995 for import of 5,200 reams of Dragon Brand white cigarette paper and the goods was inspected and verified by the Pre-shipment Inspection Agency who issued their Clean Report of Findings, vide Annexure F and after the consignment arrived at the Port of Chittagong the petitioner has presented Bill of Entry No. C13313 on 25-7-1996 for clearance of the goods on the basis of CRF value in accordance with the above mentioned SRO No. 316 dated 4-11-1994 but by impugned order dated 3-8-1996, vide Annexure K, the respondent No. 1 has decided that the assessment of customs duties and other charges on the basis of CRF value was not possible in view of SRO No. 1663/96/ Sulka dated 17-6-1996 and also as per order of the Hon'ble High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 1495 of 1995 and the consignment of the petitioner was liable to be assessed on the basis of Tariff Value.

3. The petitioner has further stated that the Customs Authority wanted to assess the consignment on the basis of Tariff Value, which he was legally not liable to in view of section 25A of the Customs Act and the SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994. According to the petitioner, section 25A of the Customs Act, 1969 shall prevail over any other provision of other sections of the Act and that ad-interim order passed in the Writ Petition No. 1495 of 1995 was not applicable to his case for, the petitioner was neither a party to it, nor was it served upon him nor the SRO No. 51 any longer is in force and therefore, the petitioner by issuing a Demand of Justice Notice has invoked the writ jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court and obtained the instant Rule. At the time of issuance of the Rule this Court has been pleased to direct the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 to allow the petitioner delivery of the imported goods upon payment of customs duties and other charges on the basis of CRF value pursuant to the SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-1994.

4. The respondents, ie, the Customs Authority, did not controvert the statements and submissions made by the petitioner in the Writ Petition by way of filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition and, as such, this court had no occasion to examine the respondents' version in the case.

5. Mr Ramjan Ali Sikder, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has taken us through the petition, annexures and the SROs in question and submits that the petitioner was entitled to have his imported goods assessed on the basis of CRF value in accordance with section 25A of the Customs Act and the SRO No. 316 dated 4-11-1994 and that the respondents cannot apply the SRO No. 1663 dated 17-6-1996, Annexure E, retrospectively and that the impugned Notification, Annexure E, has been issued without lawful authority.

6. Ms Nahid Mahtab, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, submits that in response to her duty to protect the Government interest in the case she has appeared without having any power and instructions and materials from the Customs Authority. She, however, submits that the Customs Authority had taken the correct view in respect of the consignment and the petitioner was under obligation to pay customs duties and charges on the basis of Tariff value.

7. In the Letter of Credit, Annexure D, there is distinct reference to PSI Agency and CRF Certificate and, as such, initial intention of the importer to have his goods inspected and verified by the PSI Agency is apparent which is also a pre-condition of the SRO No.316 dated 4-11-1994. The petitioner has opened the Letter of Credit on 5-6-1996 for import of his goods under the HS Code No. 4813.90.00.

8. The SRO No. 1663/96/Sulka dated 17-6-1996 provides that ".......সরকার অত্র বিভাগের ৭ই পৌষ, ১৪০২ বাংলা মোতাবেক ২১শে নভেম্বর ১৯৯৫ ইংরেজী তারিখের প্রজ্ঞাপন এস,আর,ও নং ২২৬ আইন/৯৫/১৯৪৮ শুল্ক রহিত করিয়া , কাস্টমস ডিউটি আরোপের উদ্দেশ্যে নিম্নবিধৃত কইঈঋ এর কলাম (৩) এ বর্ণিত মূল্য ভিত্তিক শুল্ক আরোপযোগ্য পণ্যের আমদানির জন্য উক্ত TABLE  এর কলাম (৫) এ উল্লিখিত ট্যারিফ মূল্য নির্ধারণ করিল ।"

9. In the SRO No. 51 dated 3-4-1995 this item, along with some other items, was put under the TABLE for the purpose of assessment on the basis of Tariff value. The SRO No. 154 dated 3-7-1995 also put the item under its TABLE to be assessed on the basis of Tariff value. Thereafter the SRO No. 226- Law /95/1648/Shulka dated 21-12-1995 again came into force containing a list of goods including this item under the TABLE for the purpose of assessment on the basis of Tariff value and the HS Code No. 4813.90 was under the TABLE. The SRO No. 1663/96/Sulka came into force on 17-6-1996 rescinding the SRO No. 226 dated 21-12-1995 but containing this item under its TABLE. It is therefore, apparent that the petitioner has opined his Letter of Credit while the SRO No. 226 was in force and before the SRO No. 1663 dated 17-6-1996 was issued. It also appears that Tariff value of this item was fixed by the SRO No. 51 in 1995 for the purpose of assessment on the basis of value prior to the opening of the Letter of Credit in question and all the subsequent SROs contained the item under their TABLE.

10. Section 25A of the Customs Act, 1969 has empowered the Government, notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of the Act, to make rules regarding Pre-shipment inspection of Imported goods and CRF Certificate thereof and in exercise of that power the Government has framed rules by the SRO No. 316 dated 4-11-1994 as a general provision and thereafter, in 1996 a specific Pre-shipment Inspection of Goods Rules, called the PSI Rules, was also issued by another SRO, namely, the SRO No. 244 and in the Schedule of that SRO too cigarette paper was kept separate from the purview of PSI and CRF for the purpose of assessment on the Tariff Value. This shows the intention of the subordinate legislature that all along from 3-4-1995 they intended to keep this item along with some other items beyond the purview of CRF. From the SRO 51 to 154 or 226 to 1663 all dealings with this specific matter of keeping certain commodities apart from the general provisions of the SRO No.316 have kept the item separate for the purpose of assessment on the basis of Tariff value.

<u>11. The petitioner, in the instant case, has opened the LC on 5-6-1996 knowing fully well that his intended commodity had been kept separate from the general provisions of the SRO No. 316 by the SRO No. 226 dated 21-12-1995 and by other previous SROs and the same shall be assessed on the basis of Tariff value.</u>

12. The SRO No. 226 dated 21-12-1995 provided that ".......সরকার  এস,আর,ও নং ১৫৪ আইন/৯৫/১৬৩৫ শুল্ক (তারিখ ৩/৯/৯৫) রহিত করিয়া কাস্টমস ডিউটি আরোপের উদ্দেশ্যে নিম্নবিধৃত TABLE  এর কলাম (৩) এ বর্ণিত মূল্য ভিত্তিক শুল্ক আরোপযোগ্য পণ্যের আমদানির জন্য উক্ত কইঈঋ এর কলাম (৫) এ উল্লিখিত ট্যারিফ মূল্য নির্ধারণ করিল ।"

13. This SRO had categorically stated that, fixation of Tariff value was for the purpose of imposition of duties on the basis of value.

<u>14. Since the LC was opened during the period when the above SRO No. 226 dated 21-12-1995 was in force, containing the item under the TABLE, the petitioner was bound to comply with the provisions of the said SRO. The argument that the SRO No. 1663 was applied retrospectively is of no substance.</u>

15. The petitioner's argument is that since he has opened the Letter of Credit relying upon the SRO No. 316 dated 4-11-1994, he therefore, had a legitimate expectation to have his goods assessed in accordance with the provisions of that SRO. But facts remain, at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit his intended commodity was not within the purview of that expected SRO No. 316 and long before the opening of the Letter of Credit it had been bundled together with some other items and put under a TABLE for the purpose of not assessing on the basis of CRF value as was provided by the SRO No. 316 dated 4-11-1994. It is a fact that the SRO No. 51 is no more in force but it is also the fact that the subsequent SRO Nos. 154 and 226 have succeeded their predecessor to the fullest extent.

16. Mr Ramjan Ali Sikder lastly, argued that the Principles enunciated in the case of Monohar Ali 2003 BLD (AD) 59 is equally applicable in this case.

17. In Monohar Ali's case, the intended commodity was not bundled together and put under a TABLE for the purpose of not assessing duties and taxes on the basis of CRF value at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit. The impugned SRO, in that case, came into force after opening of the Letter of Credit.

<u>18. We therefore find that the petitioner had neither any legitimate expectation nor any vested right in his favour by virtue of the SRO No. 316 dated 4-11-1994. The case of Monohar Ali 2003 BLD (AD) 59 is factually and substantially distinguishable from those of the instant case. In the case of Hafizul Islam vs Bangladesh, reported in 11 BLT 65 this Division has held that "Legitimate expectation is not allowed as wishful hope without lawful root".</u>

19 As regards placing reliance upon the SRO No. 316 dated 4-11-1994, section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 may be quoted.

Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provides:

"Power to make, to include power, to add to, amend, vary or rescind, orders, rules or bye-laws. Where, by any Act of Parliament or Regulation, a power to issue notifications, orders, rules, or bye-laws is conferred, then that power includes a power, exercisable in the like manner and subject to the like sanction and conditions (if any), to add to, amend, vary or rescind any notification, orders, rules or bye-laws so issued."

<u>20. In view of the above, we find no substance in the submissions and no merit in the Rule. The consignment is liable to be assessed on the basis of Tariff value.</u>

21. By order dated 25-7-2001 this Court has stayed hearing of this Writ Petition on the prayer of Mr Ramjan Ali Sikder on the ground of pendency of Civil Appeal No.102 of 2000 before the Appellate Division of this Hon'ble Court. At this stage, Mr Ramjan Ali Sikdar submits that subject matter and law applicable in that appeal and those of the instant Writ Petition are not the same and they are distinguishable.

22. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

23. The petitioner is directed to pay the difference amount on the basis of tariff value within 2(two) months from this date and in case of failure the respondents are at liberty to realise the same in accordance with law.

Communicate.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1042 of 2007.
lawyer:
Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner. 
Md Khaled Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent No. 11. 
None represented—Respondent Nos. 1-10, 12.
parties:
Amir Hossain Reza ------ Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This Petition for Leave to Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 10-6-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 5794 of 2004 discharging the Rule.

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the petitioner is the elected Chairman of Surma Union Parishad under Sunamgonj Sadar Upazila, District-Sunamgonj. He being the Secretary of Sunamgonj Sadar Upazila Awami League was nominated as a candidate in the last Parliament Election and incurred dis-pleasure and anger of the local MP belonging to the ruling BNP-Jamaat 4-party alliance. The petitioner has been discharging his duties and functions as the elected Chairman of Surma Union Parishad honestly, sincerely, properly and diligently and with full satisfaction of all concerned except his local political rivals including the local member of the Parliament. While the petitioner had been seriously involved in the relief work of the flood affected of Sunamgonj, a requisition signed by 11 members of Surma Union Parishad was submitted before the Upazila Nirbahi Officer with some allegations against him. Consequently one Md Abul Kalam Azad as Authorised Officer and Upazila Project Officer (Education) Sadar Upazila, District-Sunamgonj issued a notice upon the petitioner vide Memo No. এফ এস এস পি/সদর/সুনাম/০৪/১০০০(১৫) dated 27-7-2004 to show cause within 7(seven) days upon receipt of the same as to why decisions should not be taken in a special meeting for removal of the petitioner from the office of the Chairman of the Union Parishad. The petitioner gave reply to show cause notice on 3-8-2004 with explanation in detail and documentary evidence laying the allegations brought against him. The authorised officer then fixed a date for conveying the special meeting on 19-8-2004 at his office vide Memo No. এফ এস এস পি/সদর/সুনাম/০৪/১০৭(১৬) dated 9-8-2004 without considering the reply of the petitioner and same was sent to the petitioner. The petitioner filed an application to the authorised officer on 17-8-2004 praying for time for his appearance due to his sickness. But without paying, any heed to his prayer for time the special meeting was held on 19-8-2004 and resolution was sent to the Upazila Nirbahi Officer vide Memo No. এফ এস এস পি/সদর/সুনাম/০৪/১১৬ dated 21-8-2004 showing 10 votes in favour of the no confidence and 2 votes against the no confidence in respect of removal of the petitioner from the office of the Chairman of Surma Union Parishad. Thereafter, the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Sunamgonj Sadar received the resolution and transmitted the same to the Secretary, Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operative vide Memo No. সুনাম/সদর ইউএনও/এলজি/-১২৯/০৪/১৬৯৭(২) dated 22-8-2004 giving his opinion in favour of removal of the petitioner from the office of the Union Parishad Chairman. Upon receipt of said resolution, the Senior Assistant Secretary of the said Ministry communicated the approval order of the Ministry vide Memo No. ইপ/সাবঅ-৫৮/৯৯/৯৭৯ dated 17-10-2004 stating that the Ministry approved the no confidence motion against the petitioner under Rule 12(1) of the Union Parishad Chairman and Members (Resignation, Removal and Vacation) Rules, 1984 and directed the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Sunamgonj Sadar Upazila for publishing the matter in the official gazette within 15(fifteen) days upon receipt of the approval for vacation of the office of Chairman. Against that order, the petitioner moved the High Court Division and obtained a Rule.

3. The added respondent Nos. 6-12 contested the Rule denying the averments made in the writ petition contending, inter alia, that after being elected as Chairman, petitioner worked against the interest of the general public; that he became involved in many unlawful activities of which he incurred displeasure of the public of the concerned Union Parishad as well as the members of the Union Parishad. It was further contended that the petitioner had lost the confidence of the people and the elected members, therefore, 11 members of the said Union Parishad submitted a requisition against the petitioner to the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Sunamgonj Sadar requesting him to bring no confidence motion against the petitioner and, as such, removal process was initiated by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer. It was further con-tended that there is no iota of evidence that there has been any political influence in the matter and the statement with respect to the political connection of the petitioner is vague and false. The petitioner was involved in anti-social activities and also worked against the interest of the union parishad for which he lost the confidence of the local people as well as the elected members of the union parishad for which 11 members of the said Union Parishad were compelled to submit the requisition against the petitioner. It was further contended that notice of the special meeting was served upon the petitioner in accordance with law, the petitioner wilfully did not attend in the special meeting and the proceeding of the special meeting was done in accordance with law. It is further contended that 10 members cast their votes against the petitioner in support of the no confidence motion and 2 members cast votes in favour of the petitioner. Accordingly, the impugned order is lawful and the Rule is liable to be discharged.

4. Mr Md Nawab Ali, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that the allegations brought against the petitioner are totally false and fabricated and the petitioner replied to those allegations with documentary evidence but the respondents did not consider the said reply of the petitioner with a malafide intention to remove him from the office of the Union Parishad Chairman. On the other hand, from the materials on record it appears that all the members did not voluntarily sign or attend the so-called special meeting held at the residence of authorised officer, respondent No. 5. All the proceedings were done deploying police face at the instance of the local MP belonging to the party in power in a well planned evil political design and with the colourable exercise of the authority; that the petitioner never absented himself from the meetings of the Union Parishad and he was never involved in any activities prejudicial to the interest of the Union Parishad or of the State or he ever became physically or mentally incapacitated from performing his functions or he was never guilty of misconduct or responsible for any loss or misapplication of money or property of the Union Parishad within the meaning of section 12(1) of the Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983; that the petitioner could not attend the special meeting held on 19-8-2004 since he was sick and he filed an application through his representative along with medical certificate before the authorised officer two days before the said meeting seeking some time for holding the meeting so that he can get the opportunity to take part in the meeting and to make his representation. But the authorised officer without giving him the said opportunity proceeded against the petitioner, even the said respondent did not feel the necessity to reply to the prayer of the petitioner and thus the very hurried actions of the respondents suffer from lack of reasonableness and fairness. The impugned proceeding is therefore, a clear violation of the provision of section 12 of Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983 as well as Rule 7 of the Union Parishad Chairman and Members (Resignation, Removal and Vacation) Rules, 1984 and, as such, the impugned order approving the so-called proceeding is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority.

5. The learned Advocate further submitted that the High Court Division have committed an error of law in not holding that proceedings of the impugned no-confidence suffers from lack of application of independent mind of the respondents concerned, requisite materials on record which constitute 'misconduct' within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983, non-observance of the necessary procedures required by the law and the procedures of the proceedings having not been followed properly and correctly, the alleged proceeding had been drawn so hurriedly in a most arbitrary and capricious manner to foil and frustrate the mandate of the electorates by malafide and colorable exercise of power at the instance of his political rivals and, as such, the impugned order approving the so-called proceeding is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority.

6. Mr Md Khaled Ahmed, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the respondent No. 11, submitted that Rule 9 of the Union Parishad Rules, 1984 contains two parts, firstly, if any written explanation is submitted by the Chairman concerned it shall be considered and no personal hearing would be necessary in such case. Secondly, if no written explanation is given the concerned Chairman is to be heard in person. He further submitted that the petitioner submitted written explanation and, as such, it was not necessary to allow him time for personal hearing under Rule 9 of the Union Parishad Rules, 1984. The authority passed the impugned order on consideration of reply of the petitioner and the Rules thereunder. So, the impugned order passed by the authority is in accordance with law and the same does not suffer from legal infirmity.

<u>7. It appears from the record that 11 members of the concerned Union Parishad filed the requisition stating the grounds for no confidence against (the Chairman under section 12 (1) of the Ordinance, 1983 on 14-7-2004. The authorised officer issued a show cause notice under Rule 5 of the Union Parishad Rules, 1984 giving him opportunity of showing cause for 7 (seven) days against the declaration or resolution proposed to be made or passed with respect to him. Accordingly, the petitioner replied on 3-8-2004. The authorised officer, thereafter, convened the meeting on 19-8-2004 within the prescribed time under Rule 6 of the Union Parishad Rules, 1984 at his office after informing all concerned including the petitioner vide his memo dated 9-8-2004. The authorized officer convened special meeting for no confidence motion on 19-8-2004 in presence of 12 members of the Union Parishad under Rule 8. The no-confidence resolution was also legally passed by 10/2 votes under Rule 10. Thereafter, authorised officer sent a resolution to the Upazila Nirbahi Officer on 21-8-2004 within time and accordingly, the Upazila Nirbahi Officer sent the same to the Government on 22-8-2004 under Rule 11. The Government approved the resolution under Rule 12(1) of the Union Parishad Rules, 1984 and sent it to the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Sunamgonj Sadar for publishing in the Official Gazette within 15 days from the date of receipt of the approval under Rule 12(2). So the period contemplated in the provision of the Ordinance, 1983 and the Union Parishad Rules, 1984 was meticulously followed by the Authority.</u>

<u>8. Since a resolution of no confidence against the petitioner was taken upon due compliance of law and the resolution has been approved by the competent authority, the order of removal in respect of the petitioner removing him from the office of Chairman does not suffer from any infirmity. This view finds support in the case of Md Mosharraf Hossain (Babul) vs Bangladesh reported in 13 BLT (AD) 45.</u>

9. In view of the above, we find no substance in submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Md Nurul Amin with Md Azizul Haque Sikder, Advocates—For the Appellants.
Abdul Quayum with Md Selim Reza Chowdhury, Advocates—For the Respondents.
parties:
Hachina Begum and others ------ Plaintiff-Appellants
vs
Abdul Mannan and others ------ Defendant-Respondents.
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 29-8-1980 (decree signed on 4-9-1980) passed by the then Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal in Title Suit No. 23 of 1978 dismissing the suit.

2. The facts of the case, in-short, are that the present appellants as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 23 of 1978 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal imp leading the defendants for declaration of title on the averments that one Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs was owner of the suit land appertaining to CS Dag Nos.1194 and 1195 of Mouza Charvaduria measuring about 17.33 acres of land, who took settlement by executing a registered kabuliyat in favour of the then Government on 7-11-21. At the time of taking settlement of the suit land Abdul Kader Mia was a seasonal but collector of khash mohal; that Abdul Kader Mia died leaving behind the plaintiffs as his heirs while he was in service; that Abdul Kader Mia in connection with his service posted different station in which he assigned his full brother defendant No. 2 to look after the suit property; that the defendant No.  2 with ill motive got the suit land recorded in the name of the defendant Nos.1-4 and Abdul Kader Mia in equal share, that is, 3 arenas 4 gandas share; that the preparation of RS Khatian in the name of defendant Nos. 1-4 and Abdul Kader Mia was collusive and without any legal basis; that on the basis of wrong RS Khatian, the SA Khatian has also been pre-pared wrongly in the name of the defendants and Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land in which the defendant Nos. 1-4, in-fact, have no right, title or legal interest whatsoever; that Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs was the exclusive owner of the suit land, who used to possess the suit land through different bargadars on the basis of barga Kabuliyats and after the death of Abdul Kader Mia, the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land through different bargadars on payment of rent to the Government; that the plaintiffs demanded Nadabinama or Multiparty in respect of the suit land in which the defendants Nos.1-4 have not tile or interest whatsoever but the defendant Nos.1-4 refused to execute any Nadabi  Muktipatra in their favour in respect of the suit land on 27th poush, 1384 BS; that the preparation of the wrong record of rights have cast a cloud upon the title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and hence, the suit for declaration of title.

3. The defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint con-tending, inter alia, that Abdul Latif, the father of defendant Nos. 1-4 and Abdul Kader Mia took settlement of the suit land in the benami of his eldest son Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs; that Abdul Latif, the predecessor of the defendants got the suit land recorded during the time of PS operation of the year 1925 in Khatian No. 34 in the name of Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs to maintain benami character; that Abdul Latif Mia was a forester under Khas Mohal, when he took settlement of the suit land in the benami of his minor son Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs; that Abdul Latif Mia during his life time was in possession of the suit property on payment of rent to the Government; that Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs was a minor school going student during the RS operation of the years, 1925 and was in joint mess with his father Abdul Latif in the year 1925; that Abdul Kader Mia had no source of income to take settlement of the suit land and he never possessed the suit land before the death of his father Abdul Latif Mia; that the kabulyat dated 7-11-21 was executed and registered in the name of Abdul Kader Mia by false percolation; that Abdul Latif Mia died before RS operation and Abdul Kader Mia the predecessor of the plaintiffs used to look after the property of his father; that Abdul Kader Mia got the suit land recorded in the name of his 5(five) brothers. The daughters of Abdul Latif Mia relinquished their claim in the suit land and thereupon, the suit land was recorded in the name of 5(five) brothers including Abdul Kader Mia in equal share in which they are in possession; that the SA operation has also been made correctly in the name of the defendant Nos.1-4 and Abdul Kader Mia in equal share; that the defendant Nos.1-4 and Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs are in possession in the suit property in equal share on payment of rent to the Government; that the RS and SA khatian have been correctly prepared in the name of defendant Nos.1-4 and Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs in equal share; that the plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in the suit property relating to the shares of defendant Nos.1-4 and as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. In the course of trial, the trial Court framed the following issues:

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Is the suit barred under section 42 of the SR Act?

3. Is the suit barred by limitation?

4. Have the plaintiffs any right, title, interest and possession in the suit land?

5. Are the plaintiffs entitled to get a decree for declaration of title as prayed for?

6. To what relief, if any, are the plaintiffs entitled?

5. At the trial the plaintiff-appellants examined as many as 4 PWs. And the contesting defendant No. 2 examined 5 witnesses namely DW 1, DW 2, DW 3, DW 4 and DW 5 and both the parties exhibited a series of documents in support of their respective cases.

6. The learned trial Judge on consideration of the materials on record by his judgment and decree dated 29-8-1980 (decree signed on 4-9-1980) dismissed the suit mainly on 3 (three) counts: (1) that the suit is hopelessly barred by law of limitation. (2) that Abdul Kader Mia took settlement of the suit land in the became of his eldest son Kader Mia, who was a minor as per his service book (Exhibit 9) and the evidence of PW 1. (3) that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiffs could not prove their exclusive possession over the suit land.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 29-8-1980 (decree signed on 4-9-1980) the present plaintiff-appellants preferred the instant First Appeal before this Court.

8. Mr Md Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellants in the course of his argument has taken us through the impugned judgment and decree, deposition of witnesses, exhibits and other materials on record and then submits that the findings of the trial Court below that Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs had no source of income at the time of execution of kabuliyat dated 7-11-21 (Exhibit l) while he was a school going boy, his father Abdul Latif Mia took settlement of the suit land in the benami of his eldest son Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs is perverse being contrary to the material evidence on record. He next submits that the trial Court below having failed to consider the vital aspects of the case that Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs took settlement of the suit land from the then government on 7-11-21 and he executed and registered Kabuliyat in favour of landlord on 7-11-1921 and to prove the case the original Kabulyat was called for from the collector ate on 11-8-1979 vide order No. 27, Kabulyat was exhibited as Exhibit 1 and the settlement was acted upon vide Exhibit Nos. 1A-1G that is the chronological registered barga kabulyat which were given by abraders in favour of Abdul Kader Mia and in those deeds including Exhibit 1 the occupation of Abdul Kader has been consistently stated as service holder. He further submits that the trial Court without assigning any sound reason most illegally ignored all registered documents (exhibits "1 and 1A-1G series") which were produced from the custody of the plaintiffs and those documents are more than 30 years old documents and have strong presumptive value as per provision of section 90 of the Evidence Act.

9. Mr Md Nurul Amin, further submits that the finding of the trial Court on the point of limitation is totally perverse inasmuch as the plaintiff's suit is for simple declaration of title and the proposition of law is well settled that the limitation will start not from the date of publication of record of right, so long any dispute as to title and possession is not raised there is no reason to institute a suit and in the present case it is apparent from the record that the title of the plaintiffs was threatened in the year 1977 and the suit was filed in the year 1978 and therefore, the suit is not barred by limitation. He adds that the wrong record of right by itself does not constitute a ground of limitation, when the title is threatened or evasion only then the cause of action would arise but the trial Court below failed to appreciate this simple point of law.

10. Mr Nurul Amin, further submits that the findings of the trial Court on the point of possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land is not only against the weight of evidence on record also contrary to the well settled principle of law inasmuch. as admittedly in the present case the SA and RS record was prepared in the name of the defendants along with the name of the plaintiffs but the defendants never paid any rent to the Government, on the other hand, the PW 1, Hanif Miah used to pay rent to the Government regularly vide exhibit 2A-2F starting from 1954 to 1975 and those rent receipts are evidence of possession and the same should be used as collateral evidence of title. He further points out that the plaintiff-appellants by adducing sufficient evidence both oral and documentary have been successfully proved their right, title and possession over the suit land and on the other hand, the defendant could not show any scrap of paper in support of their title and possession in the suit land but the trial Court below without considering the vital and ancient documents namely exhibit 1 and 2 series mechanically dismissed the suit which resulted in the failure of justice.

11. Mr Nurul Amin while elaborating his submissions referred to the registered deeds including registered kabuliyat dated 7-114961 and argued that Abdul Kader Mia was in service at the time of execution of kabulyat dated 7-11-1961 and if Abdul Kader Mia found to be minor he could not be allowed to execute and register the kabuliyat on 7-11-21 in favour of the Government but the trial Court below being misdirected itself most illegally on the basis of un-corroborative testimony of the DWs held that at the time of settlement Abdul Kader was minor and Abdul Latif Mia took settlement in the benami of his minor son Abdul Kader Mia. He further submits that admittedly Abdul Kader himself executed and registered kabuliyat on 7-11-21 (Exhibit 1) and several deeds were executed in favour of Abdul Kader (Exhibit 1A to 1G series) wherein his occupation has been consistently stated as service holder, these registered documents were not considered by the trial Judge and he simply relied only on service book of Abdul Kader Mia and held that Abdul Kader Mia was minor at the time of execution of kabuliyat on 7-11-21, this finding of the trial Court below is illegal, which clearly contradicts the old registered documents. Mr Md Nurul Amin, to fortify his submission has relied on the decisions reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76, 44 DLR (AD) 162, 39 DLR (AD) 78, Abdul Hafez vs Lal Meah 1988 BLD 497 = 38 DLR 327, 6 MLR (AD) 49, AIR 1928 (Madras) 14, Sontosh Kumar Deb vs Hiron Chandra Day 1995 BLD 221, Janab Ali Mondal vs Md Anowar Hossain 2004 BLD 243, 2003 BLD (AD) 82, 7 BLT 133, 35 DLR (AD) 216, 43 DLR (AD) 55 and Md Shamsul Huda vs Bangladesh 2000 BLD (AD) 48 = 5 BLC (AD) 108.

12. Mr Md Nurul Amin, finally relying on the decision reported in 1 XP (AD) 73 submits that the original title deed is in the name of, Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiff-appellants and on the basis of that registered kabuliyat PS record was prepared in the name of Abdul Kader Mia but subsequently SA and RS record was prepared in the name of the defendants and in such situation the conflicting between kabala and khatian the earlier registered kabuliyat prevails over the subsequent record of rights in RS khatian and SA khatian.

13. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate on the other hand, appearing for the defendant respondents in the course of argument after placing the impugned judgment and decree submits that the trial Court below after discussion of the evidence on record rightly arrived at a finding that Abdul Latif Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs and defendants settled the suit property in the name of his minor son Abdul Kader Mia because he was govt. servant and it was possessed by Abdul Latif Mia during his life time and later on, his five sons possessed equally and accordingly RS and SA khatian was prepared in the name of five brothers at the instance of Abdul Kader Mia himself and all of them used to pay rent jointly. Mr Abdul Quayum, next submits that the learned Subordinate Judge, Barisal after discussion of the evidence on record rightly dismissed the suit by its judgment and decree dated 29-8-1980 on the findings that the suit is barred by limitation and Abdul Kader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs was a minor as per statement of PW 1 admitted is his evidence that his father was a student of Class X in 1925 in BM School as well as the service book of Abdul Kader Mia (Exhibit 9) shows his date of birth in 1904 and the suit is barred under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiffs do not have exclusive possession over the suit land. Mr Abdul Quayum, further submits that the plaintiffs tried to establish that the kabulyat dated 7-11-1921 is a registered document and the original was called for vide order No. 27 dated 11-8-1979 but there is no order or arrival of such record and there is nothing on record to show that registered kabulyat was produced before the Court below rather the kabulyat marked as "Exhibit 1" is an unregistered kabulyat and it was not proved by any manner as provided in the Evidence Act whatsoever.

14. He further upon placing the written objection filed by the only contesting defendant No.  2 and the evidence of DWs submits that the contesting defendant No. 2 pleaded that their father Abdul Latif Mia was a Government servant so he took settlement in the benami of his minor son from his own fund and possessed the same and after his death his 5 sons used to possess it and accordingly it has been recorded in RS and SA khatian and in that view of the matter the intention, motive and source of money, possession dealing with, preparation of RoR all the ingredients of benami transaction has been proved by the defendants by adducing evidence both oral and documentary.

15. Drawing out attention to exhibit Nos. 5-5(c) Mr Abdul Quayum submits that RS and SA khatians are public document and those document clearly speaks that the suit property has been diluviated and as per Presidents Order No. 135/72 tenants lost their title and the diluviated land vested upon the Government and no Court can pass any decree and in that view of the matter the suit abates and suffers from defect of party in not imp leading the government and for all these reasons the plaintiff-appellants are not entitled to get any relief as prayed for.

16. We have heard the learned Advocates for both the sides at length and perused the evidence and materials on record including the impugned judgment and deposition of witnesses. Now, in order to resolve the disputes, let us examine first how far the learned Subordinate Judge was justified to dismiss the suit on the findings that Abdul Kader, the predecessor of the plaintiffs was a benamder and the plaintiffs could not prove their exclusive possession over the suit land.

17. It is found that during trial the kabuliyat was proved as Exhibit 1, both the parties at the trial in their respective evidence admitted that kabuliyat dated 7-11-1921 (Exhibit 1) is a registered document. The contesting defendant No. 2, in his written statement stated as follows:

প্রকাশ থাকে যে, আবদুল কাদের নাবালক থাকায় তাহার স্থলে অপর লোক দাড় করাইয়া বিগত ৭/১১/২১ তারিখে খাস মহল কতৃপক্ষের বরাবরে একখানা কবুলিয়ত রেজিষ্ট্রী করিয়া রাখা হয়।

18. On perusal of the kabuliyat dated 7-11-1921 (Exhibit 1), it appears that there is a precondition inserted into it that no one can take such settlement in the benami of others. In this connection a portion of the kabuliyat dated 7-11-1921 (Exhibit 1) is reproduced hereunder:

যদি কবুলিয়ত দাতা কাহারও বেনামদার রুপে এই কবুলিয়ত সম্পাদন করিয়াছে ইহা প্রকাশ পায়, তাহা হইলে কালেকটর সাহেব আদালতের সাহায্য লইয়া জমিতে খাস দখল লইতে পারিবেন। সেজন্য তিনি কোন ক্ষতিপূরণ বা খোসারতের দায়ী হইবেন না।

19. From the above, it transpires that Exhibit 1, kabuliyat dated 7-11-21 is admittedly a registered document. The sole contesting defendant No. 2, (DW-2) claimed his title by virtue of said kabuliyat. During the trial no dispute was raised in the trial Court as to its registration.

20. On perusal of Exhibit 1-G series, it transpires that in those old documents the occupation of Abdul Kader Mia has been consistently stated as service. Mr Azizul Haque, the learned Advocate argues that at the relevant time if Abdul Kader Mia was found to be minor he could not be allowed to execute and register the kabuliyat in favour of the then Government. He also argues that the age of Abdul Kader Mia as mentioned in the service book (exhibit-9) was not correct and in that view of the matter the trial Court below was absolutely wrong in finding that Abdul Cadre Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs was minor having no source of income. We find consider-able merit in the above submission of Mr Azizul Haque.

21. Mr Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate in the course of his argument relying on the decision reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76 submits with force that the proposition of law is well settled that once such a document is more than 30 years old was produced from the proper custody, it may be presumed under section 90 of the Evidence Act that the document was duly executed by the executants. The exhibit 1 to exhibit 1-G series are all registered documents which were produced from the rightful custody of the plaintiffs and those documents are more than 30 years old documents and have strong presumptive value under Section 90 of the Evidence Act.

22. PW 1, AKM Hanif, PW 2, Nader Ali, PW 3, Yeasin Mia and PW 4, Abdul Hashim all these PWs. In their respective evidence categorically stated that at present the plaintiffs are possessing the suit land. Mr Abdul Quayum upon referring to the rent receipts Exhibit 2 dated 27-12-1979, Exhibit 2(A) dated 12-4-1978, exhibit 2(B) dated 31-3-1977, Exhibit 2(c) dated 12-3-1976, exhibit 2(d) dated 27-1-1974, exhibit 2(e) and exhibit-2(f) dated 25-9-1978 all those rent receipt shows that the rent has been paid in favour of all the brothers of Abdul Kader as আব্দুল কাদের গং Furthermore, it is found that PW 1, Hanif Miah, used to pay rent to the Government regularly vide Exhibit 2A to 2F starting from 1954-1975.

<u>23. In view of the above evidence both oral and documentary there is nothing on record to suggest that the plaintiffs are not in possession. Rather, the exhibited rent receipts and registered deeds in respect of the suit land demonstrate that the possession of plaintiff-appellants in the suit land.</u>

<u>24. In consideration of this material evidence on record and facts, our view is there-fore, that the reasons given by the trial Court below for passing the impugned judgment on the point that Abdul Kuader Mia, the predecessor of the plaintiffs was a benamder and the plaintiffs could not prove their exclusive possession over the suit land are not sustainable either in law or on facts. Furthermore, in his connection it may be mentioned that a kabuliyat (Exhibit 1) executed and registered in 1921 creates a presumption that the registration authority under the then British Government was satisfied that the executants Abdul Kader Mia was squarely a valid citizen to execute the kabuliyat (Exhibit 1).</u>

25. Now, let us examine how far the trial Court below was justified in holding that the suit was barred by law of limitation as well as barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiffs could not prove their exclusive possession within 12 years before the date of filing the suit.

<u>26. We have already indicated that in view of the evidence both oral and documentary on the point of possession there is nothing on record to suggest that the plaintiffs are not in possession. PW 1, Hanif Miah used to pay rent to the Government regularly vide exhibit 2A to 2F starting from 1954-1975 and those rent receipts are evidence of possession. On examination of the rent receipts vide exhibit 2A to 2F together with the evidence of PWs and DWs. We are unable to agree with the finding of the trial Court that the suit was barred by law of limitation as well as barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiffs could not prove their exclusive possession in the suit land within 12 years from before the date of filing of the suit. This finding of the trial Court below appears to be perverse and the same does not deserve to be sustained.</u>

<u>27. The proposition of law is well settled that the limitation will start not from the date of publication of record of right, so long any dispute as to title and possession is not raised and in the present case it is found from the record that the title of the plaintiffs was threatened in the year 1977 and the suit has been filed in 1978 and thus, the suit is not barred by limitation. Mr Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate in the facts and circumstance of the case rightly pointed out that the wrong record of right by itself does not constitute a ground of limitation, when the title is threatened or evasion only then the cause of action would arise but the trial Court below having failed to appreciate this simple point of law. We are inclined to agree with Mr Nurul Amin.</u>

28. At the end of the day, Mr Abdul Quayum having himself realied the fate of the case, like a drowning man, tried to catch at straw and accordingly, he has raised 2 points for the first time before this Court that RS and SA khatians "Exhibit 5-5C" are public document and those document highlights that the suit property had been diluviated and as per President's Order Nos. 135 /72 tenants lost their title and the diluviated land vested upon the Government and no Court can pass any decree and in that view of the matter the suit abates and suffers from defect of party in not impleading the government and the exhibit-1 (kabuliyat dated 7-11-1921) is an unregistered document.

29. To meet the last branch of argument of Mr Abdul Quayum, we have carefully examined the entire evidence on record and it appears that at the trial both the parties admitted in their respective testimony that Exhibit 1, kabuliyat dated 7-11-1921 executed and registered by Abdul Kader Mia. It also appears that out of 4 defendants only defendant No.  2 (DW 2) Rafiqul Alam alias Rafiqul Islam contested the suit by filing written statement, who in his written statement as well as evidence admitted about the registration of the kabuliyat dated 7-11-1921.

30. Upon a scrutiny of the evidence on record, it appears that the Exhibit 1, kabulyat dated 7-11-1921 is admittedly a registered document of 1921, the defendants also claimed their title by virtue of the same kabuliyat (exhibit-1). No dispute was raised in the trial Court as to its registration nor nay finding on this point in the judgment of the Subordinate Judge, Barisal. The records shows that the trial Court called for the original kabuliyat from the Collectoriate. Therefore, we do not find any substance in the last branch of argument of Mr. Abdul Quayum that the kabuliyat (Exhibit 1) is an unregistered document particularly when the same is nobody's case.

31. As already noticed that at the trial both the parties led evidence to prove their title and possession over the suit land. DW 1, Rafiqul Alam Rafiqul Islam, DW 2, Al-haj Asmat Ali Khan, DW 3, Haji Yakub Ali, DW 4 Md Yunus and DW 5, Md Siddique all of them in their respective testimony categorically testified that the defendants have been jointly possessing the suit land. Therefore, the plea as canvassed by Mr Quayum that the suit property had diluviated and as per President's Order Nos. 135/72 tenants lost their title and the diluviated land vested upon the Government and no Court can pass any decree and in that view of the matter the suit abates and suffers from defect of party in not imp leading the government is not only beyond the pleadings of the parties also contrary to the evidence of DWs. Hence, this contention, also, fails to the ground as the same is nobody's case.

<u>32. Be that as it may, the records of rights of the Government which at best are evidence of possession at the time when such records are prepared and not an evidence of title. This is a well-established principle of law. A registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over the other records of rights, until and unless such kabala/kabuliyat is cancelled on a specific allegation of fraud by any civil court in an appropriate civil suit.</u>

33. Mr Quayum, the learned Advocate to fortify his argument has relied on the decisions reported in 6 MLR (AD) 151, 46 DLR 35, 5 BLC (AD) 77, 44 DLR (AD) 162, 1997 BLD (AD) 45, 17 DLR 392, 6 BLC 54, 2003 BLD (AD) 82 and 19 DLR 17.

34. We have carefully gone through the cited decisions to the best of our ability but it appears to us that the principles as enunciated in those decisions have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case inasmuch as facts of those cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case.

35. On an overall consideration of the facts, circumstances and the materials on record, we are of the opinion that the impugned judgment and decree of the trial Court below suffers from illegalities in many folds, it cannot be sustained in law and is liable to be set-aside.

36. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree dated 29-8-1980 (decree signed on 4-9-1980) passed by the then Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal in Title Suit No. 23 of 1978 is set-aside.

Let a copy of the judgment along with lower Court's record be sent down at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Khurshid Alam Khan—For the Petitioner 
Nusrat Jahan, Assistant Attorney-General—For the Respondent
parties:
Zahir Miah (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Abdus Salam Mamun J : This Rule Nisi under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was issued calling upon the respondent to show cause as to why the inclusion of the property, the petitioner's House No. 31/5, Block-F, Joint Quarter, PS Mohammadpur, District Dhaka in the 'Ka' list of the Abandoned Property published in the Bangladesh Gazette (Extraordinary) dated 23-9-86 (Annexure-E) should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. The facts, as stated in this writ petition, in short, are that the property in question originally belonged to one Sagir (father of the petitioner) by virtue of the lease given to him by the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan by a registered lease deed dated 18-5-1964 for 99 years, Annexure-A. The father of the petitioner, Sagir, took delivery of possession of the said house property from the concerned authority, became its owner and started living therein with his family, paid full price of Taka 1500.00 and other charges and house rent upto 1978 and got clearance certificate and rent receipts, vide Annexure-B series.

3. On 25-9-1969 Sagir died leaving behind his wife Sakina Bibi and two sons including the petitioner as his heirs and was buried near Mohammadpur Jame Mosque, Dhaka. Since the death of his father the petitioner with two other heirs of late Sagir have been in continuous possession of the property in question. His mother died in the year 1989 and thereafter his brother died in the year 1991.

4. For the first time on 3-3-2000 the petitioner came to learn that the house in question was included in the 'Ka' list as abandoned property and the Gazette notification to that effect was made on 23-9-86 without taking over possession or serving any notice upon the petitioner for surrender of possession of the said property. During this time the Settlement Court was totally closed and, as such, it was not possible for the petitioner to go to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the said property from 'Ka' list.

5. That the petitioner is in physical possession of the house since 1964. He was never served with any notice under Article 7(3) of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and Rule 8(3) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over possession) Rules, 1972 and, as such, inclusion of the house in the 'Ka' list is without any lawful authority and illegal.

6. The lone respondent has entered appearance by filing an affidavit-in-opposition denying material allegations of the petitioner stating that the whereabouts of the original lessee Sagir or his alleged legal heirs were not known from 28-2-1972 till 1978. The original owner or legal heirs had never paid any rent as required by law. The petitioner purposefully in collusion with the unscrupulous staff of the respondent's office somehow created the papers mentioned in Annexure-B series to the writ petition which shows that the rent is paid upto 1978 by Sagir. It is further stated that all the legal formalities were observed before inclusion of the said house in the 'Ka' list under the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance, 1985 and publication of the Gazette Notification dated 23-9-86 in this regard. The question of inheritance is a disputed question of fact. There was no trace of lessee Sagir, his alleged wife and the heirs on 28-2-72 and the house was found to be occupied by others.

7. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has taken us through the writ petition and the Annexures thereof namely, the letter of allotment, lease deed in respect of the said house executed between the parties, document showing payment of price, rent receipts, clearance certificate, death certificate, succession certificate, appointment of Guardian Certificate, etc. and submitted that said  Sagir was rehabilitated by the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan as a displaced person and he was allotted the house in question where he lived till his death. He was succeeded by his wife and two sons and they were also in peaceful possession of the same, thereafter, the wife and a son of Sagir died leaving behind the petitioner alone as his successor. The petitioner is a Bangladeshi national and he never left the country at any point of time and was all along available and present in Bangladesh and in occupation of the said house. Government never took over possession of the house nor served any notice on the petitioner or his predecessor-in-interest asking for surrender of possession of the house as required under law. Only on 3-3-2000 the petitioner came to learn that the property in question was included in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned property

8. His physical possession and non-service of notice render the impugned inclusion of the house in the 'Ka' list illegal and without jurisdiction.

9. He has relied upon the case of Begum Lutfunnessa vs Bangladesh, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 86, the case of Syeda Chand Sultana vs Bangladesh, reported in 48 DLR 547 and the case of Ali Bandi vs Government of Bangladesh, reported in 46 DLR 634.

10. Mrs Nusrat Jahan, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent, submits on the other hand, that the petitioner was silent about his possession and inheritance from 1972 to 1978 and that there was no trace of Sagir at the time when President's Order 16 of 1972 came into force, so, question of serving notice on Sagir does not arise. Relying on the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Abdul Jalil and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10 she submits that the Government has no obligation to disclose grounds or basis for enlisting the house in question in the 'Ka' list and it is the duty of the petitioner to prove that the house is not an abandoned property.

11. She has produced before us the office-file maintained by the respondent in respect of this house.

12 Section 5(1) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. LIV of 1985) provided that the Government shall, after the 31st March 1986 and before the 30th day of April, 1986 publish in the Official Gazette-

(a) a List of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order; (b) a List of buildings in respect of which notice for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said Order have been issued ……..'

13. An Extraordinary Gazette was published on 23-9-1986 in accordance with section 5(1)(a) of the Ordinance containing a list of those abandoned buildings whose possession have already been taken by the Government as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 known as 'Ka' list. In this list the house in question has been listed in serial No. 217.

14.
