The rudiment of inclusion of a house in the 'Ka' List is that possession of that house has been taken over by the government sometime after 28th February 1972, the date on which the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 came into force and before 31st day of March, 1986 the date after which no notice for surrendering or taking possession of any building as abandoned property shall be issued or possession be taken except those in respect of which notices have been issued before 31st March 1986 and notices have not been issued due to pendency of suits/ proceedings as has been provided by section 4 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985.

15. The respondent in his affidavit-in-opposition has stated nothing about taking over possession of the house in question at certain point of time after 28-2-1972 and before 31-3-1986 and also as to present possession of the house. In view of definite assertion made by the petitioner in the writ petition that he is in continuous possession and the Government has never taken over possession of the house, the Government is under obligation to disclose as to whether it has taken over possession and at what point of time and whether continuing the same.

16. In the case of Begum Lutfunnessa vs Bangladesh, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 86 it was held that "The minimum the Government must show in a proceeding where the publication of the list is challenged in respect of any property by its owner, is that the property has at some point of time been taken possession of as abandoned property."

17. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Abdul Jalil and others, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10 it was held that "The onus is on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant."

18. In this case, the writ petitioners themselves stated that they had been living in the disputed building with their mother, their father having died in 1954, till June, 1974. In the second week of June, 1974 they were ousted from the said house by some goondas and subsequently, the Deputy Secretary of the Ministry of Works, one Aftabuddin, treated the property as abandoned property although the mother of the respondent writ petitioners showed her title deeds and other documents in respect of the said property .

<u>19. Admittedly, the writ petitioners in this case, were evicted from the house in the second week of June, 1974 and the Ministry of Works has taken over possession of it by treating the house an abandoned property. Facts of this case are, therefore, distinguishable from those of the instant case. The Government need not disclose basis for treating the property as an abandoned property and may not be under obligation to deny the facts alleged but it is definitely under obligation to show in a proceeding that it has taken over possession of the house and maintaining the same for, taking possession is the condition-precedent for a building to be included in the “Ka” List under section 5(1)(a) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985.</u>

<u>20. If possession is not taken by the Government the property cannot be included in the 'Ka' List. That was the view expressed by their Lordships in the case of Saleha Begum vs Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement and another, reported in 49 DLR 243 in the following words: “Unless possession of a house is taken over by the Government that cannot be included in the 'Ka' list as abandoned buildings".</u>

<u>21. To satisfy ourselves as to whether the Government has taken possession of the house in question and maintaining the same, we have perused the relevant file kept in the office of</u>

<u>the respondent and produced by the learned Assistant 'Attorney-General and to our utter surprise, found no notice, papers, records or documents whatsoever in the file relating to taking over and maintaining possession of the house.</u>

<u>22. The Government must maintain, in its file, necessary documents relating to taking over possession of the house and show the same in a proceeding. This principle was laid down in the case of Begum Lutfunnessa, referred to above, in the words: "There is not a shred of paper to show that the Government took over possession of the house at any time."</u>

<u>23. We are, therefore, constrained to hold that the respondent has not taken over possession of the house in question. Enlistment of the house in the 'Ka' list of Abandoned Buildings is thus illegal and without lawful authority.</u>

<u>24. The respondent in his Affidavit-in-opposition has stated that the whereabouts of the original lessee Sagir or his alleged legal heirs were not known from 28-2-1972 till 1978 and that the original owner or legal heirs had never paid any rent as required by law. The petitioner purposefully in collusion with the lower grade staff of the respondent's office somehow created the papers mentioned in Annexure-B series to the Writ Petition which shows the rent is paid upto 1978 by Sagir.</u>

<u>25. Mere statement of the respondent that the whereabouts of the original lessee or his legal heirs were not known from 28-2-1972 to 1978 will not absolve the respondent from his responsibility of showing that a proceeding was taken in respect of the property in question sometime after 28-2-1972 and pursuant to the proceeding possession of the same has been taken over on a certain date treating the property as abandoned property. Presumption attached to section 5(2) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 is rebuttable and Annexures to a writ petition together with the facts and circumstances of the case can rebut the presumption. The statement that somebody else was found in the house will also not absolve the respondent from serving notice upon the occupant of the house.</u>

26. Predicament of the learned Assistant Attorney-General, in spite of her best efforts, is thus due to scanty papers on record and laches of the concerned department of the Government.

27. Hearing about collusion with the lower grade staff is neither palatable nor worthy of hearing. Before making such statement the upper grade officials should have taken drastic, punitive, corrective and/or legal measures and produced those relevant papers before the court along with the affidavit-in-opposition to show that they have not in any manner indulged in or connived with it. It has become a fashion of the day to blame the 'lower grade' for escapism of the 'upper grade'

28. Mr Abdul Quiyyum, Administrative Officer, Mohammadpur and Mirpur Housing Estate, Dhaka who issued clearance certificate No. 1070 NIAA dated 14-12-1978 certifying that the entire price amount of Taka 1500 and other taxes upto 1978 has been paid in respect of House No. 31/5, Block-F, Joint Quarter, Mohammadpur Housing Estate, Dhaka, (Annexure-B), is not a 'lower grade' nor is he beyond the reach of the 'upper grade'. So also the persons who issued rent receipts, etc. We find nothing to disbelieve the Succession Certificate, appointment and/or declaration of Guardian under section 7 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, (Annexure-D).

29. In the case of Dr S Motiur Rab vs Bangladesh, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 128 their Lordships held that "Mere denial by the respondent of a fact in issue raised by the petitioner in a writ petition will not render that fact a disputed fact. But if the assertion made by the petitioner is not supported by materials to the satisfaction of the court, the court may refuse to act on such assertion".

30. We find that the petitioner has supported his assertions with sufficient materials.

31. With regard to the alternative forum the petitioner has stated that the court of settlement was totally closed and, as such, it was not possible for the petitioner to go to the court of settlement. In reply thereto the respondent has, in his affidavit-in-opposition, stated that the said statements are matters of record and hence no comment. Be that as it may. Right to property is a fundamental right guaranteed by Article 42 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

32. In the case of Alhaj Mohammad Rahimuddin Bharasa vs Bangladesh reported in 46 DLR 130 their Lordships held that "Inclusion of the disputed properties by the Gazette notification having been found to be without jurisdiction, the notification is in violation of the petitioner's right to hold property. Even if his fundamental right would not have been affected his writ petition would lie inasmuch as the alternative remedy of invoking the jurisdiction of the court of Settlement became nonexistent in the meantime."

33. In the case of Sarwari Begum vs Bangladesh, reported in 45 DLR 571 it was held that "The petitioner being a 'person aggrieved' by enlistment of her house as abandoned property can maintain a writ petition irrespective of whether she has other equally efficacious remedy or not".

<u>34. The inclusion of the petitioner's house as abandoned property vide notification in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary, dated 23-9-86 in serial No. 217 (Annexure-E to the writ petition) is thus declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.</u>

35. The respondent is therefore, directed to exclude the house under serial 217 from 'Ka' list of the Gazette Notification dated 23-9-86 vide Annexure-'E' to the writ petition within 3 (three) months from this date.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

Md Abdul Matin Khasru with Md Jahorul Haque, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan with Md Ruhul Quddus, Advocates—For the Respondent No. 8.
parties:
Zamir Hossain Master (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J : This Rule was issued on 11-1-2003 calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 6-1-2003 contained in Annexure B passed by the respondent No. 8 in Appeal No. 15 of 2003 affirming the order dated 2-1-2003 contained in Annexure-A passed by the respondent No. 4 in rejecting the nomination paper filed by the petitioner shall not be declared to have been passed illegally and without any lawful manner and is of no legal effect.

<u>2. The case of the petitioner is that he, being very popular, was elected Chairman of No. II Rajai Union Parishad, Bhaluka Upazila for three consecutive terms from the year 1983 to 1997 and he, for the Union Parishad Election 2003, also filed nomination paper for the post of Chairman but at the time of scrutiny, the respondent No. 3 illegally rejected the above nomination paper on the ground that the petitioner was a defaulter as memo dated 2-1-2003 issued by the respondent No. 7 showed that the petitioner was guarantor for the deep tubewell loan taken from Sonali Bank. Bhaluka branch against which an amount of Taka 48,889 was outstanding. The petitioner then filed appeal before the respondent No. 4 raising the grounds that (i) the petitioner himself did not take the above loan and he was a mere guarantor (ii) Kullabo Daksinpara Krishak Somabaya Samity, hereafter referred to as the Samity, took the above loan from Bhaluka Upazila Kendriy Samabaya Samity Limited, hereinafter referred to as BRDB, and not from Sonali Bank and so the above loan is not a bank loan in terms to the disqualification clause of section 7(2) of Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance 1983, hereinafter referred to as Ordinance 1983, and further (iii) Sonali Bank, having extended the period of repayment of the above loan from 31-12-2002 upto 31-1-2003 the question of default did not arise on 1-1-2003. But the respondent No. 3, by the impugned order illegally dismissed the appeal holding that (i) the petitioner is not only the guarantor but is also the President of the Samity. (ii) the Samity took deep tubewell loan from Sonali Bank and (iii) the above loan was to be repaid by 29-11-1999 and the petitioner did not repay the loan even with the extended time and so he is a defaulter.</u>

3. The added respondent No. 8 who, in view of the rejection of the above nomination paper became uncontested chairman, filed affidavit in opposition stating, inter alia, that the petitioner is the President of the above Samity and as will be evident from the contents of Annexure Y, which is a certificate dated 6-1-2003 jointly signed by the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 respectively and that the petitioner and his two full brothers took the above loan from Sonali Bank and the same not being repaid before 1-1-2003, the petitioner is a defaulter and further, even if Annexure C, which is the advertisement published in Daily Jugantor on 5-1-2003, is taken into consideration even then the petitioner, on 1-1-2003, i.e., the date of filing of the nomination paper was a defaulter because it is only on 5-1-2003 i.e. after 4 days, that the time for repayment was extended by Sonali Bank from 31-12-2002 upto 31-2-2003.

4. Even though the petitioner in the writ petition categorically asserted that the Samity took loan from BRDB and not from Sonali Bank, neither the Manager of Sonali Bank. Bhaluka Branch nor the Upazila Palli Unnyon Officer, who were made respondents in this writ petition as respondent Nos. 6 and 7 respectively, filed any affidavit in opposition asserting the Samity took the above loan from Sonali Bank and not from BRDB or that the petitioner was a defaulter.

<u>5. Mr Md Abdul Matin Khasru, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the disqualification clause as provided in section 7(2)(g) of Ordinance 1983, is to be interpreted in such a way that the democratic right of a citizen to contest in the election may not be cut clown and that the petitioner was only a guarantor and he himself did not take the loan and in several decisions both the Appellate and the High Court Division held that in such cases the nomination paper filed by the petitioner cannot be rejected on the ground of "defaulter" and further, the above loan was taken from BRDB and not from "any specified bank" as provided in section 7(2)(g) of the Ordinance 1983 and even if for argument's sake it is conceded that the petitioner himself took the above loan and loan was taken from Sonali Bank and not from BRDB, even then the time limit for repayment having been extended by Sonali Bank upto 31-1-2003 by Annexure-C, which is a follow-up of Annexure-F(2) i.e. Circular dated 31-12-2002 issued by Sonali Bank, the petitioner is not a defaulter. 18. So, at first, let us examine the cases of Indian Jurisdiction as referred above. In AIR 1952 SC 64, which is known as Ponnu Swami's case, nomination paper of the appellant for election to the Madras Legislative Assembly was rejected by the Returning Officer and so he prayed for a writ of certiorari before the High Court to quash the above order of rejection. The High Court dismissed it as unsustainable because of the bar as provided in Article 329(b) of the Indian Constitution and on appeal Indian Supreme Court affirmed the above decision. Fazle Ali J virtually spoke for the Supreme Court and explained the principle underlying in Article 329(b) as follows:

"The question now arises whether the law of elections in this country contemplates that there should be two attacks on matters connected with election proceedings, one, while they are going on by invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution (the ordinary jurisdiction of the courts having been expressly excluded), and another, after they have been completed by means of an election petition. In my opinion, to affirm such a position would be contrary to the scheme of Part XV of the Constitution and the Representation of the People Act, which, as I shall point out later, seems to be that any matter which has the effect of vitiating an election should be brought up only at the appropriate stage in an appropriate manner before a Special Tribunal and should not be brought up at an intermediate stage before any Court. It seems to me that under the election law, the only significance which the rejection of a nomination paper has consists in the fact that it can be used as a ground to call the election in question. Article 329(b) was apparently enacted to describe the manner in which and the stage at which this ground, and other grounds which may be raised under the law to call the election in question, could be urged. I think it follows by necessary implication from the language of this provision that those grounds cannot be urged in any other manner, at any other stage and before any other court. If the grounds on which an election can be called in question could be raised at an earlier stage and errors, if any, are rectified there will be no meaning in enacting a provision like Article 329(b) and in setting up a special tribunal. Any other meaning ascribed to the words used in the article would lead to anomalies, which the Constitution could not have contemplated, one of them being that conflicting views may be expressed by the High Court at the propelling stage and by the Election Tribunal, which is to be an independent body, at the stage when the matter is brought before it".

19. In the above decision, Fazle Ali J at page 71, after elaborately setting out the history in England and in India of election legislation vis-a-vis dispute-resolution, also stated as follows:

"If the language used in Article 329(b) is considered against this historical background, it should not be difficult to see why the framers of the Constitution framed that provision in its present form and chose the language which had been consistently used in certain earlier legislative provisions and which had stood the test of time."

The Indian Supreme Court then concluded as follows:

"(1) Having regard to the important functions which the legislatures have to perform in democratic countries, it has always been recognised to be a matter of first importance that elections should be concluded as early as possible according to time schedule and all controversial matters and all disputes arising out of elections should be postponed till after the elections are over, so that the election proceedings may not be unduly retarded or protracted.

(2) In conformity with this principle, the scheme of the election law in this country as well as in England is that no significance should be attached to anything which does not affect the election," and if any irregularities are committed while it is in progress and they belong to the category of class which under the law by which effect of vitiating the "election" and enable the person affected to call it in question, they should be brought before a special tribunal by means of an election petition and not be made the subject of a dispute before any court while the election is in progress."

In the case of Imtiaz Ahmed vs Gholam Ali, 15 DLR (SC) 283, the Presiding Officer, did not allow Gholam Ali, the respondent, to take oath as in the list supplied to him the father's name of Gholam Ali was shown as Muhammad Ali instead of Ali Muhammad and the. Presiding Officer subsequently gave oath to Imtiaz Ali, the appellant, as the Chairman of the Union Council. Gholam Ali then filed writ petition before the High Court of West Pakistan and after hearing, the High Court issued a writ in favour of Gholam Ali setting aside the election of appellant Imtiaz Ahmed on the ground that the Presiding Officer acted in "bad faith". Before the Pakistan Supreme Court the appellant raised the preliminary plea that the election of a Chairman could only be called in question by means of an election petition. By a majority decision the Pakistan Supreme Court took the following view:

"Ordinarily the Court in exercise of its writ jurisdiction declines to interfere in case of election because it is desirable that decision on a matter of disputed election should as soon as possible become final and conclusive so that the Constitution of the Council or Legislature may be distinctly and speedily known. There is another reason why the Court declines to enter into these questions because in such cases there are bound to be serious disputes on questions of fact which cannot be properly decided in the writ jurisdiction. If it was to do so, it would enter into a field of investigation which is more appropriate for a Tribunal rather that for a Court exercising the prerogative of issuing writ. The court has, therefore, avoided interfering with election disputes, although it cannot be said that the writ jurisdiction of the Court cannot at all be attracted in such cases. For instance, where actions are characterised as being done in bad faith, the exercise of public power may thus be called in question. Here the respondent Gholam Ali attempted to show that the Presiding Officer in refusing to administer oath to him acted malafide. Two question arise, viz, one of fact, namely, whether there was bad faith, and the other of law, namely, whether in the circumstance, the action of the public authority was illegal and void. The Court has, therefore, first to decide what was the duty which he was required to perform in relation to his duty as a Presiding Officer, and secondly, whether the manner in which he acted was a performance of duty in accordance with rules."

In the case of Presiding Officer vs Sadruddin, 19 DLR (SC) 516, which related to Basic Democracy Election, the election was challenged by filing petition under Article 98 of the Constitution and during the pendency of the hearing of the writ petition, Rule 7 of West Pakistan Democracies (Election of Chairman Rule 1960) was promulgated providing the Controlling Authority to have the sole jurisdiction to entertain an election petition and also the power to declare an election to be void and to order a fresh election. The relief sought in the writ petition could not be obtained under the old Rule but however could be obtained under the new Rule. The High Court Division, after hearing, held that the action of the Presiding Officer was amenable to correction under Article 98 of the Constitution and directed the Presiding Officer to declare the result of the election in terms of sub-rule v of Rule 5 of the Election Rules, 1960. Before the Supreme Court it was contended that it was not only incumbent upon the person seeking relief to approach the special forum and follow the special procedure provided and the High Court while acting under Article 98 of the Constitution should not interfere because by doing so it would involve itself into a field of investigation which is more appropriate for a tribunal rather than for the High Court to exercise its prerogative power. The Pakistan Supreme Court held as follows:

………………………………………………..

Article 98 confers a constitutional right to a particular kind of remedy, namely, to obtain a direction upon a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the State or a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do  ……………………………………………

This was clearly a duty cast upon the Presiding Officer by this rule and I, for my pare, am unable to see why this duty could not be enforced by a writ independently instead of filing an election petition and getting relief indirectly after taking upon himself the additional burden of having the election of the returned candidate declared void.

"So, where an officer clearly charged with the duty to declare a person, obtaining the highest number of votes at an election, elected refuses or neglects to do so upon malafide or upon wholly irrelevant considerations or in a wanton, arbitrary or fanciful manner, then I see no reason why the aggrieved party cannot seek this expeditious remedy under Article 98 of the Constitution to compel the officer concerned to declare him elected without having to resort to an election petition.’

Thus the Pakistan Supreme Court was in favour of invoking writ jurisdiction in the election dispute.

So, it appears even in cases of election disputes of Parliamentary election where Article 329(b) of Indian Constitution or Article 171 of Pakistan Constitution are applicable, the courts of this Subcontinent held that in such case the High Court can invoke writ jurisdiction but in election dispute which is beset with disputed question of facts, High Court will not enter into controversy.

In 48 DLR (AD) 128, the election dispute was in respect of Parliamentary election wherein in view of Article 125(b) of our Constitution, the principle laid down in AIR 1952 SC and AIR 1978 SC on the basis of Article 329(b) of Indian Constitution, were applicable. In 53 DLR (AD) 93, the election dispute was in respect of poll and counting of votes involving disputed question of facts i.e. "falls into a territory which vests with disputed facts" but in the present case no such disputed question of facts are involved.

35. Now let us examine the implications of non obstante clauses like Article 125(b) or Article 117 of our Constitution on the jurisdiction of the High Court in invoking jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution.

In respect of Article 125(b), it appears that there is no reported case but in respect of corresponding Article 329(b) of the Indian Constitution and Article 171 of Pakistan Constitution there are several cases some of which we have discussed above.

In respect of Article 117 of our Constitution, which more or less corresponds to Article 23A and 323B of Indian Constitution, the Indian Supreme Court in Sampath Kumar's case, AIR 1987 SC 385, and Chandra Kumar's case, AIR 1997 SC 1125 and the Appellate Division in Mujibur Rahman's case 44 DLR (AD) 111 and Shafiuddin's case 50 DLR (AD) 27, discussed this issue.

36. It appears 42nd Amendment of the Indian Constitution in 1976, Articles 323A and 323B were inserted enabling the Indian Parliament to establish by law the Administrative Tribunal in regard to civil servants and other Tribunals for settlement of disputes of some kinds, providing in clause 2(d) and 3(d) thereof respectively that Parliament may by law "exclude the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136" with respect to the disputes and complaints referred to in clause (I) of Article 323A and the matters falling under the Jurisdiction of the other Tribunal constituted under Article 323B. Accordingly, the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1985 was passed by the Indian Parliament, excluding powers of judicial review of the High Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution in section 25 thereof. This exclusion was upheld in Sampath Kumar's case AIR 1987 SC 385.

37. In Mujibur Rahman's case 44 DLR (AD) 111, the Appellate Division following the principle as laid down in Sampath Kumar's case above held as follows:

"Within its jurisdiction the Tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising out of sub-clause (a), but such tribunals cannot like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India AIR 1987 (SC) 385 (para 16) and 113 Chopra vs Union of India, AIR 1987 (SC) 357 (Para 2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(I), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2)."

38. But 11 years thereafter in Chandra Kumar's case AIR 1997 SC 1125, the Indian Supreme Court held that sub-clause (d) of clause (3) of Article 323B, to the extent they exclude the jurisdiction of the High Courts and the Supreme Court under Articles 226/227 and 32 of the Constitution, are unconstitutional and the subordinate legislations are also unconstitutional to that extent. Articles 226/227 and 32 are parts of the inviolable basic structure of the Constitution and decisions of Tribunals created under Article 323A and 323B will be prospectively subject to the Division Bench of the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the particular Tribunal falls.

39. It appears in Shafiuddin's Case, 50 DLR (AD) 27, the above decision of Chandrakumer's case reported in AIR 1997 SC 1125 was referred and the Appellate Division did no longer follow its view taken in Mujibur Rahman's case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111.

Accordingly, we are of the view that because of absence of similar provision like 125(b) in the case of dispute arising out of Union Parishad election, the jurisdiction of the High Court in hearing election disputes in respect of Union Parishad Election cannot be curtailed specially in cases where such election disputes are not beset with disputed questions of facts and the disputes may be decided from admitted facts as shown in the Annexures.

40. Further in the case of Ram and Shaym vs State of Haryana AIR 1985 SC 1147 the Indian Supreme Court held a follows:

Ordinarily, it is true that the court has imposed a restraint on its own wisdom on the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 where the party invoking the jurisdiction has an effective, alternative remedy. More often it has been expressly stated that the rule which requires on the exhaustion of alternative remedies is a rule of convenience and discretion rather than the rule of law. At any rate it does not oust the jurisdiction of the Court.

41. Moreover, it is for the apprehension that there will be opening of floodgate of writ petitions, as was argued in Dr Mohiuddin Faruq's case, that the Appellate Division answered as follows :

As to the apprehension of floodgate, the people as a whole is no doubt a flood and the Constitution is the sluice-gate through which the people controls its own entry. Our Courts will be prudent enough to recognise the people when the people appears through an application as also those who masquerade under the name of the people. Taking up the people's causes at the expense of his own is a rare phenomenon, not a commonplace occurrence.

42. It appears in Anwar Hossain's Case 41 DLR (AD) 165 ATM Afzal J : gave dissenting view on all the issues except issue No. 2 which is in respect of taking away, by amendment, the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution and deciding this issue his Lordship held as follows :

"Therefore in exercise of the power under Article 142 the Constitution cannot be destroyed or abrogated. The destruction of the Constitution will be the result if any of its "structural pillars", that is, the three organs of the Government", Executive, Legislature and Judiciary, is destroyed. The result will also be the same if any of these organs is emasculated and castrated in such a manner as would make the Constitution unworkable. For example, if the Supreme Court or a Superior Court by any name is retained but the power of judicial review as under Article 102 is taken away the result will be that the form will be there but the 'soul' of the judiciary will be gone and the Constitution will be rendered unworkable inasmuch as the balance which is struck in 'the scheme of the Constitution cannot be maintained. There can be no objection to the exercise of amending power to fulfil the needs of time and of the generation. But the power cannot be so construed as to turn the Constitution, which is the scripture of hope of a living society and for its unfolding future, into a scripture of doom".

43. So, the Election Commission's power to review under Rule 70 being no longer in existence, we are of the view that the High Court Division, in Writ jurisdiction, even after detecting from the admitted papers that the Returning Officer illegally rejected the nomination paper and his order is nullity as in the present case, instead of correction of such illegal order he should not ask the petitioner to seek relief before the Tribunal where disposal, after exhausting appeals and revision, takes long time and in many cases covers the period of five years. Further, the declaration of the respondent No. 6 as uncontested Chairman as in the present case by rejecting the nomination paper filed by the petitioner and denying the people of the Union to exercise their right to cast votes is not a step forward for upholding democracy by free and fair election.

44. Further, in Mohindar Singh's Case the effect and importance of free and fair election to uphold democracy were elaborately discussed and the pervasive philosophy of democratic elections which Sir Winston Churchill expressed in matchless words, was quoted. The above quotation is as follows:

"At the bottom of all tributes paid to democracy is the little man, walking into a little booth, with a little pencil, making a little cross on a little bit of paper—no amount of rhetoric or voluminous discussion can possibly diminish the overwhelming importance of the point."

45. In Mohinder Singh's case the Indian Supreme Court also observed as follows:

"if we may add, the little, large Indian shall not be hijacked from the course of free and fair elections by mob muscle methods, or subtle perversion of discretion by men 'dressed in little, brief authority. For, be you ever so high, the law is above you"

The old articles of the supreme lex meet new challenges of life; the old legal pillars suffer new stresses. So, we have to adapt the law and develop its latent capabilities of vovel situations, as here, are encountered. That is why in the reasoning we have adopted and the perspective we have projected, not literal nor lexical but liberal and visional is our interpretation of the Articles of the Constitution and the provisions of the Act. Lord Denning's words are instructive:

"Law does not stand still. It moves continually. Once this is recognised, then the task of the Judge is put on a higher plane. He must consciously seek to mould the law so as to serve the needs of the time; he must not be a mere mechanic, a mere working mason, laying brick on brick, without thought to the overall design. He must be an architect, thinking of the structure as a whole, building for society a system of law which is strong, durable and just. It is on his work that civilised society itself depends."

Democracy is government by the people. It is continual participative operation, not a cataclysmic, periodic exercise. The little man, in this multitude, marking his vote at the poll does a social audit of his Parliament plus political choice of his proxy. Although the full flower of participate Government rarely blossoms, the minimum credential of popular government is appeal to the people after every term for a renewal of confidence. So, we have adult franchise and general elections as constitutional compulsions. The right of election is the very essence of the Constitution (Junius). It needs little argument to hold that the heart of the Parliamentary system is free and fair election periodically held, based on adult franchise, although social and economic democracy may demand much more.

Article 324, in our view, operates in areas left unoccupied by legislation and the words superintendence, direction and control, as well as conduct, of all elections are the broadest terms"

Myriad may be too mystic to be precisely presaged, may call for prompt action to reach the goal of free and fair election. It has been argued that this will create a constitutional despot beyond the pale of accountability; a frankenstein monster who may manipulate the system into elected despotism instances of such phenomena are the tears of history. To that the retort may be that the judicial branch, at the appropriate stage, with the potency of its benignant power and within the leading strings of legal guidelines, can call the bluff, quash the action and bring order into the process. Whether we make a triumph or travesty of democracy depends on the mean as much as on the Great National Parchment, secondly, when a high functionary like the Commissioner is vested with wide powers the law expects him to act fairly and legally. Article 324 is geared to the accomplishment of free and fair elections expeditiously. Moreover, (AIR 1957 SC 896) and Harishankar (1955)1 SCR 380: (AIR 1954 SC 465) discretion vested in a high functionary may be reasonably trusted to be used properly, not perversely. If it is misused, certainly the Court has power to strike down the act. This is well established and does not need further case-law confirmation. Moreover, it is useful to remember the warning of Chandrachud, J: (at page 2465 of AIR 1975 (SC) :

But the electorate lives in the hope that a sacred power will not so flagrantly be abused and the moving finger of history warns of the consequences and inevitable flow when absolute power has corrupted absolutely. The fear of perversion is no test of power."

46. In 41 DLR (AD) 68 it was argued before the Appellate Division that the declaration of the Presiding Officer as to the person who got the highest vote was final and the power of the Returning Officer is only to consolidate the results and so the Election Commission is obliged to publish the result as shown by the Presiding Officer and it has no other option, but the Appellate Division did not accept the above argument holding as follows:

If this argument is allowed it will mean whatever happened it will be sufficient without appearing before the voters if Presiding Officer and Returning Officer are wooed and kept in good humour. This is no election and that is no democracy. Election is needed to sustain democracy and a perverse election or voterless election destroys democracy.

47. In AIR 1978 SC 851, the Indian Supreme Court also took the view that discretion vested in a high functionary may be reasonably trusted to be used properly, not perversely, and if it is misused certainly the court has power to strike down the act and observation given by Chandrachud J: to the effect that history warns that absolute power has corrupted absolutely was also considered.

48. In 45 DLR 255 it has also been held as follows:

"The Election Commission exercised its supervisory power over the conduct of its officers before the election actually started to correct an apparent exercise of power by a Returning Officer which the law never permits and thus, wholly without jurisdiction on his own admission. The Election Commissioner found the behaviour of the Returning Officer as unbecoming of an honest officer when malafide act vitiates everything. Shall the authority wait to correct this error committed without jurisdiction which is a nullity and void ab initio, till the election is over with a wrong candidate from the beginning, in spite of its being detected immediately and taken for decision before the Election Commission. The answer surely would be in the negative as otherwise, in the whole election people would be backing a horse which will ultimately be found to be a wrong horse making the whole election an exercise in futility at public expense and inconvenience.

49. We have already found that because of non obstante clause as provided in Article 329(b) of the Indian Constitution and that the concerned election dispute related to Parliamentary Election, the Indian Supreme Court took the view that the High Court invoking jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Indian Jurisdiction cannot interfere in such dispute except in case of coram non judice or malice in law whereas in our Constitution there is no such non obstante clause in respect of Union Parishad election. However, in Shah Alam's case reported in 41 DLR (AD) 68 the Appellate Division approved the above view of the Indian jurisdiction mainly on consideration that such election disputes are beset with facts and High Court will not enter into controversy and in Rafiqul Islam's case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 137 the Appellate Division allowed the appeal mainly on the ground that section 26 of the Ordinance 1983 was at least an implied bar in filing suit and further, the aggrieved candidate did not deny the fact that he failed to repay the loan taken by the bank.

50. Even if it is conceded that the High Court Division did not invoke in case of election dispute of Union Parishad except in coram non judice or malice in law let us examine whether the impugned order is bad for malice in law.

<u>51. In the present case the petitioner contended that the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 acted with malafide motive rejecting the nomination paper filed by the petitioner.</u>

<u>Regarding what is malafide in the case of Ram Chandra vs Government of West Pakistan AIR 1964 Cal 265, 272 Durgadas Basu J relying on some decisions of the Supreme Court held as follows :</u>

<u>"Malafide or bad faith: it is often said that malafide or bad faith vitiates everything and a malafide act is a nullity.</u>

<u>What is malafide? Relying on some observations of the Supreme Court in some decisions. Durgadas Basu J: held,</u>

<u>It is enough if the aggrieved party establishes: (I) that the authority making the impugned order did not apply its mind at all to the matter in question: or (II) that the impugned order was made for a purpose or upon a ground other than what is mentioned in the order."</u>

52. In the English writ jurisdiction this bad faith/malafide is used widely or rather in loose sense and in the case of Waived vs Minister of Housing and Local Government 17 DLR 755, 784, it has been held that in view of the above confusion is created. However, subsequently, the courts took the view that as an independent ground of attack, malafide (malice in fact) should be distinguished from malafide (malice in law). In the case of Shear vs Shield 1914 (AC) Viscount Haldane LC has brought out the distinction as follows:

"Between malice in fact and malice in law there is a broad distinction which is not peculiar to any particular system of jurisprudence. A person who inflicts an injury upon another person in contravention of the law is not allowed to say that he did so with an innocent mind; he is taken to know the law, and he must act within the law. He may, therefore be guilty of malice in law, although so far as the state of his mind is concerned, he acts ignorantly, and in that sense innocently. Malice of fact is quite a different thing: it means an actual malicious intention on the part of the person who has done the wrongs independent of contract a very material ingredient in the question whether a valid cause of action can be stated."

The above view was affirmed in Dr Nurul Islam's case 33 DLR (AD) 201.

সময় শেষ হবার আগে সোনালী ব্যাংকের সংশ্লিষ্ট শাখার সাথে যোগাযোগ করুন এবং বর্ধিত সময়ের সুযোগ গ্রহণ করুন। এরপরও খেলাপ��� ঋণ পরিশোধ না করা হলে সংশ্লিষ্টদের বিরুদ্ধে ব্যাংক মামলা দায়ের করবে। সমাজের নিকট আপনি হেয় হবেন কেন কাজেই আর দেরি নয়। এখনই সোনালী ব্যাংক এ আসুন।

সোনালী ব্যাংক

দরিদ্র বিমোচনে সরকারের অংশীদার ।

65. Annexure-F(2) of the supplementary affidavit dated 5-2-2003 filed by the petitioner is Memo dated 31-12-2002 issued by the Sonali Bank, Head Office by which the period for repayment of such loan was extended upto 31-1-2003 from the previous date of 31-12-2003 as fixed by Annexure-T(1) in order to enable such Samity to repay their outstanding dues by 31-1-2003 and, as it appears, on the basis of above circular, the above Annexure-C was published by the Sonali Bank. Accordingly, the time for repayment of the loan in question having been extended upto 31-1-2003, the petitioner was not a defaulter on 2-1-2003.

66. The Thana Nirbahi Officer who is the Appellate authority is supposed to know the publication of the abo re Annexure-C and also the circular of the Sonali Bank Head Office issued by Memo dated 31-12-2002, Annexure-F (2). Accordingly, it appears the impugned order is bad because of malice in law.

67. Now let us see what approach was taken by High Court Division and also the Appellate Division regarding acceptance or rejection of nomination papers in Union Parishad Elections on interpreting section 7(2)(g) of the Ordinance of 1983.

68. In the case of Abu Taher Miah vs Faraz Uddin Sarker, 41 DLR 543, the petitioner filed writ petition stating that the respondent No. 1 being a defaulter loanee was not qualified to file nomination paper for the post of Chairman of the Union Parishad and that the Returning Officer, in spite of his objection, accepted the nomination paper and the appeal filed by the petitioner before the Appellate authority was also not accepted and then election was held. Gazette Notification was published declaring the respondent No. 1 as chairman. The High Court Division invoked Jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution but discharged the Rule on merit holding that in order to attach mischief of Clause (g) of section 7(2) of Ordinance 1983 it must be shown that loan was to be repaid within the time allowed by the bank and there was nothing on record to show that the respondent No. 1 failed to repay the loan within the time allowed.

69. In the present case from the contents of Annexure-C and Annexure-F(2) it appears that loan, as referred in Annexure-A and B was to be repaid by 31-1-2003 and not before 1-1-2003.

70. Further, it appears in the following cases in respect of election disputes of Union Parishad Election, the High Court Division invoked writ jurisdiction.

71. In the case of Warish Miah vs Secretary, Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development, 41 DLR 51 the petitioner filed writ petition stating that respondent No. 5 contested the Union Parishad election suppressing that he was a defaulter and so the petitioner, raising the above ground, filed an application before the Chief Election Commissioner praying for staying publication of the result of the election of the respondent No. 5 but with no result. The respondent No. 5 in his affidavit-in-opposition stated that he merely stood as a guarantor for the loan. The High Court Division invoked jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution but discharged the Rule on merit holding that section 7(2)(g) of the Ordinance 1983 merely indicates that a person/candidate who having taken loan from any specified bank has defaulted in repayment of the same within the time so allowed by the bank is not disqualified and to insert the word "guarantor" in sub-section (g) of section 7(2) was nothing but making amendment of the said clause (g) of sub-section (2) of section 7 which is not the function of the Court and that the right of the respondent Nos. 5 to stand as a candidate or his title to office if elected cannot be taken away by allowing flexible or loose interpretation to such statutes and a statute that makes an invasion upon the right of a citizen and threatening to take away such right must be construed very strictly and the High Court Division held that respondent No. 5 who stood as guarantor, is not disqualified within the meaning of sub-section 2(g) of section 7 of the Ordinance.

72. In the case of Afzal Hossain vs Chief Election Commissioner 45 DLR 255, the petitioner filed writ petition stating that the respondent No. 8 in his nomination paper suppressed the fact that he defaulted in repaying the loan taken from Krishi Bank and apart from the objection filed by the petitioner before the Returning Officer, the Manager, Krishi Bank, who was made respondent No. 7, also issued certificate to the effect that the respondent No. 8 did no repay the loan within the specific time and the Returning Officer rejected the nomination paper filed by the respondent No. 8 and the Thana Nirbahi Officer upheld the said order of cancellation but on review the Election Commission by the impugned order dated 22-10-92 allowed the respondent No. 8 to contest the election for the post of chairman. The High Court Division invoked jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution but discharged the Rule on merit holding the bank having accepted the loan money out of time on 1-9-92 it would be deemed that the time to repay it has been extended from 21-7-92 to 1-9-92 and that a liberal interpretation of this disqualification clause needs to be given for the simple reason that on this disqualification clause created by law, the democratic right of the people should not be cut down and thus, a liberal construction in favour of the candidate be given to serve the purpose of the law concerning election.

73. In the aforesaid decision it was also held as follows:

The Election Commission in such an unforeseen compulsory circumstance which circumstance may not be defined finally but left to the circumstances of each case has enough supervisory power to act to correct an apparent wrongful exercise of power at the threshold and to keep the records clean mostly in exceptional cases, can act, on admitted facts, in spite of the provision of an Election Tribunal for deciding election disputes.

74. In the case of Abdul Jalil vs Deputy Commissioner, Comilla 45 DLR 258 the petitioner filed writ petition stating, inter alia, that the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 illegally rejected his nomination paper for the post of Chairman, Comilla Pourasava because in respect of the certificate issued in Certificate Case No. 278/87 the petitioner filed Civil Suit No. 63 of 1988 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Comilla for a declaration that the said certificate case was illegal and the prayer of the petitioner for stay of the said certificate having been rejected, the petitioner obtained an order dated 27-4-88 from High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 83 of 1988 by which all further proceedings of the said certificate was stayed till disposal of the Rule and so he owed no money to Krishi Bank and the matter being sub-judice under Article 102 of the Constitution and made the Rule absolute and directed the Returning Officer to accept the nomination paper observing that the default clause shall not be used as a clog in refusing a democratic right of seeking election by citizens, such clause should always liberally be construed for giving such right and though a finality clause is attached to the orders of the election authority in this matter of rejection, on appeal, it is final only on fact and not final on law which this court shall examine if committed at the threshold, in spite of an Election Tribunal in public interest. Of course, it will be subject to the suit and the certificate case and if he is finally decided and found on that date of filing nomination paper to be a defaulter, the law will take its course. The court however, ordered that the case before the High Court and the Civil Court may be heard, on prayer, expeditiously.

75. The Appellate Division also in the case of AFM Rashid reported in 1991 BLD (AD) 189 took similar view. In that case, the nomination paper filed by the respondent No. 6 was rejected by the Returning Officer which was also upheld in appeal and though the appellant was declared chairman uncontested but the Chief Election Commissioner by order dated 12-7-90 cancelled the uncontested election and directed the holding of by-election accepting the nomination paper filed by the respondent No. 6 and the petitioner challenging the above order dated 12-7-90 which was rejected summarily. On appeal, the Appellate Division also held as follows:

"The facts of this case are distinguishable from those of Rafiqul Alam's case. Where an authority has been designated to decide a question of qualification/disqualification of a candidate and another authority has been designated for hearing appeal and the order passed in appeal has been termed as final, and no provision has been made for any other forum to further adjudicate upon that order, none of the election functionaries, not even the Election Commission, can question the order. During the period from 24th November, 1987, till March 1989, when Rule 70 was in force, the Election Commission could arguably invoke that rule in case of an interference with an order passed under Rule 16(2), but not after 16th March, 1989, when Rule 70 was deleted. An order passed under Rule 16(2) can only be interfered with judicially either by the Election Tribunal or by the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. An aggrieved candidate may bid his time and after the publication of the result of the election in the Official Gazette can file an election petition. If he has got a clear case, that can be decided at the macro level on the interpretation of relevant law on admitted facts, not cluttered by micro questions of disputed nature, then for an efficacious and expeditious remedy he may invoke the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution.

In this case, the appellant, instead of waiting for the publication of the result of the election in the official Gazette, filed an application under Article 102 of the Constitution before the High Court Division against the order of the Election Commission. His application is no doubt maintainable. We uphold the appellant's first contention that the Election Commission acted without jurisdiction in interfering with the appellate Order made under Rule 16(2) of the Rules.

We are satisfied that no useful purpose will be served by deferring the issue of respondent No. 6's qualification to contest the election to the Election Tribunal. No further evidence on facts is necessary. On the admitted facts, the appellant has failed to show that respondent No. 6 was in any way disqualified to contest the election for the office of the Chairman of the Union Parishad concerned."

<u>76. We are also of the view that if these malafide activities are allowed to be continued on refusing exercise of jurisdiction by the High Court Division under Article 102, certainly the entire democratic process through election will remain hostage in the hands of unscrupulous bureaucrats like Thana Nirbahi Officer and Returning Officer.</u>

In the result the Rule is made absolute and the election results is set aside. The election of the added respondent No. 8 as uncontested chairman is cancelled and the Returning Officer is directed to hold fresh election upon accepting the nomination paper filed by the petitioner. There will be no order as to cost.

End.

parties:
Aysha Begum and ors ----- Defendant-Appellants
VS.
Mozibur Rahman ----- Plaintiff-Respondent
full_judgment:
M. Moazzam Husain J: This appeal, a t the instance of the defendant Nos.1-4, arises out of a judgment and order dated 23-4-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Chittagong, in Other Class Suit No. 254 of 2008 appointing receiver in respect of properties described in Kha schedule of the plaint. Facts relevant for disposal of this appeal, in short, are that the sole plaintiff filed the aforesaid other class suit against heirs of Korban Ali, his father, and heirs of late Abdul Gani, his first cousin for partition of land and structures described in schedule Ka, Kha and Ga of the plaint claiming saham of the same as ejmali property in joint possession of the co sharers. His mother was later added as defendant No.13. The appellants ie, heir of Abdul Gani and the added defendant No. 13 made their appearance in the suit but did not file written statement. At this stage the plaintiff filed an application under Order XL rule of the Code of Civil Procedure, shortly, "the Code" praying for appointment of receiver in respect of all the landed and other properties described in schedule Ka, Kha and Ga appended to the plaint. The appellants filed written objection against the application. Added defendant No.13 also filed written objection separately. Learned Joint District Judge, heard the parties on the application and upon hearing, however, was pleased to allow the application in part and appointed receiver only in respect of Kha schedule property while refused the application in respect of other properties as he was not satisfied about the ejmali character of the same.

2. The appointment of receiver, though only in respect of Kha schedule property, led the defendant Nos. 1-4 to file this miscellaneous appeal as persons directly affected by the order. For our purpose, therefore, it would suffice if we confine ourselves in the case of the parties relating to the properties described in Kha schedule only. As it appears from the plaint and the application under Order XL, rule 1 of the Code annexed as annexure A & B respectively, to an application for stay earlier made by the appellants that the land in schedule Kha comprises a hotel called- Gani Hotel Residential and other premises, nature left unclear. Plaintiff's case as transpires from the plaint and application as aforesaid, particularly in respect of Kha schedule property seems to be incomprehensive and unclear. What he said is that since the death of his father in 1967 the kha schedule properties used to be managed by Abdul Gani, predecessor of defendant Nos.1-4, ie, the appellants. Subsequently defendant No.9 (plaintiff's full brother) in connivance with defendant No.10, another full brother, and other defendants forcibly leased out the premises in September, 2007 at a monthly rental of Tk 24,000 taking an advance of Tk. 15 lakh from the lessee. From the advance and monthly rent of the premises for ten months the plaintiff was proportionately entitled to Tk. 1, 75,000 but defendant No. 9 has misappropriated the same. The other premises in the schedule ie, Gani Residential Hotel is run by defendant No.10 through an agent. Defendant No.1 has deprived the plaintiff of an amount Tk. 40,000 payable to him as his share of rental realized over ten months from the lessee of that hotel.

3. The written objections filed by the appellants as defendant Nos.1-4 and added defendant No. 13 are found as annexure-C and D to the application for stay. The case of the defendant Nos.1-4 ie, the appellants especially with regard to Kha schedule land as it appears from their written objection are a hit incomprehensive. The same read with the written objection filed by the added defendant No.13 suggests that the property was jointly purchased by Korban Ali, predecessor of the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 9-13. and Korban Ali's full brother Hachi Mia's sons ie, Abdul Gani (predecessor of defendant Nos.1-4) and others. The land was amicable partitioned by family arrangement and accordingly was recorded in the name of Gani Mia in the BS record. After the death of Abdul Gani the appellants have been in exclusive possession and enjoyment of the property. The defendant Nos.1-4 are paying rent, gas, WASA bills in respect of the Kha Schedule property and they are in exclusive possession thereof to the knowledge of all including the plaintiff. There is no joint possession or community of interest of the plaintiff and the defendant Nos.1-4 in the property.

4. The learned Joint District Judge, as is mentioned earlier, doubted ejmali character of the Ka and Ga schedule land and refused to appoint receiver with regard to those properties. He, however, was prima facie satisfied about the ejmali character of Kha schedule property and appointed receiver with regard to the same by his impugned order dated 24-3-2009 mainly on three findings firstly, plaintiff's claim is that the Kha schedule property is one acquired by joint purchase by the predecessors of the parties and the same is an ejmali property of the parties and the defendants did not directly deny this claim of the plaintiff and secondly, it is admitted that Kha schedule land is ejmali and leased out to a third party thirdly, it is not denied that any rental share of that property is not given to the plaintiff and upon the findings he concluded: 'it may be presumed that the plaintiff is being deprived of his share from the earning of that property.'

5. Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant submits at the outset that the principles of appointment of receiver, particularly in a suit for partition, is by now well-settled. It is only in extreme cases where there is apprehension that the property undergoes imminent danger of being wasted or damaged that receiver may be appointed. The present suit being one of partition is against co-sharers and admittedly the suit land is under possession of members of the family the plaintiff comes from. The dispute raised is about deception and deprivation of the rental share and profit earned from the properties. Mere dispute about share of land or rent does not offer any ground for appointment of receiver. The plaintiff has failed to make out a case that property, allegedly ejmali, was going to be wasted or damaged at the hands of his siblings and members of his extended family against whom he has sought relief. Plaintiff claims, as he did, 1/5th share from all the suit properties. His claim is concurrently denied by his mother as defendant No.13 and the appellants as defendant Nos.1-4 in the separate sets of written objections filed by them. This may, he insisted, well be settled on trial. Mr. Ali further submits that appointment of receiver as of routine has consistently been disapproved by our superior courts more so where members of a joint family are in possession of the same. In support of his contentions he cited the decisions reported in 36 DLR (AD) 97, 48 DLR (AD) 14 and 56 DLR 303.

6. Mr. Nawroz MR Chowdhury, learned Advocate, appearing on the other side tried to defend the impugned judgment by reference to the case of Mohammad Moslem Khan vs Mohammad Mohsin Khan reported in 7 BLT (AD) 101 and Nurul Hossain vs Hasan Banu reported in 35 DLR 28. He submits that in Moslem Khan's case our Appellate Division approved appointment of receiver in a suit for partition though the petrol pump in question was long in possession of the defendants. He further submits that Nurul Hossain's case is also a partition suit wherein receiver was appointed to stop realization of rent from the ejmali property and appropriation by the defendants. And a Division Bench of the High Court Division upheld the order of appointment of receiver.

7. The instant case is one of partition filed by an expatriate living in America against his full brothers, sisters, heirs of a first cousin and others. On perusal of the records it appears that suit for partition by one expatriate member of a family against all others has arisen out of a sense of deception and deprivation allegedly meted out to him by his co-owners in terms of his 1/5th share in rental and other profits earned from the suit properties. The application is ex facie ill-advised and does not lie in the fitness of things in that dislodging the rest of the family from its rightful possession of the family property on the ground of deprivation of minor rental share of a single member, even if true, cannot be a ground of appointment of receiver. A plain reading of the impugned order ipso facto suggests that the learned judge passed the same totally unconcerned about the utterly senseless dislocation that may follow in the management of family property in the event of introducing a stranger into management that too before determination of the single member's share, if any, in his family property. Furthermore the plaintiff as an expatriate living in America does not appear to be in immediate need of the money for maintaining his family.

<u>8. Law is long settled with regard to appointment of receiver in a suit for partition. Appointment of receiver in joint property of a family or co-sharers as of routine has never met the approval of the superior courts. Long line of decisions are there showing complete dis-approval to appointment of receiver in such cases merely because of dispute over the property, tainted relationship among the co-sharers or non-payment of share of rent or profit etc. accruing there from. A co-sharer in possession in ejmali property has a preferential right to remain in possession until his right is judicially determined. Receiver may be appointed in such cases only on consent or in extreme cases where refusal to do so has the single consequence of wastage, damage or destruction of the property which need be preserved for the interest of the parties.</u>

9. The finding that 'the claim of ejmali character of Kha schedule property is admitted' arrived at by the learned judge besides being no ground for appointing receiver in this case is contrary to the case of the contesting defend-ants. Defendant No. 13 has directly denied the plaintiff's claim that he is a co-sharer of the property under any of the schedules. And the absence of direct denial in the written objection by defendant Nos.1-4 is fairly attributable to poor draftsmanship not to 'admission' as is taken by the learned judge. Admission in law has a technical meaning not to be inferred from absence of any positive statement or infirmity in the narratives. Far less in case of written statements or objections as those are protected, as is done, by a protective clause containing the words, 'unless specifically admitted hereinafter every averment made by the plaintiff shall be deemed to have been denied.'

10. In the case of Faiz Ahmed vs Bakhtear Ahmed, 36 DLR (AD) 97, referred to by Mr. Mohammad Ali, our Appellate Division has taken very strict view in matters of appointment of receiver in a partition suit. Appella to Division quoted with approval the case of Gobinda Narayan Rao Desai vs Vallablirao Narayatao Desai, AIR 1920 Born 321 wherein it is held: "In a partition suit between members of a joint family the court will not appoint receiver except by consent. Especially when the family property consists of land, special circumstances must be proved before the court will make such appointment. The plaintiff must satisfy the court that the property in possession of the defendants is in danger of being wasted."

11. In the above case the Appellate Division sounded a note of caution about putting a third party in a joint family property and observed: "Law requires exercise of caution about putting a third party as receiver of property of a joint family which are being possessed and enjoyed by members of the family. if there is no fear that the property is going to be destroyed or dissipated, court should be reluctant to extend the relief."

12. Appellate Division in line with the principle laid down in Ghtilam Zainab vs Taltira Sultana, PLD 1977 Lah 492, further held: "The provision for appointment of receiver is to be considered as one of the harshest remedies for the enforcement of rights to property. It should, therefore, be exercised only in extreme cases. Where there is not merely apprehension of possible danger but the peril or danger to the property in question appears to be great and imminent, such appointment may be made."

13. In the case of Kamirziddin vs Moksed Ali, 49 DLR (AD) 14, cited by Mr. Mohammad Ali receiver was appointed by the High Court Division basically on the ground that earlier the suit land was under a receiver for a long time. On appeal the Appellate Division held: "The applicant for appointment of receiver of any property must show a prima facie case and good chance of his success and so no order should be passed to deprive a de facto possessor of the property Simply because the property in suit was under the management of a receiver for a long period of time it cannot be regarded as just and convenient ground for appointment of receiver..."

14. The case of Ali Akbar vs Sakina Begum, 56 DLR 303, relied upon by Mr Ali does not come in aid of his contention as there the members of the family were in separate possession of the suit property under a registered deed of partition and the High Court Division expressed its disapproval to appointment of receiver in such cases even if the deed was challenged as fraudulent etc. which is distinguishable with the facts of the instant case.

15. The case referred to by Mr. Nawroz MR Chowdhury reported in 35 DLR 28 is distinguishable from the instant case. In this case the plaintiffs were admitted co-shares of the property, that too female, admittedly having a considerable share in the suit property. But they were forcibly kept out of enjoyment of their property by the defendants who realized rent from the tenanted premises and continuously misappropriated the same. A Division Bench of this court took notice of the peculiar circumstances of the case and affirmed the order of appointment of receiver passed by the trial court. In the instant case the plaintiff is not admitted as co-sharer nor is forcibly kept out of enjoyment of his property as a weaker party nor is there a question of misappropriation of rental share by rightful owners of the property having had lion share, if not all. The case of M. Moslem Khan vs M. Mohsin Khan reported in 7 BLT (AD) 101 as referred to by Mr. Nawroz MR Chowdhury is all about dismissal of a leave petition against appointment of receiver by the High Court Division in respect of a petrol pump that originally belonged to one Imam Sharif, their predecessor-in-interest. High Court Division refused prayer for appointment of receiver in respect of all the properties of Imam Sharif described in schedules A to D and granted receiver only in respect of a petrol pump described in schedule C. Here in this case the parties were admitted heirs of late Imam Sharif who being a business-man left huge property behind. Still the High Court Division refused to appoint receiver in respect of all the property except the petrol pump described in schedule C definitely under fit circumstances not stated in the decision. The petrol pump as it appears was the property of Chittagong Port authority and the machine, pump etc. were the property of Jamuna Oil Co. which used to be run by late Imam Sharif as a dealer, a peculiar circumstance that might have offered grounds for such appointment to run the pump free from chaos. Furthermore, no principle is decided in this case as the Appellate Division dismissed the leave petition holding that the High Court Division's order was not passed inequitably and in violation of law. This case. Therefore, does not come in aid of the respondent's case as is far distinguishable from the peculiar facts of the instant suit.

<u>16. The primary purpose of the Order XL, rule 1 of the Code is to save the subject-matter of the suit from mismanagement and mischief with a view to safeguard interest of the parties. Here in this case no allegation of mischief, wastage or damage of the subject-matter of the suit is alleged. The allegation made consists in deprivation of the plaintiff by misappropriation of his 1/5th share in rent and other profits earned from the joint property by his immediate and extended family members. Appointment of receiver in such circumstances means nothing less than dispossessing rest of the members of a family to their utter peril from the ancestral property as against the claim of a minor share of only one of member which by no stretch of imagination can be called just and convenient as contemplated by law. Learned judge appears to have acted on the erroneous proposition of law that ejmali nature of property and deprivation of the profits earned from the joint property, if established prima facie, should offer sufficient ground for appointment of receiver no matter how inequitable and distressing that may be for rest of the family or substantial part of the family.</u>

<u>17. The impugned order is not called for in the peculiar circumstances of the case as it seeks to dislodge members of the plaintiff's extended family from their ancestral property they are long in possession as against contested claim of a minor share of the same. Furthermore the allegation of misappropriation of rental and other shares made by the plaintiff is basically against defendant Nos.9 and 10, ie, his two full brothers, whereas receiver was appointed in respect of the property possessed by the defendant Nos.1-4 on the ground of non-payment rental share against whom no such allegation is found in the application of the plaintiff. The impugned order, therefore, is manifestly erroneous and unsustainable in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case.</u>

<u>18. For the reasons stated above, we find merit in this appeal. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed. The impugned order passed by the learned Joint District Judge is set aside.</u>

There shall, however be, no order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
