He strenuously argues that the petitioner, being a government servant and his grievance being related to and arising out of his service condition, ought to have approached the Administrative Tribunal where he could have agitated all his grievances, as viewed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 5 of 2004 arising out of his earlier Writ Petition No. 4134 of 2002. He submits that it is true that the Hon'ble Appellate Division in its judgment sympathized with the entitlements of the petitioner having observed that 'some injustice has been done to him' but at the same time commented that 'it is for the government to consider the grievance of the petitioner' but he, instead of approaching the government, filed AT Case No. 163 of 2005, which was dismissed by the Administrative Tribunal and, then, he preferred an appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal and, only at that stage, the petitioner started to seek remedy from the government. He submits that since respondent no. 1 was contesting the appeal, the petitioner ought to have obtained his relief through that forum but he, instead, choose to withdraw it on 2-6-2009 on his own motion and, therefore, filing of the instant writ petition by the petitioner is clearly an attempt to reagitate the issues, which were dealt with and adjudicated upon by the Administrative Tribunal previously, which is not permissible in the law being barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence as well as hit by res judicata.

16. He next submits that Annexures I and K are mere opinions of two Ministries and such interministerial communications made in the process of reaching a decision, being uncommunicated to the petitioner, do not create any right in his favour as those do not have any force of law. He submits that making such communications falls within the administrative functions of the government which does not call for any interference by this court.

17. He finally submits that in order to enforce the performance by the public bodies of any public duty by mandamus, the applicant is required to have a specific legal right to insist upon such performance and since in the instant case the petitioner has no legal right, the petitioner is not entitled to get any order directing the respondents to enforce the performance as claimed under mandamus.

18. In support of his above submission, the learned Deputy Attorney-General seeks to rely on the cases of (1) Nur Hossain vs Secretary Ministry of Land reported in 52 DLR 275, (2) Secretary, Internal Resources Division, Ministry of Finance and Commerce vs Nasrin Banu and 5 others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 171, (3) Al-Haj Abul Basher being dead his heirs Hosne Ara Begum vs Bangladesh reported in 50 DLR (AD) 11, (4) National Engineers Ltd vs Director, Military Lands and Cantonment reported in 44 DLR (AD) 179, (5) Badal Rani Misra alias Badal Rani Goswami vs Government 27 DLR (AD) 65 and (6) Sadeque Uddin Ahmed vs Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakhya, reported in 46 DLR 205.

19. We have heard the learned advocates for both the sides, perused the writ petition, supplementary-affidavit, affidavit-in-opposition together with its annexures and the relevant laws and decisions placed before us, which have been considered carefully.

20. It appears that the issues for determination by this Court are whether the contents of the annexure I & K should be held to be the "decisions" of the government, as termed by the petitioner, or those should be held to be mere recommendations, opinions or interministerial communication, as termed by the respondents, and whether the aforesaid recommendations, opinions, interministerial opinions or decisions, whatever may be termed, are amenable under writ jurisdiction seeking its implementation in the form of mandamus and, finally, whether Article 117 debars this Court to entertain the petitioner's present writ petition.

21. In order to have a proper adjudication on the above issues, let us first see whether the impugned annexure I & K are decisions of the Government or these are mere interministerial communications/correspondence or actions taken by the government.

22. At first, we will endeavour to deal with the factual issues of the instant writ petition. For a technical reason, stated at the last part of this judgment, we will deal with the issue of maintainability of the present writ petition at a later stage, together with the case laws related to the said issue referred to by the learned advocate for the petitioner.

23. It transpires that the petitioner is a veteran freedom fighter who possesses an excellent academic background and unblemished service record. It further transpires that though on 5-10-1979 he joined as the Deputy Secretary of the Government, he was subjected to deprivation of his legitimate promotion throughout his service carrier till his retirement as evident from the fact that he was supposed to be promoted as a Secretary of the Government in the year 1993. It appears that upon receiving legal notice from the petitioner in the year 1993, the good office of the Hon'ble Prime Minister started an investigation by the NSI as to the allegations raised by the petitioner and after conducting a thorough investigation by the said agency, a comprehensive report was submitted to the Hon'ble Prime Minister who forwarded the same to the office of the then Attorney-General who prepared a "Case Summary" with some recommendations for the Hon'ble Prime Minister as evident from annexure-A to the writ petition. Pertinent part of the said recommendations contained in Paragraph 8 are as follows:

“ তদন্ত প্রতিবেদনের চুড়ান্ত সুপারিশে উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে যে, জনাব এনায়েত উল্লাহর কনিষ্ঠ উপ-সচিবগন চাকুরী রেকের্ডের ভিত্তিতে ১২/১২/৮২ইং তারিখে যুগ্ম সচিব, ৪/৩/৯১ তারিখে অতিরিক্ত সচিব ও ২১/৪/৯৩ তারিখে সচিব পর্যায়ে পদ্দোন্নতি লাভ করেছেন। দীর্ঘদিনের বঞ্চনা ও তার প্রতি অবিচারের প্রতিকারার্থে যে যে তারিখে তার কনিষ্ঠ কর্মকর্তাগন যুগ্ম সচিব, অতিরিক্ত সচিব ও সচিব পর্যায়ে পদ্দোন্নতি পেয়েছেন, উপরে বর্ণিত সেই তারিখ হতে সকল সুবিধা প্রদান করে জনাব এনায়েত উল্লাহকে পদ্দোন্নতি প্রদান করে প্রকৃত মুক্তিযোদ্দার প্রতি সুবিচার করার বিষয়টি বিবেচনার দাবী রাখে। NSI প্রতিবেদন, সংশ্লিষ্ট তথ্যাবলী, চাকুরীর রেকর্ড ও বার্ষিক গোপনীয় প্রতিবেদন পযালোচনা করে উপরোক্ত তারিখে জনাব এনায়েত উল্লাহর পদ্দোন্নতি না হওয়ার স্বপক্ষে কোন যুক্তিযুক্ত কারন নেই। কাজেই  NSI প্রতিবেদন এর অনুচ্ছেদ ১২ অনুযায়ী একটি সন্মানজনক Fellowship প্রদান ও চুড়ান্ত মন্তব্য সমূহ নীতিগতভাবে গ্রহনযোগ্য।

সংশ্লিষ্ট কাগজপত্র পুঃখানুভাবে পর্যালোচনার পর NSI পরিদপ্তরের তদন্ত প্রতিবেদনটি পরিপূর্ণ তথ্য সম্বলিত, সুষ্ঠ ও নিরপেক্ষ প্রতীয়মান হচ্ছে। প্রতিবেদনটি পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় যে, একজন মুক্তিযোদ্দার প্রতি দীর্ঘ ২১ বছর চরম অবিচার করা হয়েছে। এর জন্য তিনি অবশ্যই ক্ষতিপূরন পাবেন। অতএব, অনুচ্ছেদ ৮ এ বর্ণিত সুপারিশমালা অনুমোদন করতঃ অনতিবিলম্বে পোষ্টিং প্রদান করে একজন বিশিষ্ট মুক্তিযোদ্ধার প্রতি সুবিচার প্রদর্শনের জন্য মাননীয় প্রধান মন্ত্রীর নিকট বিনীতভাবে পেশ করা হলো।”

24. The said recommendations being approved by the Hon'ble Prime Minister was forwarded to the Ministry of Establishment for taking necessary action. It transpires from para-graph 3 of the Annexure-B to the writ petition, which runs as follows: ৩। মাননীয় প্রধানমন্ত্রী ক���্তৃক অনুমোদিত সার সংক্ষেপের উপর প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহনের জন্য প্রধানমন্ত্রীর কার্যালয়ের ২৪/১২/১৯৯৬ ইং তারিখের স্মারকমূলে সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রনালয়ে প্রেরিত হয়। ১৫-৩-১৯৯৭ ইং তারিখে সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয় জনাব এনায়েত উল্লাহকে অতিরিক্ত সচিব হিসাবে পদ্দোন্নতির আদেশ জারী করলেও মাননীয় প্রধানমন্ত্রী কর্তৃক অনুমোদিত সার সংক্ষেপের একটি নির্দেশ ও বাস্তবায়িত হয় নাই। that on the basis of the Prime Minister's order, which arose out of NSI report and recommendation of the then learned Attorney-General, the Ministry of Public Administration withdrew the petitioner from OSD, whereon he was placed for a period of 5 years, and promoted him to the post of Additional Secretary and eventually appointed him as a Member of the Privatization Commission.

25. It further appears that when the petitioner was legitimately expecting that he would go on retirement as a Secretary of the Government as per recommendations made by the then learned Attorney-General being approved by the Hon'ble Prime Minister, on 11-5-2002, he was sent on retirement and, under the circumstance, he filed a writ petition to the High Court Division challenging the non-implementation of the remedial measures quoted hereinbefore (quotation in Bengali) as well as seeking the legality and propriety of the order of his retirement dated 11-5-2002 wherein the petitioner was successful to obtain a direction from this Court for implementation of those remedial measures albeit without any relief as to the order of his retirement.

26. Being aggrieved with the High Court's direction the government preferred an appeal. The Appellate Division though found the petitioner's case to be worthy of consideration but was of the view that since the writ petition was not maintainable the petitioner should seek remedy from the government. It appears that the petitioner then unsuccessfully moved to Administrative Tribunal and, then, he, having preferred an appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, simultaneously started to try getting remedy from the government by making representation.

27. It transpires that immediately after assuming the office of the present Hon'ble Prime Minister, the petitioner's case again got momentum to move from the Hon'ble Prime Minister's Office to the Ministry of Public Administration, Ministry of Law and Justice and Ministry of Finance. It appears that the petitioner's case upon being forwarded by the present Prime Minister office on 22-3-2009, as evident from annexure-G to the writ petition, the concerned dealing ministry (Ministry of Public Administration), which is vested with the power of implementation of the petitioner's case, sought opinion, at first, from the Ministry of Law and Justice who provided a detailed opinion of 31 paragraphs vide annexure 'I' to the writ petition recommending the implementation of the remedial measures. The Paragraph No. 24 is the concluding opinion, contents of which are as follows:

“২৪। এমতাবস্থায়, নোটানুচ্ছেদ ২১ এ উল্লিখিত অর্থাৎ সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রনালয়ের যাচিত বিষয়ে নিম্নরুপ মতামত প্রদান করা যায়ঃ-

(ক)২৩-১১-১৯৯৬ তারিখে বিজ্ঞ অ্যাটনি জেনারেল জনাব কে,এস নবী কর্তৃক উপস্থাপিত সার সংক্ষেপ মাননীয় প্রধানমন্ত্রী স্বাক্ষর করায় এবং উক্ত সার-সংক্ষেপের ৯নং অনুচ্ছেদের প্রস্তাব সমূহ সম্পর্কে প্রয়োজনীয় কার্যক্রম গ্রহনের জন্য সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রনালয়কে নির্দেশনা প্রদানের প্রেক্ষিতে উক্ত বিষয়ে প্রয়োজনীয় কার্যক্রম গ্রহন করার বাধ্যবাধকতা থাকে। সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রনালয়ের সার সংক্ষেপ  উল্লেখিত বিষয় বাস্তবায়নে সংগত কোন কারনে প্রতিবন্ধকতা সৃষ্টি হলে তা সরকার প্রদান হিসাবে মাননীয় প্রধানমন্ত্রী সমীপে উপস্থাপনক্রমে প্রাপ্ত সিদ্ধান্ত মোতাবেক কার্যকরন সমীচীন হবে।

28. Thereafter, again the said Ministry of Public Administration sought clearance as to getting the required fund for the petitioner from the Ministry of Finance, which also opined in favour of the petitioner (Annexure-K) in the following words:

“উপযুক্ত বিষয় ও সূত্রের প্রেক্ষিতে বিজ্ঞ এ্যাটনী জেনারেল কর্তৃক উপস্থাপিত এবং মাননীয় প্রধানমন্ত্রী কর্তৃক অনুমোদিত সার সংক্ষেপ এবং আইন, বিচার ও সংসদ বিষয়ক মন্ত্রনালয়ের মতামতের ভিত্তিতে জনাব এ,কে,এম এনায়েত উল্লাহ, আইডি নং-৩২৩, সাবেক অতিরিক্ত সচিবকে সংস্থাপন মন্ত্রনালয় কর্তৃক ভুতাপেক্ষ পদ্দোন্নতি বিষয়ে বিবেচনা করলে প্রাপ্যতা অনুযায়ী তাকে বেতন ভাতাদি প্রদানে অর্থ বিভাগের সন্মতি নির্দেশক্রমে জ্ঞাপন করা হল।

29. It appears that previously in the year 1996 the Office of the Prime Minister once directed Ministry of Public Administration on the basis of the NSI report as well as the recommendations of the then Attorney-General and, pursuant thereto, the said Ministry placed the petitioner on regular posting from OSD and promoted him to the position of Additional Secretary but did not implement the remedial measures in full. Again the Ministry of Public Administration being directed by the Prime Minister in the year 2009 took some steps in a bid to implement the remaining remedial measures by seeking legal opinion from the Ministry of Law and Justice and approaching the Ministry of Finance for funds to be paid to the petitioner and both of the Ministries complied with the request of the Ministry of Public Administrations. Thus, we are unable to concede to the submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the Ministry of Public administration was not aware of the NSI report or communications between the then learned attorney General and the Prime Minister.

30. From the above discussions, it clearly appears that annexure "I" is a legal opinion given by the Ministry of Law and Justice as sought by the Ministry of Public Administration and annexure "K" is an interministerial correspondence of the Ministry of Finance to the Ministry of Public Administration and, thus, may not be any "decision" of the government but the aforesaid legal opinion and correspondence, collectively, amount to a positive action of the government and the said action of the government imposes a duty upon it to go ahead for further action towards its implementation.

31. This takes us to deal with as to whether the aforesaid "actions" of the government creates any right to the petitioner. In view of the fact that the Ministry of Law and Justice in the process of providing the legal opinion for the petitioner vide annexure "I" impliedly insisted, if not said expressly, the petitioner to withdraw his AAT Appeal No. 92 of 2007 and thereby made a promise to the petitioner to the effect that a decision in respect of the petitioner's matter will be eventually made by the government and, accordingly, when the petitioner withdrew his case giving up his right to proceed with the appeal, the Ministry of Public Administration should not have ignored its duty to take further action to make a decision on the petitioner's matter inasmuch as, the Ministry of law was engaged by the Ministry of Public Administration to give a legal opinion. Seemingly, the said Ministry of Public Administration took further steps by asking the Ministry of Finance to opine on the petitioner's matter but refrained from taking further steps since obtaining clearance/opinion from the Ministry of Finance, which the said Ministry can not do in view of the fact that the matter of the petitioner was initiated from the Office of the Hon'ble Prime Minister and the Ministry of Public Administration is duty bound to make a decision on the petitioner's claim, whether it goes in favour or against the petitioner given that the Prime Minister, as per the rules of business, is the Chief Executive of all the Ministries of Bangladesh and whenever any matter is forwarded by the Prime Minister to any Ministry, it becomes imperative on the part of the concerned Ministry to make a decision on the said matter or, in the alternative, to place the matter before the Prime Minister for her decision thereto.

32. Moreover, since by channeling the petitioner's matter from one Ministry to the other Ministry aiming at disposal of the same, the said Ministry of Public Administration acted in a manner, which raised a legitimate expectation in the mind of the petitioner that the said Ministry will make decision on his claim and, furthermore, since in the said process of moving from one Ministry to the other Ministry, his AAT Appeal No. 92 of 2007 was withdrawn to his disadvantage and, by now, nearly 4(four) years have elapsed since the time of placing the petitioner's application to the Prime Minister on 22-3-2009, the Ministry of Public Administration is estopped from stepping back in making a decision on the petitioner's matter.

33. Thus, though annexures I & K cannot be equated with the status of "decision", nonetheless, those being "actions" taken by the government, it was imperative upon the government to conclude the said actions by arriving at a final decision by the Ministry of Public Administration.

34. Now, let us deal with the question as to whether Article 117 is a bar to the instant writ petition.

35. The learned advocate for the petitioner makes the following submissions as to the maintainability of the instant writ petition; that the instant writ petition is maintainable in view of the fact that the petitioner seeks a direction from this Court in the form of mandamus for implementation of the remedial measures and, therefore, this Hon'ble Court is the only forum to deal with this matter as the Administrative Tribunal is not competent to pass the kind of order as prayed for by the petitioner; that in view of the fact that the petitioner's fundamental rights have been violated for not treating him in the same manner as the government did for the other freedom fighter civil servants and, therefore, he is entitled to come to this Court instead of going to the Administrative Tribunal; that the High Court Division should not turn inward as it deals with the question whether the petitioner can come before it to protect his fundamental rights and if it does, it would fail to perform its duty as imposed upon it under the Constitution; that if this Court shrugs off its responsibility, the spill-over effect will impinge on the jurisdiction of this Court specially vested under the Constitution and it will be a considerable setback to what is an extremely promising trend to exercise the jurisdiction; that a number of Division Benches of the High Court Division are presently entertaining this type of writ petition and, subsequently, the Rules are also being made absolute; that there are numerous decisions of this Court as well as the Apex Court where invoking writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution in respect of the matters relating to, or arising out of, the terms and conditions of service of government servants have been held to be maintainable on the ground of violation of fundamental rights, corum-non-judice, malafide or malice in law and refers to the case of M Abu Raihan vs Secretary, Ministry of Science and Technology reported in 7 BLC 44. Then, he refers to the case of Abdul Wahab Sarkar vs Bangladesh reported in 17 BLC 365 and the case of Md Alimuzzaman   Chowdhury vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 32 BLD 228 = 17 BLC 722, an unreported judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 1405 of 2011.

36. Per contra, Mr Md Al-Amin Sarkar, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents submits that this writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution is not maintainable because the petitioner was in the service of the Republic and the matters brought before this Court relate to the terms and conditions of his service, which is not amenable under the writ jurisdiction as Article 117 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has ousted the jurisdiction of this Court in clear and unambiguous words and since there is an alternative Constitutional forum, as opposed to other alternative forums under ordinary law, available to the petitioner, the present Rule is liable to be discharged on this ground alone and in support of his above submissions, he supplies us a list of cases of our Apex Court and submits that it is the consistent view of our Appellate Division that no writ petition lies regarding any matter relating to or arising out of service matter of a government servant.

37. In order to appreciate the submissions as to the incompetency of the Administrative Tribunal to deal with the matter and as to the ambiguity in the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980, let us look at Article 117(1)(a) of the Constitution concurrently with the provision of section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980.

Article 117(1)(a): Administrative Tribunals.—(1) Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, Parliament may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of- (a) the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic, including the matters  provided for in Part IX and the award of penalties or punishments. ;

38. Section 4. Jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunals—(l) An Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine applications made by any person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority.

39. From a plain reading of the words "any person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority" and "in respect of the terms and conditions of his service " it appears that (a) the applicants of the Administrative Tribunal must be government servants and (b) the matters to be dealt with and adjudicated upon by the said Tribunal must be related to or, arising out of, the terms and conditions of their service.

40. First, admittedly, the petitioner before us is a former government servant. We have purposefully used the words "government servant" as it includes any one employed in the service of the Republic as well as under Statutory Public Authority meaning "any authority, corporation or body the activities or the principal activities of which are authorised by any Act, ordinance, order or instrument having the force of law in Bangladesh" as provided for in Article 152 of the Constitution and, thus, not the "Statutory Public Authority" as defined in the definition clause of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980. We took the aforesaid view as the definition of Constitution shall override and, therefore, prevail over an Act of parliament. We refrain from comprehensively discussing the issue for now and await to deal with this inconsistency between a Constitutional word and statutory word in a fit case at an appropriate time.

41. Second, whether the matter before us is "related to" or "arising out of (the words as used in Article 117(1)) the terms and conditions of service of the petitioner. Unhesitatingly, we hold that the matter before us is "relating to" the terms and conditions of service given that though the petitioner's apparent prayer is to implement the remedial measures proposed by the then Attorney-General, which was forwarded by the Hon'ble Prime Minister for the disposal by the relevant Ministry of Public Administration who took some actions towards disposal of the petitioner's matter but yet to make a decision on it. Therefore, under a camouflage, though, he seeks a direction from this Court, but from the averments of the petition it clearly appears that in hindsight the grievance of the petitioner is with regard to his matter, which is related to his service condition. In fact, both the words "relating to" and "arising out of are applicable in the case of the petitioner. It is not out of place to note here that taking resort to the Constitutional word "relating to", Tribunal can bring any service related dispute within its jurisdiction, even it may be remotely connected to the "terms and conditions of service" of the government servants.

42. From a careful reading of section 4(1) of the Administrative Tribunal Act 1980, it appears that the legislature has consciously used the words "shall have exclusive jurisdiction" to give effect to the words used in the Constitution in Article 117(2) "no court shall entertain any proceedings". It is to be noted here that in both the laws, the word "shall" has been used in order to avoid any ambiguity as to its jurisdiction. Then, the Constitution itself by Article 117(I)(a) prescribes the matters to be dealt with by the Tribunals " to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of (a) the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic, including the matters provided for in part IX and the award of penalties or punishments". Thus, from the language used in the Constitution "matters relating to or arising out of...." we find that with regard to any matter of a person in the service of the Republic relating to or arising out of his service during the period of his service or after his retirement from service, shall be dealt with by the Administrative Tribunal inasmuch as by using the words "including the matters provided for in Part IX", an indication has been given that Administrative Tribunal shall have exclusive jurisdiction over all service related disputes/matters of the persons in the service of the Republic as the said part IX deals with " reorganization of the service of the Republic by the creation, amalgamation or unification of services " which seem to be very serious and important national issues, nevertheless, those have been made subject matters to be heard and adjudicated upon by the Administrative Tribunals.

43. It clearly appears that Parliament never intended to leave any subject to be tried or dealt with by any other court or Tribunal other than the Tribunal established under Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 save and except striking down any law and allegation as to clear violation of fundamental rights. So, we do not find that the Tribunal was incompetent to deal with the petitioner's case.

44. We also do not find substance in the other submission advanced by the learned advocate for the petitioner that the Administrative Tribunal is incompetent to direct the government or any of its authority to implement any decision in that nowhere in the said Act there is any provision prohibiting the said Tribunal from passing such order of direction. Furthermore, when both the Laws, i.e., Constitution and the said Act empower the Tribunal by saying that "any matter relating to or arising out of there should not be any hesitation to hold that the Tribunal is amply empowered to deal with any matters except striking down any law. Also, since the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 has specifically vested the Tribunal with the power of implementing its decision under section 8 and while section 9 empowers it to penalise any person for causing obstruction in the performance of its function, it can not be said that the Administrative Tribunal cannot issue any direction. Furthermore, under section 7 of the said Act, the powers of the Administrative Tribunals are like a civil court as enshrined in the said section "a Tribunal shall have all the powers of civil courts, while trying a suit under the code of civil procedure". Since a civil court has the power to pronounce a declaration and grant consequential relief, we hold that the Administrative Tribunal is not less empowered than the former, specifically in view of the fact that the Tribunal is established under the direct mandate of the Constitution. Therefore, the Tribunals are not powerless to give any necessary direction to the concerned authority when required.

45. With regard to Mr Azmalul Hosain's submission that there are numerous Decisions of our Apex Court in favour of entertaining writ petition in respect of service matters of a person in the service of the Republic, let us examine the Decisions of our Apex Court.

46. For convenience of our analysis and discussion on the relevant Case Laws, the same may be divided into four categories. First, the Cases which have been dealt with the challenge to the vires of any law on service. Second, Cases where the Appellate Division has dealt with the issues of malafide, corum-non-judice and malice in law. Third, Cases where Appellate Division did not find any element of challenge to the vires of any law or allegation of violation of fundamental rights. Fourth, Cases which were filed by the employees of projects under the government and thereby not treating or conceiving them as persons in the service of the Republic.

47. Now, let us deal with the first category of cases of our Appellate Division.

48. In the recent case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Mosharraf Hossain reported in 32 BLD (AD) (2012) 66 = 64 DLR (AD) 21, the Appellate Division was persuaded on the issue of maintainability as the writ petitioner in the said case, who is a Bench Reader of the Appellate Division, had challenged the vires of the "“ বাংলাদেশ সুপ্রীমকোট (আপীল বিভাগ) এর কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারীদের নিয়োগ বিধিমালা, ২০০০” together with his grievance of discrimination in treating him as Third Class Non-Gazetted Officer.

49. In the case of Molla Md. Anwarul Huq vs Government of Bangladesh reported in VIII ADC (2011) 782, the Appellate Division held the writ petition to be maintainable as it found that the guidelines under challenge, having been published in Official Gazette, had the force of law.

50. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Shamsul Huq reported in 59 DLR (AD) 54, the writ petition, which was filed by the Personal Officer of the Supreme Court, was held by our Apex Court to be maintainable on the ground that the impugned Notifications had the force of law.

51. In the case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27, the vires of some Rules, Regulations and Notifications were challenged and the Appellate Division held the writ petition to be maintainable.

52. We have noticed from our personal experience while sitting in Writ Benches that the learned advocates of this Court very often quote the last paragraph of the aforesaid case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 "The supplemental, as opposed substitutional, role of the Tribunals constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution was already conceded and permitted to the Tribunals in Mujibur Rahman case, no power of judicial review under Article 102(2) was conceded to the Tribunal in that case" and endeavours to submit that in view of the aforesaid observations the Administrative Tribunals have been given only a supplemental or an additional role to the High Court and, thus, a government servant may invoke Article 102 of the Constitution instead of going to the Administrative Tribunal. In reply to the aforesaid argument, our observation is that in spite of the words 'the Supplemental' which means 'Additional', used in the last Para of the case, Bangladesh vs Saifuddin, we find in the body of the judgment no actual deviation from the view that was held in Mujibur Rahman's case. In Para 88 of the said judgment it is observed "The writ petitioner did not argue any case of supersession in the High Court Division nor did make out any case that they should be promoted with restoration of their respective seniority as per gradation list. If they had done so they would have been out of the writ jurisdiction, because by a constitutional mandate the Administrative Tribunal would have been the proper forum for determination of the question of supersession and seniority." In Para 95 of the same judgment the Appellate Division has further observed: "Mr Amirul Islam did not notice that Article 44(1) of the Constitution was in all fairness brought to the notice of his Court by the Government respondents themselves in that case (vide paragraph 47 of the Report) and the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal to strike down an order for infringement of fundamental rights or any other law (but not the jurisdiction to strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality) was conceded"

53. In the case of Bangladesh vs Azizur Rahman reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19, the writ petition was held maintainable by the Apex Court as the vires of the Bangladesh Ad-hoc appointees Rules 1990 was challenged together with the petitioner's grievance as to his seniority. In this case, as the vires of law was challenged, the Apex Court in answering the question as to non-invocation of Article 102 (1), replied that "It is found from the facts of the writ petitioners that the question of fundamental right invoked therein has been so mixed up with the facts and statutory Rules that the question of fundamental right cannot be extricated for exclusive consideration in a petition for enforcement of fundamental right. Therefore, the High Court Division rightly held the writ petitions to be maintainable under Article 102 (2) ".

54. In the case of Mujubur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) III, the constitutionality of section 3(3) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 together with the judgment of the Administrative Tribunal was challenged. In Para 48 of this reported case, the Apex Court, in outlining the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunals, observed that—

"within its jurisdiction the Tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising of sub-clause (a), but such tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1937 SC 386 (Para 16) and JB Chopra vs Union of India AIR 1987 SC 357 (Para 2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117 (2)."

55. Having found ourselves in full agreement with the observation made in Para 48 of the Mojibur Rahman's case, we would like to-add that any civil Court or Administrative Tribunal of our land may not be armed to enforce the fundamental right but while dealing with civil cases is empowered to examine any factual complaint relating to violation of fundamental rights. We find that the right to property is a fundamental right, which is being dealt with by our civil Courts every day. Similarly, the Special Tribunals, set up under the Anti-Corruption Act or Money Laundering Act, 2011 closes down a business or freezes money of businessmen but for that reason an allegation of violation of fundamental right as to his right to profession cannot help him to invoke Article 102 of the Constitution. We hold that judicial review is a discretionary or extra ordinary judicial power of this Court and the said power cannot be invoked where the jurisdiction has been specifically ousted by the Constitution itself as there is a difference between judicial power and jurisdiction. In this connection we like to refer the cases of State vs Ziaur Rahman PLD 1973 (SC) 49, Federation of Pakistan vs Sayeed Ahmed PLD 1974 (SC) 151 and Fauiji Foundation vs Shaminur Rahman PLD 1983 (SC) 457.

56. Thus, from the discussions of the above decisions of the Appellate Division it transpires that if vires of any Act of Parliament or Rules, Regulations and Government Guidelines or Notifications having force of law is challenged, then a writ petition under Article 102(1) of the Constitution is maintainable.

57. Now, let us examine the cases of our Appellate Division where writ petitions without challenging vires of law were allowed.

58. In the case of Md. Abdur Rashid vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 12 BLC (AD) 142, the writ petitions, which were filed by the Bench Officers of this Court, were held to be maintainable by the Appellate Division as it found that the same were filed invoking Article 102 (1) of Constitution for enforcement of fundamental rights, not challenging any action or failure to do an act under Article 102(2) of the Constitution.

59. In the case of Secretary, Ministry of Health vs Parvin Sultana reported in 57 DLR (AD) 111, the writ petition was entertained by the High Court Division wherein the Rule was made absolute by the said Division and, subsequently, the same was affirmed by the Apex Court, though no vires of any law was challenged. Interestingly, there is no discussion or observation in the judgment about the issue of maintainability though the petitioner was a government servant and her grievance was as to her transfer.

60. In the case of Secretary, Ministry of Establishment vs Md Jahangir Hossain reported in 51 DLR (AD) 148 it was held that " can come to the High Court Division not for enforcement of legal right but for enforcement of their fundamental right." It appears from the facts of this case that the writ petitioners were not in the service of the Republic in true sense in light of the fact that their prayer was to make them government servants by absorbing them in the service of the Republic.

61. Now, let us examine the cases of the Apex Court where issues of corum-non-judice, malafide and malice in law were discussed.

62. In the case of Shaheda Khatun vs Administrative Appellate Tribunal reported in 3 BLC (AD) 155, the writ petition, which was filed against the judgment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, was held to be maintainable on the ground that the formation of tribunal by two members was void in the eye of law and held that "the Appellate Tribunal seems to be totally unaware of the settled law that notwithstanding the ouster of jurisdiction of the High Court Division by any legislative provision or even under Article 102 itself the High Court Division is yet entitled to exercise its power of judicial review under Article 102 if the action complained of before the High Court Division is found to be corum-non-judice, with-out jurisdiction or taken malafide." It appears that the aforesaid writ petition was filed against the judgment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal and the aforesaid ground of "corum-non-judice" was conceded by the Apex Court for invoking writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution where the Tribunal was not formed as per the prescription of law. Thus, it should be mentioned here that it was not a kind of case of "corum-non-judice", where an impugned order/letter was signed by a government functionary other than the assigned one, as very often in some cases the learned advocates of this Court attempt to argue.

63. In the case of (i) Khandoker Mostaq Ahmed vs Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR (AD) 223, (ii) Jamil Huq vs Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR (AD) 125 and (iii) Kh. Ehtashamuddin Ahmed vs Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR (AD) 154, it was observed by our Apex Court that the High Court's jurisdiction under Article 102 may be exercised if the authority of a disciplined force or Courts/Tribunal under the Army Act or other law relating to disciplined forces acts malafide or without jurisdiction or is not properly constituted. It is to be noted here that though all the aforesaid three cases laid down the above principle of invoking writ jurisdiction overriding the exception of Article 102(5) of the Constitution, but, interestingly enough, in all of the cases, writ petitions were rejected summarily, which were upheld by the Appellate Division. Furthermore, since all the three cases were in relation to criminal convictions through the Tribunal set up under MLO No. 9 of 1982 and Paragraph 19(2) of the Fourth Schedule of the said MLO which made provision for this Court to review actions and proceedings of the tribunals and, therefore, there was scope in the said MLO itself to review the actions of the Martial Law Tribunals. Also, from the facts of the cases and conclusion arrived at by the Apex Court, it is our view that the aforesaid principle seems to be applicable only to the criminal cases.

64. The case of Abdur Rouf and vs Abdul Hamid Khan reported in 17 DLR (SC) 515 was regarding a dispute over land properties, which was sent to the Deputy Commissioner as a reference under a Regulation (Frontier Criminal Regulation) for adjudicating upon the matter and, as per section 10 and 60 of the said Regulation, the order of the Deputy Commissioner was final. Then, question arose as to whether the dispute was at all referable to the Deputy Commissioner and it was found by the Supreme Court that the matter was sent as a reference to the DC under misconception of law and, therefore, the order passed by the DC was without jurisdiction. Thus, the principle laid down in the above case is not relevant at all to service matters and, as such, it cannot be applied here inasmuch as our jurisprudence on the word "malafide" or "without jurisdiction" has subsequently developed in clear terms making the word applicable in specific situation/case.

65. In the case of Nur Mohammad vs M Ahmed reported in 39 DLR (AD) 1, which is a case on acquisition, the argument of malafide was made in spite of imposing a clear bar to file any suit in the statue and it was rejected by the majority decision of the Appellate Division. In this case it was observed that "This is a wellknown proposition of law which this Court has yet no occasion to depart from or express any disagreement with it. The point, however, is whether any bar of suit imposed by the legislature can be disregarded to make such suit which is so barred, maintainable in order to try an issue on malafide alleged in the plaint. It may, at least in some cases be seen that hardship, or even injustice, may result it, in spite of evident truth in the allegation of malafide, the suit is held to be not maintainable because there is a bar against such suit in the statute concerned. But, seeker of justice in a court of law should become aware, if not already so, that justice is done according to law, A Judge may have sympathy for a litigant's suffering due to technicalities of law made by the legislature, still in view of the express legislative intention, he must follow the "hands-off doctrine". Otherwise chaos and anarchy would prevail leading to all sorts of complexities and confusion. Whatever the legislature says, unless it is contrary to the Constitution, its mandate, either express or implied, has been obeyed by Court.

66. Malafide was also argued in the cases of (i) Miah Mohammad Latif vs Province of West Pakistan reported in PLD 1970 (SC) 180 = 22 DLR (SC) 98, (ii) Federation of Pakistan vs Syeed Ahmed reported in PLD 1974 (SC) 151 and (iii) Ali Jan vs Bangladesh 37 DLR (AD) 161. It is pertinent to mention here that the facts of all the aforesaid 5 cases are with regard to requisition of property where it was alleged that the said properties were requisitioned not for bonafide purpose but for collateral purpose. Furthermore, in those statutes the decision of the authority/appellate authority was made unquestionable in any court and, therefore, the argument in those cases to examine the allegation of malafide sounds good given that the highhandedness of the authority would remain unexamined. But, here the Tribunal can look into the allegation of malafide, which is an opposite scenario to those cases where the doors for judicial scrutiny as to the allegation of malafide were closed by a statutory provision. Therefore, the principles laid down in those cases appears to be applicable only in other matters including the civil cases inasmuch as, the ouster of writ jurisdiction in service matters of the government servants has been done by a Constitutional provision, not by any statute. Thus, the facts and law in the present case are entirely on different lines, which, therefore, do not attract the application of the aforesaid cases of malafide in service matters.

67. In the landmark case of Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201, the vires of section 9(2) of Public Service Retirement Act, 1974 was challenged together with the order of retirement from service. In this case "malice in law" was found by the Apex Court and the writ petition having been discharged by the High Court Division, was allowed by the Apex Court. Since the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 did not come into force on the date of pronouncement of judgment of this case on 9-12-1980, the issue of maintainability of the writ petition did not come under attack though the petitioner Dr Nurul Islam was in the service of the Republic and the grievance was with regard to his condition of service.

68. However, subsequently in the case of Taposhi Bhattacharje vs Bangladesh reported in 24 BLD (HCD) 365 = 9 BLC 613 it was held that "When the question of malafide is alleged with reference to the conduct and grudge of the authority concerned, it may become a question of fact which may not be decided under Article 102. But when there is allegation of malice in law that can be decided and considered by this Court in a summary proceeding under Article 102. Thus every writ petition with an allegation of malafide may not give jurisdiction to this Court if that allegation is required to be decided on the basis of evidence and in such a case the proper forum will be the Administrative Tribunal. But where the allegation is about malice in law and such question can be decided without going into any disputed question of fact, this Court can assume jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. " We find that although the style and manner applied in the aforesaid case to deviate from a series of decisions of our Apex Court seems to be sound and impressive but since against the said judgment, leave was granted by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition For Leave to Appeal No. 1557 of 2002 in order to examine the point as to whether 'malice in law' can stand as a ground for entertaining the writ petition of a person in the service of the Republic, but till date the aforesaid point has not been tested by our Appellate Division, particularly after the Administrative Tribunal Act came into operation on 16-1-1982, we find it difficult to accede to the decision of the aforesaid case.

69. Administrative Tribunal being established under the direct mandate of the  Constitution as a court of first instance adequately equipped with all the components for conducting a trial, is competent to adjudicate  upon all types of service related matters involving the issues of malafide, malice in law and  corum-non-judice.

70. Now, let us deal with the cases where the Appellate Division answered the question of maintainability of a writ petition of a person in the service of the Republic in respect of any matter arising out of his service in the negative.

71. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs SM Fariduddin reported in 54 DLR (AD) 95, which was a case with regard to transfer order, the Appellate Division found that since there was no complaint in the Rule against violation of any fundamental right, the order passed by the High Court Division in the writ petition was found to be, on its face, illegal. In this case the Appellate Division criticised the concerned Bench of the High Court Division for issuing such a Rule and subsequently making it absolute.

72. In the case of Delwar Hossain Mia (Md) vs Bangladesh reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120 it was held that: "A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2)."

73. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Mohammad Faruque reported in 51 DLR (AD) 112 it was held that: "Violation of all kinds of laws is not violation of fundamental right. Violation of terms and conditions of service may indeed be a violation of law, but if a specific remedy is provided in the Constitution for remedy then that specific remedy shall be availed of by the aggrieved person".

74. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Abdul Halim Miah reported in 9 MLR (AD) 105 = 9 BLC (AD) 134 it was held that: "No vires of Rules has been challenged but certain decisions taken in the meeting of the standing committee and placement in the gradation list and publication in the official Gazette has been challenged by way of an application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. The right of judicial review under Article 102(2) of the Constitution is neither a fundamental right nor a guaranteed right. Similarly, the judicial review of an administrative action is neither an all weather remedy nor a remedy for wrongs but is only available only when there is no other equally efficacious remedy. The writ petitioners have challenged the impugned decision to have infringed their fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 27 and 29 of the Constitution, but in view of the provision of Article 117(2) of the Constitution the Parliament has set out up Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 for exercise of the functions enumerated in Article 117(1) i.e. by setting of the Administrative Tribunal to exercise the jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic etc. Article 117(2) of the Constitution provides that no Court shall entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such Tribunal".

75. In the case of Jihad Ahmed vs Bangladesh Power Development Board reported in 52 DLR (AD) 75 it was held that: "The argument that the fundamental right of the petitioners as provided in Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution have been violated cannot be accepted for the simple reason that the order of transfer from one place to another is really a matter connected with the terms and conditions of the service of the petitioners".

76. In the case of Junnur Rahman vs Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha reported in 51 DLR (AD) 166 it was held that: "The writ petition was not maintainable because the petitioner did not seek to enforce any fundamental right and it was within the competence of the Administrative Tribunal to entertain the grievance of the petitioner ".

77. Now let us deal with the fourth category of cases, which are (i) Chief Engineer, the LGED vs Kazi Mizanur Rahman reported in 17 BLC (AD) 91 and (ii) unreported decisions of the Apex court in CPLA Nos. 767, 769, 1084-1085 of 2011 where the writ petitioners, being employees of projects under the government, invoked Article 102 directly without going to the Administrative Tribunal out of their apprehension of outright rejection of their application by the said Tribunal as their service status was not under the revenue budget and considering them not to be a public servant. All the cases were disposed of by our Apex Court with a direction upon the respondents to consider the writ petitioners' prayer as to absorption under the revenue budget.

78. Interestingly, in none of these cases, the issue as to maintainability was ever raised by the government. It might be that under a preconceived notion, "project employees" are not government servants and, as such, their grievances as to the terms and conditions of service are not amenable to the Administrative Tribunal. Had this issue been raised, then there would have been occasion to examine whether they also do come within the purview of the Administrative Tribunal in view of the provision of Article 117(1)(a) of the constitution "....including the matters provided for in Part  IX " and the said Part IX of the Constitution includes Article 135(4) "Where a person is  employed in the service of the Republic under a  'written contract and that contract is terminated by due notice in accordance with its terms, he shall not, by reason thereof, be regarded as removed from office for the purposes of this article".

79. If the employees of projects under the government are held to be barred from applying to the Administrative Tribunal for not being in the service of the Republic, even then there should not be any difficulty to invoke jurisdiction of civil courts unless in a statute there is any ouster clause like section 14A of (Emergency) Requisition of property Act, 1948, section 44 of the Emergency Requisition Ordinance, 1982, section 30 of SAT Act, 1950, section 45 of the Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 and so on. For mere violation of any contractual right as to absorption after completion of projects, or on the ground that they continued to be employed in the project under government based on its promise to eventually include in the revenue set up and thereby having legitimate expectation thereto, or violation of any Law or Rule can well be dealt with by the civil courts unless they intend to challenge any vires of law or raise a clear case of violation of fundamental right for which they are to seek judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution.

80. We do not wish to discuss on this aspect any further and await to see a proper adjudication of the issue by our Appellate Division in an appropriate case.

81. Thus, our understanding of the observations made in the cases discussed hereinbefore, particularly Mujibur Rahman's case, Azizur Rahman's case, Shafiddin's case, Mohammad Faruque's case and the recent case of Mosharraf Hossain 32 BLD (AD) (2012) 66 = 64 DLR (AD) 21 are that the Administrative Tribunal might be empowered to hear and adjudicate upon the said issue of violation of fundamental right of a government servant by the government or any higher authority during his service, but the High Court Division is always a better forum to examine any complaint as to violation of fundamental rights.

<u>82. From a plain reading of the above Appellate Division Cases, which we have categorized in four groups, namely (1) cases where writ petitions were held to be maintainable on the ground of challenging vires of Law, (II) cases where Corum-non-judice, malafide and malice in law have been discussed (iii) cases where Appellate Division has outright rejected writ petitions to be not maintainable and (iv) writ petitions which have been held to be maintainable on the ground of being employees under project of the government, it is our understanding that it is the consistent view of our Appellate Division that writ petitions by government servants are maintainable if they  challenge vires of any law or in a situation where the government servants successfully  make out a clear case of violation of fundamental rights, as opposed to a case of merely mentioning some Articles of part III of the Constitution. Although the cases referred to by the learned advocate for the petitioners are recent pronouncements of the High Court Division, nonetheless, we do not' think it would be a profitable exercise to discuss those cases here in view of the Rulings of the Appellate Division discussed hereinabove, apart from expressing our own view that until on the decision of the instant case, which is being delivered by this Bench, and the aforesaid decisions of the High Court Division referred to by the learned advocate for the petitioners, where writ petitions by the government servants on service matters have been held to be maintainable, our Appellate Division lays its hands, it would continue to create a scope for the government servants to circumvent the Administrative Tribunal with a plea that a petition under Article 102 is more efficacious alternative remedy to redress their grievance. It is to  be borne in mind that the argument of efficacious remedy should not be conceded to by this Court for service matters of the government  servants inasmuch as it is not applicable where  the Constitution has made a specific forum for government servants. Administrative Tribunal is not an ordinary forum as has been provided  in other laws of our land, such as, Customs Act,  Income Tax Ordinance, Public University Ordinance/Acts etc where in spite of providing appellate forum, this Court often tends to entertain writ petitions despite not approaching the original forum or preferring the appellate forum as laid down in those Acts/Ordinance, considering the exigencies of the facts of the  cases. However, we hope that in a fit case in an appropriate time, our Appellate Division would give a guideline for dealing with writ cases relating to government servants' service matters inasmuch as there should not be contradictory judicial pronouncements by different Benches of the High Court Division on a single and the same point of law as has been directed by our Appellate Division in the case of Chief Engineer, the Local Government and Engineering Departments vs Kazi Mizanur Rahman reported in 17 BLC (AD) 91 where it has been observed that "There should not be conflicting opinions of different Benches of the High Court Division sitting on coordinate jurisdictions. When there will be different opinions on a particular point, it will be difficult for the executive to follow the directions. Whenever, a Division Bench of the High Court Division is called upon to decide question of law, it becomes its duty to ascertain whether any pronouncement of the High Court Division exists on the point and the best procedure is to follow the said opinion. If it does not accept the decision as correct, it may refer the matter to a Full Bench after formulating the point on which it differs on the point of law. If the facts are distinguishable then it can decide the question of law on the facts of the given case. In these cases we noticed that though their attention was drawn to the earlier pronouncement, each Bench expressed its own opinion ignoring earlier opinions".</u>

83. In the present case, the grievance of the petitioner is with regard to implementation of his promotion and other financial benefit while he was serving the Republic. When the respondents apparently acknowledged that the petitioner deserves some compensation in the form of giving retrospective effect of his seniority and, with that aim, the respondent took some actions in respect of the petitioners claim and, thus, the government was expected to take further step towards arriving at the decision in order to dispose of the petitioner's claim, it was the duty upon the petitioner to make a written representation to the higher authority as per the Proviso under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act and, thereafter, on non-action on the said representation the petitioner could have approached the Tribunal.

84. We hold that by not giving effect to the remedial measure in full, as was proposed by the then learned Attorney-General being approved by the Prime Minister and, later on, again when after few years the petitioner's matter got momentum, and by not taking the required action, the relevant authority, who halted it, might have violated the law but in no way it can be held that the authorities have violated the petitioner's fundamental rights. The allegation as to violation of the petitioner's fundamental right guaranteed under Article 27 of the Constitution for not treating him equally with the other freedom fighter civil servants appears to us to be of bereft any substance in that the background of those civil servants are completely different from that of the petitioner and, thus, the petitioner being not at per with the said civil servants cannot make an allegation of unequal treatment. In dealing with the complaints by the government servants as to their violation of fundamental rights, the High Court Division should bear in the mind the observations made by the Appellate Division in Para 49 of the Mujibur Rahman's case where the High Court Division has been reminded by the Apex Court to be cautious and mindful to entertain a writ petition on service matters on the plea of violation of rights guaranteed under part III of the Constitution and thereby enforcing the same by invoking Article 102(1) of Constitution by desperate litigants or busybodies in the following language "An aggrieved person may, out of desperation or just for taking a sportive chance in the summary writ jurisdiction, allege contravention of some fundamental right which may turn out to be frivolous or vexatious or not even remotely attracted in his case. The Court is, however, to be on guard so the great value of the right given under Article 102(1) is not frittered away or misused as a substitute for more appropriate remedy available for an unlawful action involving no infringement of any fundamental right". We find that the fact of the present case is almost similar to the fact of the case of Government of the Bangladesh vs Md Abdul Halim Miah reported in 9 MLR 2004 (AD) 105 = 9 BLC (AD) 134 where the writ petition was held to be not maintainable.

<u>85. It is relevant and profitable to quote a passage from Para 90 of the landmark case of Mujibur Rahman where their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed that "Administrative Tribunals have been established all over the common law countries to relieve the High Court from the congestion of cases." Thus, in our view, by entertaining writ petitions in respect of government servants' grievance, as is very often done by some Division Benches of the High Court Division, this Court impliedly assumes the functions of the Administrative Tribunal upon gratuitously extending the jurisdiction of the High Court Division. We find that entertainment of these sorts of petitions is causing congestion in this Division, which is already overwhelmingly overburdened with huge backlog of cases.</u>

86. For the reasons recorded hereinbefore, which clearly demonstrate that the facts and circumstance of the case at hand entirely being beyond realm of writ jurisdiction, we are of, the view that the present writ petition is not maintainable.

87. However, in view of our findings that the case of the petitioner appears to be a long history of deprivation and grave injustice by the Government since his return from the UK to Bangladesh after the Liberation War and the petitioner has never been treated by the respondents with the dignity and the honour that he deserves as a Freedom Fighter, particularly when the government has taken a number of initiatives for the betterment and welfare of the freedom fighters including increasing of their service age up to 60 years, making provision of reserved employments for their children, monthly endowments for the unemployed freedom fighters etc., we would expect that the respondents shall dispose off the petitioner's claim at their earliest convenience.

88. Since, we have already hold that the instant writ petition is not maintainable, we refrain from passing any order of direction and leave the matter upon the good conscience of the respondents for their consideration in the back drop of the scenario that the government, who being seemingly sympathetic to the petitioner took all the initiatives for accommodating him with his legitimate entitlements, will not abstain from taking further steps and actions towards arriving at a decision on the petitioner's claim and, particularly, when this Court has hold that it has been a legitimate expectation of the petitioner that the Ministry of Public Administration will make a decision on the petitioner's claim either by its own or by placing it before the Hon'ble Prime Minister.

With the above discussions and observations, the Rule is disposed off without any order as to costs.

End.

Dr Kamal Hossain with Subrata Chowdhuri with Tanzib-ul-Alam with Saikat Acharjee—For the Petitioner. 

ABM Nurul Islam with Giasuddin Ahmed—For Respondent Nos. 1 and 3. 

Zaman Akhter, Assistant Attorney-General—For Respondent No. 2.
