full_judgment:
Md Hamidul Hoque J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why rules 25 and 29 of the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1979 should not be declared to be unconstitutional and void as being violative of the fundamental rights of the petitioner guaranteed under Articles 27, 28, 31 and 38 of the Constitution and why the impugned dismissal order dated 26-2-2002 as contained in Annexure R should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

2. Dr Kamal Hossain, the learned Senior Counsel, appeared on behalf of the petitioner. Mr ABM Nurul Islam was specially appointed by respondent No.1 to represent the same respondent.

3. Dr Kamal Hossain, in support of the Rule, has submitted that the petitioner was a Senior Staff Nurse at Shahid Suhrawardy Hospital, Dhaka. She was placed under suspension by an order issued by respondent No.3 on 7-10-2001 on the allegation that the petitioner in order to create an opinion against the Caretaker Government participated in a meeting on 15-9-2001 in the Audit Bhaban and thereby she violated the provisions of rules 25 and 29 of Government Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1979 and a proceeding was drawn up against her under Rule 11 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985. Dr Kamal Hossain has pointed out that this allegation of participation of the writ petitioner in a meeting held on 15-9-2001 is totally baseless because there was no meeting at all at the Audit Building on that date as alleged in the suspension order. In this connection he has further submitted that a news item was published in the daily আজকের কাগজ on 16-9-2001 wherein it was mentioned that the present petitioner along with some other Government servants participated in that meeting and delivered speech. Dr Kamal Hossain has pointed out that the petitioner sent a rejoinder to the Editor of the said newspaper on 18-9-2001. Then a reply was given to that rejoinder in which it was mentioned that the reporter himself was not present in that meeting and, as such, there might be some confusion or doubt about the names of the persons present in that meeting. Dr Kamal Hossain next submitted that departmental inquiry was held by a Deputy Director of Commercial Audit Directorate and in his report he mentioned that no meeting was held in the Audit Bhaban on 15-9-2001.

4. After referring to all the Annexures, Dr Kamal Hossain submitted that the allegation was about a non-existent fact and, as such, it was malafide from the very beginning Dr Kamal Hossain has also pointed out about some illegalities in the proceeding itself and has submitted that when there was violation of the rules which are apparent from the Annexures the petitioner had no other alternative but to come before this Court invoking its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. He has pointed out that according to the Rules of 1985; the petitioner was not given opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses. He has also pointed out that in the charge which was communicated to the petitioner there is no reference of distribution of any objectionable leaflet by the petitioner whereas in the inquiry report emphasis was given to the fact that the petitioner was involved in distribution of objectionable leaflet. Lastly, Dr Kamal Hossain has submitted that Rule 25 of the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1979 is violative of the fundamental rights as guaranteed under Articles 27, 28, 31 and 38 of the Constitution. In this connection he specially referred to the provision of sub-rule (7) of rule 25 and has argued that this sub-rule has given a sweeping power to the Government to decide whether any movement or activity falls within the scope of this rule. So, according to him at least this sub-rule (7), which is violative of fundamental rights as guaranteed under the Constitution, should be struck down.

5. Mr ABM Nurul Islam, the learned Advocate on behalf of the respondent No. 1 on the other hand, has submitted that the proceeding was drawn up against the petitioner in accordance with the Rules and as the question of disciplinary action against the Government servant is a question relating to his/her condition of service, writ petition cannot be maintained under Article 102 of the Constitution. In fact, Mr Islam confined his argument on the question of maintainability. He has also submitted that when this writ petitioner was first suspended, she also filed a writ petition but the writ petition was summarily rejected on the ground that the matter relates to condition of service. So, according to him, the present writ petition in which the order of dismissal of the petitioner has been challenged, the same is liable to be discharged on the ground that it cannot be maintained. Mr Islam has also pointed out that after filing of the writ petition the writ petitioner, in violation of the rules applicable to the Government servants, approached international bodies and tried to make her suspension and dismissal an issue before International Labour Organisations. In this connection, Mr Islam referred to some of the correspondence made with the international bodies and has submitted that the conduct of the petitioner is malafide and she has not come with clean hands before the Court.

6. In reply, Dr Kamal Hossain by referring to the case of Majibur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh as reported in 44 DLR (AD) 114 and also the case of Shaheda Khatun vs Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka and others as reported in 3 BLC (AD) 155 has submitted that the High Court Division in its writ jurisdiction can decide the question of malafide action on the part of any authority. He has also pointed out that as a vires of rule 25 of the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1979 has been challenged; the Administrative Tribunal has no authority to decide the same. Dr Kamal Hossain also referred to the case of Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh as reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201. As against the submissions of Dr Kamal Hossain, Mr ABM Nurul Islam has submitted that the question of malafide is a question of fact which can be decided by the Administrative Tribunal and, as such, on this ground alone the writ petition cannot be maintained. He has also referred to paragraph 49 of the judgment delivered by the Appellate Division in the case of Majibur Rahman vs Bangladesh as reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111 and has submitted that the petitioner has taken a sportive chance by challenging vires of a rule on the allegation of violation of fundamental rights. In fact, according to him, there was no violation of fundamental rights in the whole process of the dismissal of the petitioner.

7. Mr Zaman Akhter, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, appeared on behalf of the other respondents but has made no separate submissions as Mr ABM Nurul Islam was specially engaged in this matter on behalf of the respondent No. 1.

8. The main contention is, whether a writ petition can be maintained by a Government servant in respect of a matter relating to condition of his service by invoking jurisdiction of this Court as given under Article 102 of the Constitution. The gist of the argument of Mr Islam is that the proper forum to challenge the dismissal order is the Administrative Tribunal. On the other hand, the main argument of Dr Kamal Hossain is that the whole action was malafide and the petitioner was highly prejudiced due to the provision of sub-rule (7) of rule 25 of the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1979 and, as such, the petitioner had to challenge the vires of rule 25.

9. We may mention here that on the question whether a Government servant can come before this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution in respect of any matter relating to his service, the Appellate Division has given several decisions. The gist of the decision of the Appellate Division on this question has been summed up in the case of Delwar Hosain vs Bangladesh as reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120. In this case the paragraph 8 of the judgment may be quoted below.

The question is no longer res integra. It has been answered by this Court in Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 111 in the following terms. Within its jurisdiction the Tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution or of any other law. in respect of matters relating to or arising out of sub-clause (a) but such tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1987 (SC) 385 (Para 16) and JB Chopra vs Union of India AIR 1987 (SC) 357 (Para-2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1) but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 177(2), we find no reason to revise our earlier view. That averments of the writ petitioners' grievance is that by the impugned order of promotion their seniority has been affected. Seniority and promotion of civil servants being the terms and conditions of service the Administrative Tribunal is possessed of the exclusive jurisdiction to hear the dispute in such matters,"

10. On perusal of this decision it is clear ‘o us that a person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental rights for challenging the vires of law may seek his remedy under Article 102 and in all other matters he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117. It appears to us that the question whether an action which is challenged on the ground of malice in law can be decided by this Court under Article 102 has not been decided in this judgment. On this point, we may refer to another judgment of the Appellate Division as reported in 3 BLC (AD) 155. In this case the Appellate Division laid down the principle that notwithstanding the ouster of jurisdiction of the High Court Division by any legislative provision or even under Article 102 itself, the High Court Division is yet entitled to exercise its power of judicial review under that Article if the action complained of before the High Court Division is found to be coram non-judice without jurisdiction or taken malafide. We may also mention here that a Division Bench of this Court by its judgment delivered on 31-10-2001 in Writ Petition No. 2529 of 2001 made a Rule absolute in a case filed by the petitioner challenging order of compulsory retirement. In that judgment, one of us was a party and in that case the Division Bench mainly relied on the above decision of the Appellate Division as reported in 3 BLC (AD) 155.

11. In the instant case before us the petitioner challenged the vires of a Rule and also challenged the action on the ground that it was malafide. Dr Kamal Hossain by referring to the case of Dr Nurul Islam has submitted that malice in law means doing of a wrongful act intentionally without just cause or excuse. In this connection he referred to paragraph 107 of the judgment.

12. Dr Kamal Hossain has elaborated in his submission how the action was malafide. In this connection, he referred to the inquiry reports of the concerned departments and also to the reply of the newspaper editor about the allegation of the participation of the petitioner in a meeting held on 15-9-2001 in the Audit Bhaban. He has argued that knowing fully well that no meeting was held at all, the authority started the proceeding and without any evidence ultimately found her guilty and dismissed her from service. So, according to him the whole process was malafide and there was colourable exercise of power by the authority who initiated the proceeding and passed the order of dismissal.

13. Now, let us consider the submission made by Dr Kamal Hossain. We shall first consider whether rule 25, specially its sub-rule (7), of the 1979 Rules is violative of fundamental rights as guaranteed under Articles 27, 28, 31 and 38 of the Constitution. To decide this question the entire Rule is reproduced below:

"Taking part in politics and elections (I) No Government servant shall take part in, subscribe in aid of or assist in any way, any political movement in Bangladesh or relating to the affairs of Bangladesh.

(2) No Government servant shall permit any person dependent on him for maintenance or under his care or control to take part in or in any way assist, any movement or activity which is, or tends directly or indirectly to be subversive of Government as by law established in Bangladesh.

(3) No Government servant shall canvass or otherwise interfere or use his influence in connection with or take part in any election to a legislative body, whether in Bangladesh or elsewhere.

Provided that a Government servant who is qualified to vote at such election may exercise his right to vote, but if he does so, he shall give no indication of the manner in which he proposes to vote or has voted.

(4) No Government servant shall permit any member of his family dependent on him to act in a manner in which he himself is not permitted by sub-rule (30) to act.

(5) A Government servant who issues an address to electors or in any other manner publicly announces himself or allows himself to be publicly announced as a candidate or prospective candidate for election to a legislative body shall be deemed for the purpose of sub-rule (3) to take part in an election to such body.

(6) The provision of sub-rules (3) and (5) shall, so far as may be, apply to election to local authorities or bodies, save in respect of Government servants required or permitted by or under any law, or order of the Government, for the time being in force, to be candidate at such elections.

(7) If any question arises whether any movement or activity falls within the scope of this rule, the decision of the Government thereon shall be final."

14. Dr Kamal Hossain has pointed out that sub-rules (1) and (7) are definitely violative of the fundamental rights as guaranteed under Articles 27, 28, 31 and 38 of the Constitution because sweeping power has been given to the authority to decide whether any movement or activities falls within scope of the rule. In this connection, Dr Kamal Hossain again reiterated about the principle laid down in the Nurul Islam's case and also referred to the case as reported in 44 DLR where similar question of absence of any guideline was considered by the High Court Division and then by the Appellate Division. Mr ABM Nurul Islam has taken an objection on the ground that the rules of 1979 are by now 23 years old and by this time many actions were taken under these Rules by the Government and there is no scope of challenging the vires of the Rules at this stage. We cannot agree with the submission of Mr. Islam. Any person may come before this Court by way of challenging the vires of the above Rules at any time; no time limit can be fixed for challenging the vires.

15. Now, it appears to us that the Rules of 1979 cannot be interpreted independently or separately, these should be read together with the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 because any proceeding which is drawn up against a Government servant is drawn up under Rules of 1985. A Government servant may be proceeded with on any of the grounds as mentioned in rule 6 of the Rules of 1985. One of the grounds on which a Government servant may be proceeded with is the ground of misconduct. The present writ petition was also proceeded with on the ground of misconduct. This "misconduct" is defined in section 2(f) of the Rules of 1985 which is quoted below:

"(f) Misconduct means conduct prejudicial to good order or service discipline or contrary to any provision of the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1979 or unbecoming of an officer or gentleman and includes—

(i) disobedience to lawful orders of superior officers;

(ii) gross negligence of duty;

(iii) flouting of Government Orders, circulars and directives without any lawful cause, and

(iv) submission of petitions before any authority containing wild, vexatious, false or frivolous accusation against a Government servant."

From this definition we find that misconduct means conduct prejudicial to good order or service discipline or contrary to any provision of the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules, 1979. So, if any Government servant acts contrary to the provision of any rule of 1979 Rules that will amount to misconduct and he may be proceeded with in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Rules of 1985.

16. Now, in rules 6 and 7 of the Rules of 1985 detailed procedure has been laid down as to how the Government servant is to be proceeded with if he is accused of committing any misconduct. Next, rule 10 provides how inquiry is to be held and in this rule it has been clearly provided that the allegation has to be proved by adducing both oral and documentary evidence, the accused shall be entitled to cross-examine the witnesses against him and the accused shall also be entitled to adduce evidence in support of his case. So, there is no scope of taking disciplinary action under the Rules of 1985 against any Government servant without giving him the above opportunity. In view of the legal position, it appears to us that whatever sweeping power has been given to the Government under rule 25(7) of the 1979 Rules that power has been limited by bringing the violation of any those rules within definition of misconduct in the Rules of 1985 and by giving full opportunity to the accused to represent his case or defend himself by way of furnishing reply and cross-examining the witnesses. We like to make it clear that independently under the Rules of 1979; no action can be taken against any Government servant because there is no scope of taking action against a Government servant without following the provisions of Rules of 1985. We are of the view that the provisions of the Rules of 1979 though may appear at the first reading to be violative of fundamental rights but when it is considered that no action can be taken under these Rules without following the procedure laid down in the Rules of 1985 and the procedure laid down there has secured the rights of the Government servants on final analysis, it cannot be said that the Rules of 1979 are violative of the fundamental rights. So, we cannot accept the argument of Dr Kamal Hossain that rule 25(7) is ultra vires of the Constitution on the ground of its being violative of fundamental rights.

17. So, after our discussion as made above the only question left is whether the action taken was malafide or there was any malice in law. We have carefully gone through paragraph 107 of Dr Nurul Islam's case as reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201. In that paragraph the Appellate Division has made it clear as to what should be considered as malice in law. The quotation included in that paragraph is also very important. It has been observed that a person who inflicts an injury upon another person in contravention of the law is not allowed to say that he did it with an innocent mind. He is taken to know the law and must act within the law. He may, therefore, be guilty of malice in law although, so far as state of his mind is concerned, he acts ignorantly, and, in that sense, innocently. ABM Nurul Islam also referred to the case of Smt. SR Venkataraman vs Union of India and another as reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 49 to impress upon us that the allegation of malafide is to be proved but in above case we find that the Court has observed that the malice in its sense means malice such as may be assumed from the doing of a wrongful act intentionally but with just cause or excuse or for want of reasonable or probable cause. So, we find that when an injury upon a person is caused in contravention of the law that will amount to malice in law. Now, let us see whether there is any malice in law in the instant case before us.

18. We have already noticed that the proceeding was drawn up against the petitioner under the Rules of 1985. This is also evident from the charge Annexure-E which was brought against the petitioner. Under the heading "subject", it is clearly mentioned that it was the charge framed under Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985. In the last paragraph it is also mentioned that the petitioner was accused of misconduct under rule 3(b) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985. When the proceeding is drawn up against a Government servant under provisions of those Rules the proceeding must be concluded also in accordance with the provisions of those Rules. Now, from the inquiry report of the Inquiry Officer which we have found at Annexure O at pages 89, 90 and 91, it appears that the Inquiry Officer believed the allegation of attending in the meeting by the petitioner on the basis of the report published in the daily আজকের কাগজ on 16-9-2001. The Inquiry Officer considered the report as the basis of starting the inquiry. We also find in her report that some Senior Staff Nurses and one Supervisor expressed their willingness to depose before her and thereafter she (the Inquiry Officer) issued notice upon those witnesses to appear before her and to depose in the proceeding and accordingly, the Inquiry Officer admitted their statement in evidence. So, it is clear from the inquiry report itself that the Inquiry Officer allowed some persons to give evidence in the case who volunteered themselves to be the witnesses. This is not the law. As to how the inquiry is to be held Rules of 1985 are very much clear and the procedure has been laid down in rule 10. The entire rule 10 is reproduced below:

"Procedure to be followed by Inquiry Officer (1) The Inquiry Officer shall hear the case from day to day and no adjournment shall be given except for reasons to be recorded in writing.

(2) In an inquiry conducted under this rule the Inquiry Officer shall hold an inquiry at which oral evidence shall be heard and recorded as to such of the allegations as are not admitted and documentary evidence relevant or material in regard to the charge shall be considered. The accused shall be entitled to cross examine the witnesses against him to give evidence in person and to have such witness called for the defence as he may wish. The person presenting the case in support of the charge shall be entitled to cross-examine the accused and the witnesses examined in his defence. The accused may also consult relevant file,, but he shall not have access k he note portion of the files.

Provided that the Inquiry Officer may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, refuse to call for a particular witness or to summon or admit a particular evidence.

(3) In an inquiry under this rule, the accused may, if he so desires, adduce oral evidence in his defence which shall be subject to such cross-examination as may be necessary.

(4) The authority may nominate any person to present the case in support of the charge before the Inquiry Officer. (5) If the Inquiry Officer is satisfied that the accused is hampering or attempting to hamper the progress of the inquiry, he shall administer a warning and if thereafter he is satisfied that the accused is acting in disregard of the warning, he shall record a finding to that effect, and proceed to complete the inquiry in such manner as he thinks best fitted to do substantial justice.

(6) If the Inquiry Officer is satisfied that the conduct of the accused amounts to contempt of his office, he shall record the relevant facts and circumstances relating to such contempt and inform the authority on the matter, whereupon the authority may, if it deems fit, proceed against the accused separately under rule 3(b).

(7) The Inquiry Officer shall, within seven working days of the conclusion of the proceedings, submit his findings and the grounds therefore to the authority.

(8) The Inquiry Officer shall give his findings stating whether the accused is guilty or not guilty on each charge and he shall not give any recommendation regarding punishment or otherwise.

(9) The authority may, in any case it deems fit, instead of appointing an Inquiry Officer under these rules, appoint a Board of Inquiry consisting of three persons, and where a Board of Inquiry is appointed references in this rule to an Inquiry Officer shall be construed as reference to the Board.

(10) No proceedings or decision of a Board appointed under sub-rule (9) shall be invalid or be called in question merely on the ground of absence of any member thereof in any sitting of the Board."

<u>19. From sub-rule (2) we find that the Inquiry Officer shall hold an inquiry at which oral evidence shall be heard and recorded and the accused shall be entitled to cross-examine the witnesses against him and to give evidence in person and he may also call such witnesses as he may wish. It further appears from sub-rule (2) that the prosecution is required to nominate a person of the department concerned to present the case and this has been made clear in sub-rule (4) wherein it is provided that the authority may nominate any person to present the case before the Inquiry Officer in support of the charge. So, from these provisions it is quite clear that the nominated officer while presenting the case will produce the witnesses and those witnesses shall be examined in presence of the accused and the accused should be entitled to cross-examine those witnesses. The Inquiry Officer, in the present case, entirely violated all the provisions. We have noticed in Dr Nurul Islam's case that even the ignorance of law will not make the action as lawful. Moreover, we cannot believe that a person who has been appointed as Inquiry Officer is not aware of the provisions as laid down in rule 10. It is clear from the report that the petitioner was found guilty on the basis of statement of some persons who volunteered themselves to be the witnesses. This shows clearly that the Inquiry Officer did not follow the procedure as laid down in rule 10. So, the action of the Inquiry Officer can definitely be considered as malice in law. When the law itself provides that an opportunity be given to the accused to cross-examine the witnesses, then no witnesses can be examined behind the back of the accused without giving him or her such an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses. In this connection Dr Kamal Hossain referred to a case reported in 32 DLR (AD) 46. In this case also it has been clearly observed by their Lordships that witnesses who are examined in a departmental proceeding should be examined in presence of the delinquent employee after giving him an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses. So, we have no doubt that the present case is a case in which we can say that there is malice in law.</u>

<u>20. Mr ABM Nurul Islam has argued that the questions raised in this writ petition are question of fact which can be decided by the Administrative Tribunal where there is a scope of adducing evidence by both the parties. Mr. Islam is correct to some extent. The question of malafide becomes a question of fact when one party alleges it and the other party denies it. In the instant case, the question raised is that, the action taken is malafide because it was taken deliberately in contravention of law. When such allegation is made, this Court in exercise of its power of judicial review is empowered to decide such a question. Moreover, in the instant case, vires of a rule is also challenged which cannot be decided by the Administrative Tribunal.</u>

21. Next question raised by Mr Nurul Islam is that the petitioner did not exhaust. the forum which is provided in the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985. In this connection, he referred to rule 17 of the above Rules and has submitted that the petitioner ought to have preferred an appeal against the order of dismissal. Dr Kamal Hossain has submitted that as the proceeding was initiated due to the order of the secretary, respondent No. 1 and as the appeal is to be filed before him, the petitioner did not expect any relief from him and in this regard Dr Kamal Hossain has also submitted that when action is malafide the party may come before this Court without availing the forum of appeal.

<u>22. It is true that there is provision of appeal in rule 17 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985. In some cases, our Appellate Division has given decision to the effect that even where appeal lies, the High Court Division may look into the legality of a decision and if it is found that the decision was taken on no evidence the High Court may declare the same to have been taken without any lawful authority. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Tazul Islam reported in 49 DLR (AD) 177, the Appellate Division has observed that the writ Court will not examine and weigh the aggrieved persons' case on merit as an Appellate Court but the High Court Division has power to see whether the person has been given a fair deal by the authority in accordance with law. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Jalil as reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10, the Appellate Division has observed that the High Court Division was not a Court of appeal required to make determination of facts on its own, it could interfere with the findings of a Tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 only if it could be shown that the Tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence. In the case before us, the Inquiry Officer arrived at a finding of guilty on the basis of no evidence. The word "evidence" implies only legal evidence. We have found from the report of the Inquiry Officer that there was no legal evidence before her. The statement of the witnesses before the Inquiry Officer are not the evidence according to law. So, the decision of the Inquiry Officer was given on no evidence. In view of this position, this Court, in exercise of its power of judicial review, can see whether the decision of the Inquiry Officer was in accordance with law and we have found that it was not in accordance with law because the proceeding was conducted in violation of the provisions of rule 10 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985. For the reason stated above, the present writ petition can be maintained though the petitioner did not prefer any appeal.</u>

23. Mr ABM Nurul Islam has also argued that this Court is not competent to give a finding as to whether a meeting was held on 15-9-2001 in the Audit Bhaban and whether the petitioner participated in that meeting or not. We agree that this Court is not competent to give any finding as to whether the petitioner participated in the meeting or not or whether the meeting was held or not but the Court is competent to see whether the proceeding was conducted in accordance with law or not and we have exactly done the same, we have not given any finding on the question whether any meeting was held in the Audit Bhaban and whether the petitioner participated in, meeting.

24. Mr Nurul Islam has also pointed out even after filing of the writ petition, the petitioner moved some international bodies for getting relief and it is malafide. Mr Islam, in this connection, referred to Annexures 4, 5 and 6 of the affidavit-in-opposition. However, Dr Kamal Hossain submits that this was not done by the petitioner herself but by an organisation namely, Bangladesh Diploma Nurses Association. We find from the writ petition that the petitioner was also connected with that Association. We disapprove such venture of approaching any international body to vindicate any cause without waiting for relief which may be obtained in the country. When the writ petition was filed there was no reason to approach any international body. The petitioner being a member of that Association should have prevailed upon her colleagues not to make such venture. However, we do not think that this conduct of the petitioner can be considered as a reason for discharging the Rule.

<u>25. Lastly, we may refer to another argument of Mr ABM Nurul Islam. He has submitted that when the petitioner filed a writ petition against her order of suspension the smile was summarily rejected by a Division Bench in which one of us was a party. We have been taken through the judgment of that writ petition. We have perused the judgment. The earlier writ petition was filed against the order of suspension. Suspension is not considered as punishment. Moreover, at that time the Court found no illegality in the order of suspension and considered the same to be a matter within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal. Now, In the present writ petition, the petitioner challenged the order of dismissal on several grounds such as malice in law, constitutionality of one of the rules under which action was taken and we have found that there was malice in law and this is one of the circumstances under which jurisdiction under Article 102 can be invoked. We may mention here that when the question of malafide is alleged with reference to the conduct and grudge of the authority concerned it may become a question of fact which may not be decided under Article 102 but when there is allegation of malice in law that can be decided and considered by this Court in a summary proceeding under Article 102. So, every writ petition with an allegation of malafide may not give jurisdiction to this Court if that allegation is required to be decided on the basis of evidence and, in such a case, the proper forum will be Administrative Tribunal but if the allegation is only about malice in law and if such allegation can be decided without deciding any disputed question of fact, and if it is apparent from the action itself that there is malice in law, then this Court definitely can assure jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

26. In view of our above discussion, we are of the view that the present writ petition is maintainable. We have found that there is malice in law and, as such, the Rule is liable to be made absolute.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned order of dismissed of the petitioner (Annexure-R) is declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam J: At the instance of the petitioners Nazma Sarwar and others, this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 15-5-2008 passed in Special Case No. 11 of 2008 (arising out of Gulshan PS Case No. 26 (1)08 by the Special Judge, Court No. 7, Dhaka should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

2. None appeared for the petitioner when the matter was taken up for hearing. Mr Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned counsel for the respondent No. 3, the Anti-Corruption Commission, however, submits that the petitioner in the instant writ petition did not surrender before the trial Court and he is a fugitive from justice. The learned Advocate submits that the Rule is not maintainable. In support of his contention he referred to the decision of the Anti-Corruption Commission vs Md Hossain 61 DLR (AD) 17, Anti-Corruption Commission vs Dr HBM Alamgir 1998 BLT (AD) 266 and vis-a-vis 15 BLC (AD) 44 and also an unreported decision of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 411 of 2009 judgment delivered on 14-3-2010.

3. Since the petitioner is not represented we do not propose to go into the merit of the case. We have gleaned the entire situation and it appears that the petitioner did not surrender before the appropriate Court and he is a fugitive from justice. In this regard it would be profitable to quote from 61 DLR as referred to above, where it was held: 

"Cardinal principle of the Criminal jurisdiction is that the person concerned should submit to the process of justice before he can claim the right of audience provided in law as well as judicial convention which is very much effective in the Court of law. Enunciating the age-old maxim that a man who seeks justice from the Court of law must come before the Court to agitate his grievance and must surrender first to the process of justice, otherwise he remain to be fugitive from justice and could not seek aid or assistance of the process of justice in girder to claim right of audience against the process of Court issued against him" 

4. Reflection of this principle has been echoed in all other decisions as referred to above.

 5. In ACC vs HBM Iqbal 15 BLC (AD) 44 Justice SK Sinha observed:  

"Admittedly the writ petitioner was a fugitive from justice on the date he moved the writ petition. He was away from the country and craved permission of the Court to affirm affidavit on his behalf by one HBM Shoave Rahman. The permission was given and the learned Judges issued Rule Nisi as above. It is now settled that a fugitive from Justice is not entitled to obtain a judicial order defying the process of the Court. Besides, the learned Advocates who move applications for the fugitives shall also have to face the consequence of committing contempt of Court.  This principle is being followed for over 60  years in this sub-continent:  References in this connection are Chand Shah vs Crown, 8 DLR (FC) 24, Gul Hasan vs State reported in 21 DLR (SC) 109, ACC vs Mahmud Hasan 61 DLR (AD) 17" (underlined by us) 

6. In Civil Petition for leave to appeal No 411 of 2009 relying on the decision of 15 BLC (AD) referred to above the Appellate Division reiterated the same principle.

 7. In a subsequent judgment of the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 22 of 2010 it was held as follows: 

"It is well settled that when a person seeks remedy from a Court of law, either in writ jurisdictions or Criminal appellate, revisional or miscellaneous jurisdiction under section 561A, of the Code of Criminal Procedure he ought to submit to the due process of justice. Let it be made clear to him, if it is not already known that the Court would not act in aid of an accused person who is a fugitive from law and justice" 

8. The principle of criminal jurisprudence is that the person 'concerned should submit to the process of justice before he can claim the right of audience provided in law as well as the judicial convention, which is Very much effective in the Court of law as the age Old maxim goes person Who seeks justice froth the Court of the law must come before the Court to agitate his grievance and  must surrender first to the process of justice, otherwise, he remains to be fugitive 'froth justice and could not seek aid or assistance Of the process 'of justice order to claim right of audience against the process of the Court issued against him them. In this case the petitioners have been convicted in absentia and warrant for the execution of sentence under section 389 of the Code of Criminal Procedure hanging upon them arid, as such, the petitioners have .no. locus: standi to file the instant writ petition. This view is the age-old judicial norm and convention :in our Court from the time immemorial and this view finds support in the decision in the case of Chand Shah vs Crown reported in PLD 1956 FC 43 = 8 DLR (FC) 24. 

9. In the case of Gul Hassan vs State reported. in 21-DLR (SC) 109 it has been held that Lawyers grave responsibility: involving contempt of Court in appearing: for fugitive convict., Attorneys and members of the' Bar mind the serious consequence of committing contempt of Court in moving on behalf of A prisoner who is a fugitive from law. The appeal filed by the counsel on the basis of the power of attorney executed by Gul Hassan in favour of Khawaja Mohammad Khan before his absconsion was thus not properly constituted and had been dismissed by the High Court on that ground alone. 

10. When an accused had been convicted of an offence he or she immediately becomes wanted by that Court in order to give effect to the order of the Court. His or her appearance is ensured by means of a warrant if necessary. If he does not surrender to the process nor his arrest is secured, then the execution of the order of the conviction and sentence in dispensation of justice is defeated. He remains a fugitive from justice. In the case of Chand Shah vs Crown reported in 8 DLR (FC) 24 it has been held that it was an essential condition of an administration of Justice, in a case affecting an individual or individuals, that the persons concerned should submit to the due process of jus-tice. It has been further held in the Chand Shah's case that the Attorney-General who appeared to secure the interference of the Court on behalf of fugitives, without ensuring that such persons conform to the judicial orders applicable to them, was not acting in accordance with his proper duty to acting in furtherance of justice. 

11. In the instant case the petitioners were fugitive from justice when they moved the writ petition and obtained the Rule Nisi. In view of the above, at the time of 'motion' hearing this Division wrongly entertained the writ petition and stayed judgment and order of conviction and sentences passed against the writ petitioners. 

12. Now, it has been reaffirmed by our Appellate Division in a series of cases that convicted persons were required to appear before the Court passing the order of conviction and sentences against them to enable that Court to give effect to its judgment and order. In view of 
the discussions made above we are of the view that a fugitive has no right to seek any kind of redress as against grievances, if any, against the judgment and order of a Court convicting his/her to imprisonment. 

13. Fortified with all these decisions as dis-cussed above we hold that the instant writ petition is not maintainable and accordingly the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. 

14. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated. 

Let a copy of this judgment be transmitted to the Court concerned at once. 

End.

 Vs

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 23-8-1994 passed by the 2nd Court of the Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Rajbari dismissing Title Appeal No. 14 of 1992 upon affirming the judgment and decree dated 5-1-1992 passed by the Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Rajbari decreeing Title Suit No. 674 of 1985 should not be set aside or such other or further Order or Orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 674 of 1985 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Rajbari impleading the present petitioner as defendant and opposite party Nos. 2-11 as proforma defendants praying for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit land, as described in the schedule to the plaint, alleging, inter alia that the suit land belonged to Dharani Dhar Sarkar and was accordingly recorded in the RS khatian in the name of the said Dharani Dhar Sarkar who while in possession granted settlement of the suit land appertaining to RS khatian No. 302 and 303 on the basis of rent receipt dated 28th of Chaitra 1358 BS and 10th of Ashwin 1360 BS to one Matiur Ralunan and put him in possession on receipt of rent from him and that the said Matiur claimed title and possession in the suit land on the basis of the settlement and subsequently transferred the suit land to one Mafizuddin Mistry by a registered kabala dated 23-12-1966 and the said Mafizuddin recorded his name in Mutation Case No. 1618 of 1966-1967 and paid rent to the Government and while in possession the said Mafizuddin Mistry transferred the suit land to the plaintiff by a registered kabala dated 3-1-1978 and put the plaintiff in possession of the suit land. The plaintiff also mutated his name in the government Tahsil office and has been paying taxes to the government and the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land. The principal defendants have no right, title or possession in the suit land but in the last part of 1391 BS the principal defendants made a false claim as regards title to the suit land and the plaintiff on an enquiry came to learnt that the SA record of the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of Dharani Dhar Sarkar which has cast a cloud on the plaintiff's title and hence the suit.

3. The principal defendants contested the suit by filing a Written statement contending that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was owner in possession of the suit land and that he died leaving behind 2 sons in Kanti Ram Sarkar and Dhirendra Nath Sarkar and that Dharani Nath Sarkar himself used to cultivate the suit land in khas and after his death, his sons were in possession of the suit land by cultivating the suit land themselves by their own plough and while in such possession Kanti Ram Sarkar and Dhirendra Nath Sarkar sold 40 decimals of Kha schedule land to defendant No. 1 by the registered kabala dated 13-11-1972 and out him in possession and that Dhirendra Nath Sarkar who was in possession, transferred his 8 annas share in Ka schedule land by registered deed in favour of Harmuza Bibi who is proforma defendant No. 6 and Mallika Bibi, who is defendant No. 7 and put them in possession. Kanti Ram Sarkar also transferred his 8 annas share in the Ka schedule land by registered sale deed dated 20-7-1974 to one Hazrat Ali and Shajahan and put them in possession. The contesting defendants alleged that the plaintiffs alleged case of settlement granted by Dharani Dhar Sarkar in favour of Matiur Rahman was false, frivolous and collusive and that the owner Dharani Dhar Sarkar never granted any settlement of the suit land and that he died leaving behind his 2 sons, who sold the suit land to the defendants and the plaintiff by creating false documents instituted the suit and prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. The trial Court framed necessary issues and on consideration of the evidence on record came to the finding that the plaintiff has succeeded in providing the case of settlement by Dharani Dhar Sarkar to Matiur Rahman by the rent receipts and that the plaintiffs also proved the transfer made by Matiur Rahman by a registered kabala dated 23-12-1966 to Mofizuddin and that the subsequent transfer made by Mafizuddin in favour of the plaintiff by a registered kabala on 3-1-1978. The trial Court therefore, concluded that the plaintiff acquired title to the suit land. The trial Court then considered the evidence of PWs and DWs and came to the conclusion that the plaintiff has proved his possession in the suit land. Accordingly, by judgment and decree dated 5-1-1992 the learned Assistant Judge decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff.

5. The contesting defendants then prefer-red Title Appeal No. 14 of 1992 before the learned District Judge, Rajbari. The learned Subordinate Judge, (now Joint District) First Court, Rajbari who heard the said Appeal concurred with the trial Court that the plaintiff has proved his title and also his possession in the suit land and the defendants failed to prove their title and also their possession in the suit land. Accordingly, by judgment and decree dated 23-8-1994 the learned Joint District judge dismissed the Appeal and affirmed the decision of the trial Court.

6. Being aggrieved thereby the contesting defendants as petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present rule.

7. Mr A Wahab, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has taken me through the impugned judgments of the Courts below and submits that the Courts below committed error of law in failing to consider that the plaintiff neither in his plaint nor in his evidence asserted whether Dharani Dhar Sarkar was a superior landlord or a Zamindar or Talukder or he had any right to settle the suit land as pattandar as alleged in the plaint and that the alleged story of settlement could not be proved by the plaintiff by producing cogent evidence and thereby the plaintiff did not acquire any title by his purchase from Mafizuddin who did not acquire any title by his purchase from Matiur Rahman and Matiur Rahman did not acquire any title on the basis of settlement from Dharani Dhar Sarkar. The learned Advocate also submits that the Courts below committed a gross error of law in failing to consider that the alleged Dakhilas were not properly proved by the scribe or by any attesting witnesses or by any employee of the executants of the Dakhilas and the Dakhilas not having been proved are not admissible in evidence and the said Matiur Rahman did not acquire any title on the basis of the said Dakhilas. In support of his submission of his submission the learned Advocate for the petitioners Mr A Wahab has relied on a decision in the case of Kalimuddin Sarder vs Assistant Custodian, Energy property, reported in 35 DLR 129. The learned Advocate has also relied on a decision in the case of Sree Birendra Nath Singh vs Md Mokbul Shah, reported in 43 DLR 77. Mr A Wahab further submits that decision of the Courts below with regard to plaintiff's possession is beyond the pleadings of the parties and the evidence of PW 1 and also PW 2 and 3 and, as such, the decree passed in the suit is not sustainable. The learned Advocate for the petitioners further submits that the Courts below committed a gross error of law in failing to correctly read the pleadings of the parties and the evidence, both oral and documentary and arrived at an erroneous conclusion which has resulted in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.

8. Mr Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, supports the decision of the Courts below and submits that the brother of the scribe proved the Dakhilas as the scribe was then dead at the time of deposition and both the Courts have concurrently held that the Dakhilas granted by 'Dharani Dhar Sarkar in favour of Matiur Rahman was genuine Dakhilas and Matiur Rahman got possession of the suit land from Dharani Dhar Sarkar and thereby became a raiyat in suit land and subsequently while in possession transferred the suit land to the plaintiff's vendor Mafizuddin Mridha and subsequently plaintiff acquired title on the basis of a registered kabala from Mafizuddin Mridha and also got possession as proved by all the PWs and found by both the Courts on consideration of the evidence on record. Mr Bhuiyan submits that the findings of the Courts below being concurrent and being based on consideration of evidence may not be disturbed by this division in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction.

<u>9. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the impugned judgments and all other evidence on record. The trail Court and the lower appellate Court found that admittedly the suit land belonged to Dharani Dhar Sarkar. The DW 1 also admitted in his evidence that the suit land belonged to Dharani Dhar Sarkar. The plaintiff has produced Dakhilas exhibit 4, 4 Ka and 4 Kha which was proved by PW 5 Biswanath Sen, who is a brother of scribe of the Dakhilas and this PW 5 deposed that he knows the signature of his brother and his brother wrote the Dakhilas. Both the Courts below considered this aspect of the evidence and accepted the plaintiff's case that Dharani Dhar Sarkar being the admitted owner in possession of the suit land granted settlement of the suit land in favour of Matiur Rahman. This finding of fact of the Courts below being concurrent, I do not find any reason to disagree with the said concurrent finding of fact. The submission that the Dakhilas are not genuine documents could not be substantiated by the contesting defendants by producing any evidence, mere saying that the Dakhilas are not genuine is not sufficient to prove that the Dakhilas are forged. When the defendants alleged that the Dakhilas are not genuine documents, the onus shifted on the defendants to prove the plea that the Dakhilas are not genuine documents and this onus could not be discharged by the contesting defendants. I therefore accept the concurrent finding of the Courts blow that by the Dakhilas Exhibit 4 series Matiur Rahman acquired title on the basis of settlement from admitted owner Dharani Dhar Sarkar and that the said settlement holder transferred the suit land by a registered kabala in favour of Mafizuddin Mridha on 23-12-1966. Since the contesting defendants did not challenge the title and possession of Dharani Dhar Sarkar, I do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners that there is no evidence that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was the landlord or Talukder or pattandar of the suit land inasmuch as the contesting defend-ants having admitted title of Dharani Dhar Sarkar could not raise the plea that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was not the owner of the suit land and unless the ownership of Dharani Dhar Sarkar is not disputed or challenged rather admitted by the contesting defendant such plea is not acceptable. The RS khatian shows that the suit land was recorded in the name of Dharani Dhar Sarkar. This RS khatian has not been challenged or disputed by the contesting defendants. In that view of the matter, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the plaintiff could not prove that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was the Jaminder or Talukder or pattander of the suit land is of no substance. The decision reported 35 DLR 129 has no application in the facts of the case before us. In the said decision a single Bench took the view that the plaintiff in Order to prove the settlement must prove the dakhilas by its scribe or by the executants or by the attesting witnesses. In the present case the dakhilas Exhibit 4 series have been proved by the brother of the scribe and both the Courts have accepted dakhilas as genuine documents. The contesting defendants could not produce any evidence disproving the dakhilas Exhibit 4 series and thus the said decision report in 35 DLR 129 has no application in the facts of the case. The learned Advocate has than relied on another decision reported in 43 DLR 77. In the said decision the learned Single Judge construed the provision of Order VII, rule 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure and held "The policy underlying the Order is to exclude evidence the existence of which at the date of the suit is doubtful and as to the genuine of which suspicion may arise because it was produced at the late stage. The sub-ordinate judge exercised his discretion on sound judicial principle in refusing to admit the Kabuliyat at the late stage of the suit". This is again not the case here in the present matter. Both the Court's have considered Exhibit 4 series and the evidence of PW 5 and concluded that by Exhibit 4 series the admitted owner Dharani Dhar Sarkar granted settlement of the suit land in favour of Matiur Rahman in 1358 and 1360 BS respectively. This Exhibit 4 series were proved by PW 5 Bishwanath Sen who is the brother of scribe of the dakhila as the scribe was then dead. The learned Advocate for the petitioner then relied on a decision in the case of Md Naimuddin Sarkar Q Naimuddin Sarkar vs Md Abdul Kalam Biswas Basiruddin Abul Kalam Azad reported in 39 DLR (AD) 237.1 have perused the said decision and it appears that the said decision relates to Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore not applicable in the present case which is one under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. But then the principle enunciated in the said decision is very much applicable as it held "Plaintiff in Order to succeed must establish his own case to obtain a decree and weakness of defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff." This proposition of law is established since long over a decade and is applicable in most of the civil litigation where the Courts are already taking the view that the plaintiff must prove his own case to get a decree and cannot rely on the weakness of the defence case. In the present case, both the Courts have concurrently held that the plaintiff has proved his case of title and possession and accordingly both the Courts have concurrently granted a decree in favour of the plaintiff. I do not, therefore, find that the decision referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioners has any application in the facts of the case before us. The learned Advocate for the petitioner then relied on a decision in the case of Sultanuddin Chowdhury vs Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, reported in 32 DLR 252. In the said decision a Division Bench took the view "The records of rights of Government which is best evidence of possession at the time when such. This is a well-established principle of law. A registered kabala is an evidence of title which will prevail over the other records of rights as such until and unless such kabala is cancelled on a specific allegation of fraud by any Civil Court in an appropriate Civil suit." In the said decision their lordships also held that a Kabala executed and registered in Bangladesh in 1975 carries a presumption that the executants was a citizen of Bangladesh as no Indian national could transfer any property in Bangladesh by way of registered deed. This decision is also of no help to the learned Advocate for the petitioner but it helps the learned Advocate for the opposite party as the record of right being RS khatian stands recorded in the name of the admitted owner Dharani Dhar Sarkar and this may be treated as a piece of evidence that Dharani Dhar Sarkar was in possession of the suit land when the RS record was prepared. Both the Courts have found that the plaintiffs succeeded in proving his possession in the suit land and that the contesting defendants could not prove their possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate then relied on a decision in the case of Md Naimuddin Sardar alias Naim-uddin Sardar vs Md Abdul Kalam Biswas alias Md Abul Kalam Nasiruddin alias Abul Kalam Azad, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 3. The Appellate Division in the said decision construed the provision of section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the power of the High Court Division in interfering with a finding of fact of the Courts below. This decision is also not applicable in the facts of the case before us. The learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr A Wahab lastly relied on a decision in the case of Abdur Rahim Chowkider Abdur Rahman Sheikh since deceased vs Raji Haider, reported in 58 DLR 470. A Single Bench took the view "Finding on possession, concurrent by the Courts below being not passed on the evidence, oral and documentary and law cannot be binding in revision." The proposition of law is not disputed. The facts are distinguishable. In the present case, both the Courts have considered the evidence of PWs and have accepted the evidence of the PWs assigning cogent reason and held that the plaintiff has proved his possession in the suit land. The lower appellate Court has noticed the evidence of PW 2 and 3 who was bargadar in the suit land under Matiur Rahman for about 14 years and then under Mafizuddin for about 12 years and then PW 2 barga cultivated the suit land under the plaintiff for about 12 years. The lower appellate Court has found that this PW 2 has been in possession of the suit land for about 38 years under Matiur Rahman and then under. Mafizuddin and thereafter under the present plaintiff. This was the evidence of PW 3 also. The lower appellate Court considered the evidence of all the PWs and held concurrently with the trial Court that the plaintiff has proved his possession from the time of Dharani Dhar Sarkar. This being the position, it is not a case that the concurrent finding of facts are based on non-consideration of evidence and is permitted to be disturbed by the High Court Division in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. Since the finding of fact relating to title and possession is concluded by both the Courts and such findings of facts are based on consideration of the evidence, I do not find any substance in any of the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. I do not, therefore, find any merit in this Rule.</u>

<u>This Rule is accordingly discharged wit out any Order as to costs. The Order directing the parties to maintain status quo at the time of the issuance of the rule is vacated.</u>

Send down the LCR.

End.

parties:
Mostafa Kamal ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Md kamal Hossain and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Leave was granted at the instance of defendant No. 7 petitioner, to consider whether the impugned judgment and order dated 24-4-2005 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Bankruptcy Court, Dhaka, rejecting Civil Revision No. 364 of 2004 and affirming those of dated 15-7-2004 allowing an application under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure (briefly as the Code) in Title Suit No. 178 of 2003 suffers from an error of law, resulting in an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice.

2. Materials facts are that on 11-5-2003 plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 178 of 2003 in the second Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka against defendants for declaration that memo dated 30-4-2003 issued under the signature of defendant No. 6, cancelling the allotment of shop is illegal, void and not binding upon him and also for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from evicting him from the suit premises.

3. In suit, plaintiff by an application dated 18-52004 sought to amend his plaint under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code for incorporating some facts regarding dispossession during pendency of the suit and relief regarding recovery of khas possession which was allowed by trial Court and affirmed in revision by the impugned order. Hence the Petition.

4. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that by the proposed amendment nature and character of the suit has been changed. In support of his contentions the learned Counsel refers the case of Abdul Wadud Contractor vs Nazir Ahmed, 48 DLR (AD) 120 held:

"The proposed amendment introducing new facts and subsequent cause of action different from those made in the plaint if allowed condoning the delay will change the nature and character of the suit. Amendment was therefore rightly refused."

5. The learned Counsel next refers that case of Bangladesh vs Md Aslam, 44 DLR 69 held

"The Court will not allow either party to make any departure from the earlier pleadings set forth in the plaint of written statement"

6. The learned Advocate lastly refers that case of Ismail Mohammad vs Motasim Ali Chowdhury 45 DLR 123 held:

"Amendment of plaint allowed by the trial Court as a matter of course and without satisfying itself whether the same in necessary for determining the controversy between the parties is to be discarded."

7. Therefore, the Courts below without appreciating settled principles of law by allowing the application for amendment committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

8. No one appears on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 to oppose the petition.

9. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 3-7 by filing a counter affidavit supported the contentions advanced by learned Counsel for petitioner.

10. In order to appreciate their submissions I have gone through the record, and given by anxious consideration to their submissions.

11. The point for consideration whether the impugned order calls for interference by this Court.

12. On going to materials on record it transpires that it is the definite case of plaintiff that during pendency of suit he was dispossessed. Therefore, he sought for incorporation of some facts relating to his dispossession during pendency of suit and recovery of khas possession.

13. For the convenience of understanding the Provisions of Order VI Rule 17 of the Code reads as hereunder:

"17-The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties."

<u>14. Therefore, Order VI Rule 17 of the Code provides that the Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such term as may be just and necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties. The proposed amendment would settle the question whether during the pendency of suit the plaintiff was dispossessed. This will end all pending controversies between the parties and will not amount to a change in the nature and character of the suit.</u>

15. It transpires to me that proposed amendment will in no way change the nature and character of the suit, rather the plaintiff wants to amend his plaint by proposed amendment for proper and complete adjudication of the suit which do not appear to be inconsistent, irrelevant, immaterial or contradictory of the facts of plaint. I find that one of the fundamental principles governing the amendment of the pleadings is that all the controversies between the parties as far' as possible should be included and multiplicity of the proceedings avoided.

16. Therefore, I hold that the proposed amendment is necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversies between the parties and proper adjudication of the suit. Moreover, the respective party will prove their own case by adducing evidence and other party has the ample opportunity to file additional written statement against such amendment and to prove their case at the time of hearing.

17. In the case of Abdul Mutaleb vs Ershad Ali 1998 BLD (AD) 121= 4 BLC (AD) 150 held:

"Since all rules of the Court are intended to secure the proper administration of justice, it is essential that they should be made to serve and be sub-ordinate to that purpose so that full powers of amendment may be enjoyed and, as such, it should always be liberally exercised. The only limitation in allowing an amendment of the plaint is that the proposed amendment should not change the fundamental character and nature of the suit. The settled law is that amendment of pleadings may be allowed at any stage of the proceeding for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversies between the parties."

18. This view receives support in the cases of Md Khaledur Reza Chowdhury vs Saleha Begum 1997 BLD (AD) 86 = 2 BLC (AD) 20, SN Roy Chowdhury vs A Jabber 1994 BLD 229 = 46 DLR 273. Moyjuddin Mondal vs Bena Rani Das 45 DLR 145 and MA Jahangir vs Abdul Malek 41 DLR 389.

19. Therefore, the Courts below after appreciating the materials on record by allowing the application for amendment committed no error of law.

20. It appears that findings arrived at by Courts below having been rested upon considerations and discussions of materials on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of legal aspects involved in suit. So, the finding of facts arrived at by the Court of appeal below as a final Court of fact are not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division in exercise of power under section 115(4) of the Code.

21. Moreover, the impugned order in its entirety is well founded in the facts and circumstances of the suit. So, the grounds urged and contentions advanced by learned Counsel for the petitioners are not the correct exposition of law and facts. However, I have gone through the decisions reported in 48 DLR (AD) 120, 44 DLR 69, 45 DLR 123, as referred by him. I am in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated therein but the facts leading to those cases are distinguishable to that of the instant case. Therefore, I am unable to accept his submissions.

22. In the light of discussions made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above, I am of the view that the impugned judgment and order suffers from no legal infirmity, which calls for no interference by this Court. Thus the petition having no merit fails.

23. In the result, leave granted earlier is discharged The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

The office directed to communicate the order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
ABM Altaf Hossain J: The Rule under adjudication, issued on 26-7-2009, was in the following terms:

"Let a Rule be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Government Circular purportedly issued by the Ministry of Education Vide Memo No. Shim/Sha: 11/19-2/(MPO)/2007/757, dated 15-5-2008, so far it relates to imposition of discriminatory embargo making it compulsory for every non BED Secondary School Teachers, to obtain BED training only from the Government Teachers Training Colleges (Annexure-D) and government decision purportedly taken by the Ministry of Education in its meeting dated 4-1-2009, so far it relates to direction to the Vice-Chancellor, National University, to cancel affiliation of 38 colleges marked as red (Annexure-F), shall not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper".

2. The averment figured in the petition generating in brief:

The National University (in brief "the University") has been established under the National University Act 1992(Act 37 of 1992), by its provisions, the University per-forming supervisory and regulatory function all over the colleges and institutions of the Country, and there are provisions in the Act of 37 of 1992 that Teachers Training colleges (in brief "TTCs") will be affiliated by the University, and their affiliation will be renewed yearly in accordance with the law. The petitioners TTCs obtained temporary affiliation in the year 2006, and subsequently, renewed its affiliation in due course of time. After affiliation from the University, the TTCs started to admit students in accordance with the prevailing law of the University, and there are number of students already got admission and have secured good results in the past B. Ed Examinations. It is stated that the University policy is to be increased the percentage of trained teachers in order to maintain the standards of the educational institutes. In order to maintaining the standards of the teachers of the Country, the University has increased students by establishing the TTCs and they are running their functions very smoothly. Before affiliation of TTCs, there were only 10 Government Teachers Training Colleges in the Country, which were insufficient to coup with increasing demands of the day, and, as such, considering the necessity and viability of the Act of 1992 the University affiliated and recognised Private TTCs in the Country to coup up the demands of the day.

3. There are 105 private TTCs imparting the BED course and the Private TTCs are giving B.Ed training up to 75% of the total Teachers each year. The syllabus, teaching methods and examinations systems are being done by the University, and there is no separate academic curriculum for the TTCs. All on a sudden, 15-5-2008, a Circular purportedly issued by the Ministry of Education Vide Memo No. Shim Sha 11/19-2(MPO)/2007/757, dated 15-5-2008, made it compulsory for every non-BEd Secondary school Teachers to obtain BEd training only from the Government Teachers Training colleges, and publishing a discriminatory list of 38 colleges marking as red 17, colleges as green, 15 colleges as yellow, 31 colleges as grey and, thereby barring hundreds of Private TTC around the Country to admit B Ed students. It is stated that Private Teachers Training Colleges Association made representation to the respondents, requesting to withdraw and/or cancel the impugned circular dated 15-5-2008, but respondents did not make any response on it whatsoever. The petitioner being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the decisions of the respondents preferred the instant writ petition and obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr Yousuf Hossain Humayun with Md Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Counsels appearing on behalf of the petitioners, while Mr Biswajit Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondents.

5. Mr Yousuf Hossain Humayun, the learned Counsel for the petitioners submits that by the impugned order, the respondents directing the National University to cancel affiliation of 38 Private Teachers Training Colleges is discriminatory, and nauseating violation of Article 27 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh guaranteed as fundamental rights to the petitioners.

6. Mr Humayun further submits that no opportunity of being heard was ever given to the petitioners before taking such illegal and mala fide decisions and as much every TTC was entitled to have a chance of a reasonable opportunity of being heard and to make effective representation. Further to that he submits that it is enshrined in the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh that to enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen. Every person for the time being within Bangladesh and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law, and as such every authority is law bound to afford an opportunity of being heard, but in this case it was not done, which in violation of Article 31 of the Constitution as well as the principle of natural justice. He prays for making the Rule absolute.

7. Mr Biswajit Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney-General (briefly "DAG") with Mr. Shawrup Kumar Deb, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared on behalf of the respondents without filing any affidavit-in-opposition. Mr Roy, the learned DAG submits that the respondents, have rightly issued the impugned notification and the instant Rule is liable to be discharged.

8. At the time of hearing, we have considered the submissions of learned Counsels for the petitioners and the learned Deputy Attorney-General and also perused the substantive writ Petition along with others material on records.

9. In order to attain a proper adjudication, we would first consider the issue of legitimate expectation, so far it relates to Annexure- "D" to the writ petition.

10. The doctrine of legitimate expectation imposes in spirit a duty on public authority to act fairly by taking into consideration all relevant factors relating to such legitimate expectation.

11. The doctrine of legitimate expectation has been judicially recognized by the Apex Court of the different jurisdictions in Commonwealth Countries and this recognition has paved the way for the development of a broader and more flexible doctrine of fairness.

12. In the Common law jurisdiction the doctrine had been traced to an obiter dictum of Lord Denning MR in Sehmidt vs Secretary of Home Affairs reported in (1969) 1 All ER 904. Lord Denning observed in Sehmidt:

"The speeches in Ridge v Baldwin show that an administrative body may, in a proper case, be bound to give a person who is affected by their decision an opportunity of making representations. It all depends on whether he has some right or interest or I would add, some legitimate expectation, of which it would not be fair to deprive him without hearing what he has to say."

13. The model elucidation of legitimate expectation appears from the speech of Lord Fraser in Council of Civil Service Unions vs Minister for the Civil Services ("GCHQ"), reported in 3 All. ER 935, wherein it was held that:

"Legitimate, or reasonable, expectation may arise either from an express promise given on behalf of a public authority or from the existence of a regular practice which the claimant can reasonably expect to continue".

14. The governing principles are to be found in the decision of the Court of Appeal in R v North and East Devon Health Authority ex p Coughlan [2001] QB 213. At paragraph 57 of Coughlan three categories, of case were identified:

a. Those where the public authority was only required to bear in mind its previous policy giving weight, but no more, if it thinks right to the promise before deciding to change course.

b. Those where the promise is of consultation before a particular course is adopted.

c. Those where the promise has induced a legitimate expectation of a benefit which is substantive.

15. In the first category of case the Court of Appeal held that it could only intervene on traditional Wednesbury [1948] 1KB 223, sense. In the second category of case the consultation has to be given unless there is an overriding reason to resile from the promise. Here the Court judges what fairness requires. In the third category of case the Court will require the promise to be performed if to frustrate the promise is so unfair as to amount to an abuse of power. The Court weighs up the requirements of fairness against any overriding interest relied upon for the change of policy.

16. In R (on the application of Nadarajah) and Abdi vs Secretary of State for the Home Department (2005] EWCA Civ 2363, the Court of Appeal after reviewing the authorities suggested that the applicable test was as follows:

"The principle that good administration requires public authorities to be held to their promises would be undermined if the law did not insist that any failure or refusal to comply is objectively justified as a proportionate measure in the circumstances."

17. The Court of Appeal went on to state, at paragraph 69:

"Proportionality will be judged, as it is generally to be judged, by the respective force of the competing interests arising in this case. Thus where the representation relied on amounts to an unambiguous promise; where there is detrimental reliance, where the promise is made to an individual or a specific group; these are instances where denial of the expectation is likely to be harder to justify as a proportionate factor".

18. There is a recent and significant decision of the Court of Appeal in R (Bhatt Murphy) vs Secretary for the Home Department [2008] EWCA Civ 755, wherein it was held that:—

"The power of public authorities to change policy is constrained by the legal duty to be fair (and other constraints which the law imposes). A change of policy which would otherwise be legally unexceptionable may be held unfair by reason of prior action, or inaction, by the authority".

19. In Navjyoti Coop. Group Housing Society vs Union of India (1992) 4 SCC 477, the Supreme Court recognized that by reason of application of the said doctrine, an aggrieved party would be entitled to seek judicial review (Id. At 494),

"if he could show that a decision of the public authority affected him of some benefit or advantage which in the past he had been permitted to enjoy and which he legitimately expected to be permitted to continue to enjoy either until he was given reasons for withdrawal and the opportunity to comment such reasons".

20.
