A total stranger unconnected with the authority or a person who had no previous dealings with the authority and who has not entered into any transaction or negotiations with the authority, cannot invoke the doctrine of legitimate expectation, merely on the ground that the authority has a general obligation to act fairly".

21. The Supreme Court referred to its earlier decision in Union of India vs Hindustan Development Corporation (1993) 3 SCC 499, wherein the Court has, inter-alia, held: —

"It is generally agreed that legitimate expectation gives the applicant sufficient locus standi for judicial review and that the doctrine of legitimate expectation is to be confined mostly to right of a fair hearing before a decision which results in negativing a promise or withdrawing an undertaking is taken".

22. Very recently in case of Sethi Auto Service Station vs Delhi Development Authority (2009) 1 SCC 180, it has been reiterated that:

"32 that the golden thread running through all these decisions is that a case for applicability of the doctrine of legitimate expression, now accepted in the subjective sense as part of our legal jurisprudence, arises when an administrative body by reason of a representation or by past practice or conduct aroused an expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfil unless some overriding public interest comes in the way".

23. In Golam Mostafa vs Bangladesh 2007 (XV) BLT (HCD) 128, it was observed that:

"The upshot of the decisions noted above are that judicial review may be allowed on the plea of frustration of legitimate expectation in the following situations:

i) If there is a promise by the authority, expressed either by their representations or by conducts.

Ii) The decision of the authority was arbitrary or unreasonable within the Wednesbury principal.

iii) There was a failure on the part of the concerned authority to act fairly in taking the decision.

iv) The expectation to be crystallized into a legitimate one, it must be based on clear facts and circumstances leading to a definite expectation and not a mere anticipation or a wish or hope and also must be reasonable in the circumstances".

24. In AKM Kawser Ahmed vs Bangladesh, 65 DLR 277, wherein it was observed that:

"67. The potentially important point is that change of policy should not violate the substantive legislative expectation and if does so it must be as the change of policy which is necessary and such a change is not irrational or perverse".

25. In BTMC vs Nasiruddin Chowdhury cited in 5 BLC (AD) 144, the Apex in a detailed discussion accepted the position that a legitimate expectation cannot be defeated by the executive action unless public interest clearly requires negation of such expectation, but at the same time found that such an expectation can be given effect to by the court only when the facts of the case clearly and unambiguously give rise to such an expectation.

26. In view of the above extracted principle of legitimate expectation the particular manifestation of the duty to act fairly is that part of the recent evolution of administrative law which may enable an aggrieved party to evoke judicial review if he can show that he had 'a reasonable expectation' of some occurrence or action preceding the decision complained of and that reasonable expectation was not fulfilled in the event.

27. We now proceed to examine that the present case, mainly annexure-"D" in light of the above extracted principle and relevant law.

28. After hearing the learned counsels for the parties, it is emerged that the University has been duly affiliated some 38 TTCs for 2006-2007 academic years and subsequently the affiliation was renewed by the University. It is apparent from Annexure-"A" to the writ petition that on 6-6-2006 after availing all formalities, e.g. by the approval of the Vice Chancellor, the Affiliation Committee, the Syndicate and Academic Council 38 private Teachers Training Colleges were established. It also appears from the Annexure-"Al" that as per terms of the affiliation, the University renewed the temporary affiliation in due course of time. Afterward, the TTCs of the petitioners were maintaining the highest level of standards and ensuring the training for the school teachers at their level best. Admittedly, the number of students already got admission and secured good result in the past B.Ed examinations.

29. In the case of the petitioners, when they obtained affiliation from the University, there were certain terms and conditions stipulated in the affiliation letter dated 6-6-2009. The petitioners started keeping in view of the future prospects of the colleges on the basis of terms and condition of affiliation letter. To the change and/or stop the affiliation cannot be put under "Paripatra" dated 15-5-2008, which has changed the conditions of affiliation and altered the advantage of the students of the TTCs.

30. The doctrine of legitimate expectation provides that the statements of policy or intention of the Government or its Department in administering its affairs should be without abuse or discretion. The change of law and or/Rule could not be disregarded unfairly or applied selectively for the reason that unfairness in the form of unreasonableness is parallel to violation of natural justice. It means that said actions have to be in conformity of Article 27 of the Constitution of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh, of which non-arbitrariness is a second facet. Public Authority cannot claim to have unfettered discretion in public law as the authority is conferred with power only to use them for public good. Generally legitimate expectation is essentially procedural in character as it gives assurance of fair play in administrative action, but it may in a given case be enforced as a substantive right. But a person claiming it has to satisfy the Court that his rights had been altered by enforcing a right in private law or he has been deprived of some benefit or advantage which he was having in the past and which he could legitimately expect to be permitted to continue unless it is withdrawn on some rational ground or he has received assurance from the decision making Authority which is not fulfilled.

31. It is evident from Annexure-"B" to the writ petition that there are good numbers of students those who have been secured satisfactory result in the past BEd examinations. Even it appears from the annexure-"C" to the writ petition that private TTCs are giving BEd training up to 75% of the total teachers of Secondary School levels per year. It is pertinent to be mentioned here that the syllabus, curriculum, examinations system and method of teaching are same in the vein of public teachers training Colleges. Prior to issuance the impugned "Pariparta", the private TTCs were governed by the Rules of the University. This past practice had been in mode/trend for a numbers of years and it can be said that the expectation of the petitioners that TTCs would be permanent in near future.

<u>32. While we have closely scrutinized annexures, we found that there was no prior notice or warning given to the petitioners in this regard. Even the respondents utterly failed to explain the necessity and/or public interest to change the terms and conditions of the affiliation letter. The aforesaid expectation cannot be termed or being based on sporadic or casual or random acts of the respondents, or as an unreasonable or illogical or invalid expectation. This expectation can be said to have arisen in the mind of the petitioners in the normal course, in view of the consistent past practice of the respondents as reflected in the "affiliation letter dated 6-8-2006". In our view, this expectation was legitimately entertained by the petitioners and acquired vested right in the matter of continuing the TTCs. It is for the decision maker to justify its decision to change the policy in the manner it did, by showing overriding public interest. But in the present case, the respondent failed to do so. Therefore, we have no difficulty in concluding that the "Paripatra" seeks to serve a purpose which would help in achieving benefit of the government teacher training college and must be treated as a positive discrimination. We are unable to appreciate as to what is the purpose sought to be achieved by the "Pariptra" to changed the terms of the affiliation letter, which unduly restricts the rights of the petitioners.</u>

33. Pertinently the respondents have not disclosed, either by filling an affidavit in opposition or even by making submissions before us as to what is the justification for changing the terms and conditions of affiliation of the petitioners. The provision of the "Paripatra" contains restriction upon the TTCs, by making compulsory for every non B.Ed. Secondary School Teachers both the government and Non-Government to obtain B. Ed. training only from Government Teachers Training Colleges (Annexure-"D"). We are in the view that in terms of the petitioners' legitimate expectation extracted from the above mentioned ratio of the decisions, the restriction introduced by the impugned "Paripatra", dated 15-5-2008 (Annexure-"D") is ultra vires the Constitution and also discriminatory as it offend Articles 27 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

34. In terms of the Annexure-"F", it appears that it is a mere recommendation by the Ministry of Education and it has no mandatory force at all. In this regard, we are of the view that since it has no binding force to implement upon the University, this impugned recommending (Annexure-"F") is premature.

35. Having regards to the discussions made in above, the Rule is made absolute in part.

36. In the result, the Rule is made absolute in part. Therefore, the Government Circular purportedly issued by the Ministry of Education Vide Memo No. Shim/Sha: 11/19-2/(MPO)/2007/757 dated 15-5-2008, so far it relates to imposition of discriminatory embargo making it compulsory for every non B.ED Secondary School Teachers, to obtain B.ED Training only from the Government Teachers Training Colleges (annexure-'D') is hereby declared to have been passed without law authority and to be of no legal effect and government decision purportedly taken by the Ministry of Education in its meeting dated 4-1-2009, so far it relates to direction to the Vice-Chancellor, National University, to cancel affiliation of 38 colleges marked as red (annexure-'F') is hereby discharged.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Tapan Kumar Chakraborty with Swapan Kumar Dutta, Advocates—For the Petitioners 
Sucharita Sen Gupta, AAG—For the Opposite-Party
parties:
Shamir Chandra Sajwal and others ------ Plaintiff-Respondent-Petitioners.
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh ------ Defendant- Appellant- Opposite-Party
full_judgment:
The Rule issued on an application filed under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners calling upon the Opposite-Party to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 3-11-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 114 of 2009 allowing the appeal and setting-aside those dated 19-4-2009 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Muladi, Barisal in Title Suit No. 106 of 2005 should not be set-aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the land measuring 1.92 acres appertaining to CS Khatian No. 3 in plot No. 272 of Mouza-Shaheber Char, under police station Goumadi at present Muladi, District-Barisal originally belonged to one Avoy Sajwal, Kanu Sajwal and Gopal Sajwal in equal shares. 1.59 acres of land of entire CS plot No. 273 of CS Khatian No. 4 of the said Mouza belonged to one Harachandra, Durgacharan and Sreecharan Sajwal in equal share. 2.13 acres of land of plot No. 274 in CS Khatian No. 35 of the said Mouza belonged to one Kukuri Sajwal, Bhagaban Sajwal, Brindaban Sajwal and Prosannya Sajwal in equal share. 9.49 acres of land of plot Nos. 173, 174, 175, 176, 177, 178, 179 & 180 of CS Khatian No. 66 originally belonged to one Dasharath Sajwal in 3 annas 4 gandas share, Hari Charan Sajwal in 9 annas 12 gandas share and Mohonbashi, Golak Bashi Sajwal in 1 arena 12 gandas share each. The land measuring 9.28 acres of CS plot Nos. 142, 143, 144, 145, 146, 147, 148 & 149 in CS Khatian No. 93 originally belonged to one Fadu Sajwal in 5 annas 2 karas 2 kerantis share, Ram Charan Sajwal, Adhar Chand Sajwal along with Jagabandhu Barik each in 2 annas 13 gandas 1 kara 1 keranti sahres and Rajani Barik, Jamini Barik, Bhadra Chandra Barik and Dukhi Barik each in 13 gandas 1 kara 1 keranti shares. The CS recorded tenant Gopal Sajwal died in his tender age living behind 2 full brothers Avoy Sajwal and Kanu Sajwal. The two brothers died unmarried and their property devolved upon their cousin Kukuri Sajwal. On the death of Kukuri Sajwal his only son Bhadra Kanta Sajwal became the sole owner. Subsequently Bhadra Kanta Sajwal died living behind only son Chandra Kanta Sajwal and on his death the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 remains his heirs.

In the RS operation 0.03 acres of land of CS plot No. 272 recorded in hal plot No. 1358 of RS Khatian No. 71. The plaintiff Nos.1-3 acquired 1.89 acre of land in equal shares which has been recorded in hal plot Nos. 1364 and 894 in 54 decimals and 1.35 acres of land respectively. The CS recorded tenants Harachandra and Durga Charan died living behind their sons Rashik Chandra and Prohalad Chandra. The CS recorded tenant Sree Charan Sawjal being unmarried died and his share devolved upon his two nephews namely Rashik Chandra and Prohalad Chandra in equal shares. On the death of Rashik Chandra his only son Upendra Sawjal inherited the property and after the death of Upendra Sawjal his son the plaintiff No. 9 Uttam Kumar Sawjal inherited the property left behind him. On the death of Prohalad Sawjal his son plaintiff No. 10 Ananta Kumar Sawjal inherited the property and in this way the plaintiff Nos. 9 and 10 each acquired 0.79½ acres of land in equal shares. The further case of the plaintiffs is such that the recorded owner of CS Khatian No. 35 Proshanna Kumar Sawjal died living behind only son the plaintiff No. 5 Jogendra Nath Sawjal and on the death of Brindaban Sawjal his only son Rajani Sawjal became the heir. On the death of Rajani Sawjal his son Mukunda Nath inherited the land of Rajani and on the death of Mukunda Nath plaintiff No. 4 Lakshmi Kanta as his only son inherited. During RS operation 2.13 acres of land in CS plot No. 274 under CS Khatian No. 35 has been recorded in hal plot No. 894 which is also the suit land. During RS operation although some part of 9.42 acres of land in CS plot Nos.173-180 under CS Khatian No. 66 was recorded in the names of the predecessors of the plaintiffs along with some others in RS Khatian Nos.17/18 corresponding to SA Khatian Nos. 24 and 25 in hal plot Nos. 170, 171, 168, 169, 187, 148, 166, 167, 149, 150, 151, 152, 153 and 154, but 0.09 acres of land out of 0.20 acres from plot No. 176, the entire 1.67 acres of CS plot No. 177, 0.03 acres out of 0.59 acres of CS plot No. 178, 0.10 acres out of 0.81 acres of land in CS plot No. 179 and 0.84 acres out of 1.69 acres of CS Plot No. 180 in all 2.73 acres of land recorded in hal plot No. 894. The CS recorded tenant Dasharath died unmarried living behind only brother Haricharan Sawjal, who died unmarried living behind his nephew Chandra Kanta Sajwal. On the death of CS recorded tenant Goalak Bashi and Mohon Bashi their total shares devolved upon their nephews in absence of their sons and daughters in equal share. The aforesaid nephews are one Rajani Kanta and Jogendra Nath, who is the plaintiff No. 5 of the suit. During RS operation though some part of 9.28 acres of land of CS plot Nos.143-149 under CS Khatian No. 93 recorded in the names of the predecessors of the plaintiffs along with some others in RS Khatian No. 37 corresponding to SA Khatian No. 48 in hal plot Nos. 140-147, but the entire 0.83 acres of land of CS Plot No. 143 the area measuring 2.48 acres of CS plot No. 144, 0.27 acres of CS plot No. 145, 0.32 acres out of 0.86 acres of land in CS plot No. 146, 0.71 acres out of 1.00 acre in CS Plot No. 147 in all 4.61 acres of land recorded in hal plot No. 894, which is part of the disputed land. Plaintiff's further case is such that the owner of the 1/3rd share of CS Khatian No. 93 Fasu Sawjal died as widow without any issue living behind only nephew Bhadra Kanta. On the unmarried death of Adhar Chand 2 annas 13 ganda 1 kara 1 kranti share devolved upon his nephew Ram Doyal. Ram Doyal being the owner of 5 annas 6 gandas 2 karas 2 kerantis share died living behind 2 sons Sumon and Dhiran. On the death of Sumon Sawjal his share devolved upon his only son the plaintiff No. 6 Krishna Kanta and on the death of Dhiran his share devolved upon his 2 sons the plaintiff Nos. 7 and 8. After the death of Rajani, Jamini, Bhadra Kanta and Dukhi Chandra Barik their entire share devolved upon their nephew Bhadra Kanta Sawjal and after the death of Bhadra Kanta his 3 sons the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 inherited the property. In this way out of the entire suit land measuring an area of 12.95 acres of land, the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 acquired 2.73½ acres of land each. The plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 acquired 0.80 3/4 acres of land each, plaintiff No. 6 acquired 0.76 3/4 acres of land, plaintiff Nos. 7 and 8 acquired 0.38¼ acres of land and plaintiff Nos. 9 &10 each acquired 0.79½ acres of land and they have been enjoying the same peacefully and uninterruptedly since the day of reappearance of the land by way of cultivation. In the RS operation, the said land, recorded in hal plot Nos.1364 and 894 as 0.54 acres and 12.41 acres respectively. It is the positive case of the plaintiffs that the suit property went under water of the river Arial Kha in the year 1339 BS and its diluvion was completed in the year 1445 BS. Subsequently the land re-appeared again in the other side of the river within 10 years. As the RS operation of the corresponding area was started in the year 1346 BS corresponding to 1939 AD and finally published in 1358-1359 BS, in the remark column, the suit property was wrongly shown as river and used by the public at large. Subsequently SA record was also prepared in the aforesaid manner as it was a table work relying upon the RS Khatians. The suit property was wrongly shown under water of the river Arial Kha, despite the same has already been reappeared long before. Being inspired by the said wrong record the Tahashilder of the defendant government of Bangladesh on 15-11-2005 claimed the suit disowning the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs. Hence the plaintiffs filed the original suit for declaration of title.

3. The contrary case of the defendant in short is thus, that the suit property went under water of the river Arial Kha in the year 1939 BS and it remained under water for a period of 70/75 years. As such due to the sikasti (diluvion) character of the property a note in the remark column of the corresponding and RS and SA Khatian was given showing the suit property in the river and being used by public at large, which is correct. The suit property started to reappear just before 3/4 years and the defendant government is under process of its allotment. The further case of the defendant-appellant-opposite party is such that the suit property remained under water of the river Arial Kha for a period of 70/75 years and as a result the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession therein. After reappearance of the land in hal plot No. 1364, the defendant allotted the same in favour of third party vide Miscellaneous Case No. 1862/60-61 and some new Khatians has also been opened in the names of those allottees. The land of hal plot No. 894 also allotted to different persons and the suit property is yet to be fit for cultivation and the same is still a lower shore of the river Arial Kha and in near future as the suit property would become fit for cultivation, the plaintiffs filed the suit for illegal gain.

4. The Trial Court, i.e. learned Assistant Judge, Muladi, Barisal in Title Suit No. 106 of 2005 after framing four issues as to the maintainability of suit, right, title and interest of the plaintiffs and entitlement of the plaintiffs to have the suit be decreed examining three witnesses for the plaintiffs and one witness for the defendants decreed the suit on contest.

5. Being aggrieved the defendant prefer-red an appeal being Title Appeal No. 114 of 2009 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Barisal, which was heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal and the learned Appellant Court below by the impugned judgment and decree dated 3-11-2010 allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Trial Court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained this Rule with an interim order of status quo.

7. Mr. Tapan Kumar Chakraborty with Mr. Swapan Kumar Dutta, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mrs. Sucharita Sen Gupta, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared on behalf of the opposite party.

8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned Appellate Court below during disposal of the appeal committed gross illegality and irregularity in deciding the merit of the appeal. The learned Advocates further submits that during disposal of the appeal there has been glaring misreading and non-reading of the evidence and non-consideration of the material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocates also submits that the findings on possession of the Trial Court not at all reversed by the Appellate Court below and the possession inasmuch as, in favour of the plaintiffs as observed by the Trial Court is unrebutted, the impugned judgment is not sustainable in law. The learned Counsels further submit that the possession follows the title and non payment of rent does not extinguish title of the plaintiffs in the suit property. Without reversing the findings and decisions of the Trial Court the decision of the Appellant Court below as transpires is not in accordance with law and in this context the learned Advocates referred a decision of our Apex Court reported in 16 MLR (AD) 4 in the case of Abdur Rashid vs Afzal Gazi The learned Advocate lastly submits that the defendant to the suit during examination of the plaintiff's witness as because not cross-examined the witness specially the PW No.1 (plaintiff No. 1) upon the year of diluvion and alluvion of the suit land, the observation and findings of the lower Appellate Court have no leg to stand as per section 137 of the Evidence Act and, as such, the specific contention on the fact of alluvion and diluvion of the land as stated from the side of the plaintiffs has become admitted by the act of the adversary. In this connection another decision has been referred from the side of the petitioners decided in the case of Mst. Zarjan vs Mst. Nazmunnessa reported in 1969 PLD 118. The learned Trial Court after thorough assessment of evidence and appreciation of law and on careful consideration of the facts, circumstances and papers on record decreed the suit, but the lower Appellant Court without reversing the findings of the Trial Court in consultation with the evidence on record reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Muladi, Barisal illegally and that the Appellate Court below committed an error of law in not considering that the revisional survey in the field conducted in between the years 1933-1942 while the land was on the verse of reformation and the RS Khatian was published in the year 1952 within which the land has been completely reformed. The learned Joint District Judge also erred in law having failed to consider that the disputed land has reformed in situ within statutory period and, as such, before the promulgation of part V of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the land in dispute was reformed as a whole and become fit for cultivation.

9. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Counsels for the petitioners the learned Assistant-Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the opposite party opposing the Rule submits that the learned Appellate Court below while disposed of the appeal on merit considered all the evidence adduced including the oral and documentary evidence and circumstantial evidence. The learned Assistant-Attorney-General further submits that the Court of Appeal below committed no illegality or irregularity in holding that the land in dispute was under water of the river Arial Kha more than 40 years and under Presidential Order No. 135 of 1972 the land after its reappearance has become the government Khas land. From the year 1339 BS the suit property has been under the diluvion process and for 70/75 years the process was going on and the plaintiffs never possess the land as alleged. The learned Assistant-Attorney-General lastly submits that the property in dispute while become fit for cultivation it has been leased out in favour of several allottees by settlement cases and the property in the suit plot Nos. 1364 and 894 being Khas property of the government has been settled with many landless people but the plaintiffs on false allegation to grab the property instituted the suit.

10. While the matter is taken up for deli-very of judgment the leaned Assistant-Attorney-General filing a counter affidavit on behalf of the government submitted some papers stating that the property in dispute has been settled in favour of different settlement holders and at present they have been able to find out the connected papers. The settlement cases have been taken up for collection of lease money and 46 holdings have been opened. Photocopies of the said holdings have been annexed as Annexures '2' series. The learned Assistant-Attorney-General finally submits that on behalf of the defendant government she prays for an order of remand to the learned Trial Court so that the government can avail of the opportunity to prove it's case by adducing evidence and marking the papers Exhibits.

11. In view of the above submissions of the learned Assistant-Attorney-General the learned Counsels appearing on behalf of the petitioners controverting the submissions of the learned Assistant-Attorney-General submits that there is no scope in legal arena and factual aspects of the suit to consider the submission on remand and acceptance of the papers produced at this stage on behalf of the Government. The learned Advocates in this connection also submits that the papers annexed with the counter-affidavit has no manner of application in the instant suit since the suit land does not attract the papers inasmuch as, the mention of plot numbers as appears in the papers produced are not identical with that of the suit plots. Apart from this, under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure the defendant cannot get any opportunity for remanding the case record to the trial Court for preemptory hearing since as a matter of right remand cannot be allowed to fill up the lacuna which has already been accrued in favour of the present petitioners. Remand as contemplated under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure is to be dealt with cautiously specially when a lacuna transpired in any parties pleadings to fill up the same order of remand cannot be entertained. The learned Counsels relied upon the following decisions of our Apex Court reported in 54 DLR (AD) 74 and 41 DLR (AD) 124. Regarding the admissibility of the documents produced at this stage as additional evidence the learned counsels referred another decision reported in 50 DLR (AD) 17.

12. Scrutinizing the relevant laws along with the decisions referred to above I have every reason to incline such a view that the submissions of the learned counsels for the petitioners is consistent and have got much substance to admit the proposition as to admissibility of the documents along with the order of remand as sought for.

13. On perusal of the original case records along with the Exhibited papers including the deposition of the witnesses it transpires that the plaintiffs in support their respective case produced the relevant CS Khatians, RS Khatians, SA Khatians, plot index and the certified copies of the approved Sketch Map (Kalami Naksha) of the government and those papers were duly marked Exhibits. The pertinent question in the instant suit is, as to when the suit property reappeared from the garb of the river Arial Kha. The Trial Court relied upon the testimonies of the witnesses and the witnesses specially the witness no. 2 Arun Mandal and 3 Santosh, who are the inhabitants of the concerned area Saheber Chor. These two competent, credible witnesses specifically asserted that from their boyhood they are finding the suit property under cultivation of the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs are enjoying the same uninterrupted. The defendant government alleged that in Miscellaneous Case No. 1862 of 60-61 some allottees obtained allotment of the suit property from the government as 'Khas' land and the allottees since their allotment are in possession over the same. But it appears from the case record that no authentic paper or any competent credible oral evidence is coming from the side of the government supporting the same. The positive case of the plaintiffs is such that the property in dispute reappeared within ten years from the date of diluvion which is long before part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The diluvion process starts in the year of 1339 BS and continued up to 1345 BS and within 10 years from 1345 BS the land reappeared which is the positive case of the plaintiffs while the defendant's plea that the property remained under water for 70/75 years and it has started to re appear only 3-4 years before filing of the original suit is not supported by any documentary or oral evidence. The learned Trial Court positively held that the testimonies of the plaintiff's witnesses makes it clear that the land in dispute in fact reappeared from the bed of the river Arial Kha within ten years from the diluvion process which was continued up to 1345 BS vis-a-vis; we have came across from the solitary oral evidence from the side of the defendant opposite-party that the witness Md. Serajul Islam states in the deposition that the land went under water in the year 1339 BS and some portion of the land subsequently reappeared and settlement process is going on for the said portion, which has be-come fit for cultivation. This witness Serajul Islam is an official of Upazila land office, Muladi. He is a formal witness and as surveyor he joined in the office on 15-9-2005 AD. He admits that, supporting the case of the government no paper submitted save and except the written statement. On the contrary the witness No. 1 of the plaintiffs is Samir Chandra Sawjal, who is the plaintiff No. 1 of the suit. He corroborated their plaint case as a whole to the genealogy along with their acquisition of the property by way of inheritance from their predecessors in interest. It is not denied from the side of the defendant-opposite party that the predecessors of the plaintiffs were the original owners of the property and that the CS record in their names is correct. The plaintiff No. 1 in his testimony categorically states at a stage that the land in dispute went under water within the years 1339-1345 BS and thereafter within ten years it reappears. Finally in the year 1355 BS the land has become fit for cultivation. The other witnesses of the plaintiffs i.e. the witnesses No. 2 and 3, who are the possession witnesses corroborated the plaintiffs in respect of their possession in the disputed property.

14. On perusal of the impugned judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court it appears that the learned Joint District Judge during disposal of the appeal utterly failed to consider the point of controversy between the parties as well as the criterion of the suit. There is no dispute regarding the time of diluvion of the suit property in the bed of the river Arial Kha. As regard alluvion of the property i.e. reappearance of the same the dispute runs and in this context it is noticed that the contention advanced from the side of the plaintiffs is acceptable since it is proved by sufficient competent, credible, tangible evidence. The leaned Trial Court during disposal of the original suit in his findings and observation most emphatically pointed out that when and between how may years the land in dispute reappeared from the bed of the river Arial Kha. But the learned Appellate Court below without reversing the positive findings of the trial Court in a hasty evasive manner decided that the plaintiff's claim is not proved, while the defendant government has made out their case in respect of the property claimed. Not only this; the leaned Appellate Court during disposal of the appeal was misconceived and relied upon illegally on the testimony of the defendant's witness, who is not at all a competent credible witness and measurably failed to establish the bonafide of the defendant.

15. If we concede the written statement of the defendant-opposite party; it can be easily held that by the said statement of facts, the defendant-government categorically admits the case of the plaintiffs regarding reappearance of the suit property in any time before 1960-61.

16. I have already discussed earlier that the plaintiff No. 1, who deposed as witness No. 1 for the plaintiffs despite in his examination-in-chief specifically corroborated their case the defendant-government by cross-examining him failed to establish their plea as stated in their written statement rather failed to make the testimony of the plaintiff's witnesses shaky. As regard inheritance the witness No. 1, i.e. the plaintiff No. 1 corroborated their pleadings in his deposition and also adverts in support of their respective case regarding alluvion and diluvion of the property.

<u>17. The failure to cross-examine the plaintiff's witness to falsify the case of the plaintiffs or controvert the positive assertion of the witness No. 1 in his examination-in-chief; tantamounts to admission from the side of the defendant-opposite party. The learned Advocate Mr. Swapan Kumar Dutta in this context relied on the decisions rightly in the case of Zar Jan vs Mst. Najmun Nisa, reported in PLD 1969 Peshawar 118 and another decision in the case of Nur Mohammad vs Sultan Ahmed, reported in 40 DLR 369.</u>

18. Having regard to the contents of the decision along with the evidence on record I have the reason to constrained such a view that the facts deposed by the plaintiff's witnesses about the genealogy, possession and inheritance in favour of the plaintiffs since not questioned in cross-examination; it is to be presumed that the same has been admitted from the side of the defendant. Under the purview of section 58 of the Evidence Act the facts admitted need not to be proved. It requires to be mentioned here that a fact need not be proved in any proceeding which the parties thereto or their agents agrees or agree to admit at the hearing, or which, before the hearing, they agree to admit by any writing under their hands, or which by any rule or pleadings in force at the time they are deemed to have been admitted in their pleadings.

19. In the instant case the Trial Court being satisfied decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs and the Appellate Court below without reversing the observation and findings of the Trial Court in a hasty way and evasive manner reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court without any proper consultation and assessment of evidence in it's true perspective.

20. From the discussion and findings referred to above I have every reason to draw such inference that the decision of the lower Appellate Court is based upon gross misreading and non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision and it is apparent from the face of the Records that on misconception and misinterpretation of documents and evidence adduced from the side of the plaintiffs the learned Joint District Judge decided the merit of the appeal in favor of the defendant-appellant and against the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners, which is perverse and contrary to law, evidence and material on record.

21. Having regarded to the facts and circumstance of the case the Rule has got much substance to succeed.

22. In the result, the Rule having merit is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 3-11-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 114 of 2009 allowing the appeal and setting-aside those dated 19-4-2009 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Muladi, Barisal in Title Suit No. 106 of 2005 is hereby set-aside.

23. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance the Rule stands vacated.

24. However, there will be no order as to costs.

Let a copy of the judgment along with the Lower Court's Record be sent down at once.

End.

lawyer:
Idrisur Rahman, Advocate-For the Petitioner. 
Khair Ahmed, Advocate-For the Respondent No. 1 & 2.
parties:
Abdul Kalam (Moulavi)  ----- Petitioner
Vs
Administrator of Waqfs ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Quddus J : Rule Nisi under Article 102 (2) (a) (ii) of the Constitution was issued calling upon Respondent No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 10-6-99 (Annexure-K to the petitioner having been passed in violation of the Proviso to the Section 32 and Section 38 of the Waqf Ordinance 1982 and in violation of the Article 29 and 31 of the Constitution behind the back of the petitioner should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Munshi Ana Miah grandfather of the petitioner created the Waqf Estate by registered deed dated 15-2-1951 and Munshi Md Sayeed, father of the petitioner was made Mutwalli of the same stipulating that Munshi Md Sayeed would work as Imam of the Mosque known as Shayesta Nagar Nesar uddin Mosque and would work as Mutawalli during his life time. And on his death his son who may be found fit would be the Mutawalli. The Waqf Estate comprises a mosque, grave yard, Idgah and total 98½ acres of land in which there are some agricultural lands dedicated by concerned wakifs namely Ana Miah, Mofia Khatun, A. Aziz and 2 others Omed Ali Kurbai Ali by 11 registered deeds of various dates. Munshi Md Sayed originally appointed Mutwalli by all above wakifs discharged his duties as such and, thereafter died on 13-3-1981 and present petitioner was nominated by said Munshi Md Sayeed as Mutawalli of the Estate and the petitioner applied on 1-4-1981 for enrollment of the wakf at the office of Respondent No. 1 and also for appointment of the petitioner as Mutwalli. After proper enquiry the Respondent No. 1 enrolled the Estate being EG No. 15941 and appointed the petitioner as Mutawalli for 3 years or until further order vide order dated 10-11-81 (Annexure A and A).

3. On 11-10-85 the petitioner filed an application to Respondent No. 1 for extension of his tenure as Mutawalli to Respondent No. 1 who directed the petitioner to furnish audit and Accounts of the year 1388-91 which the petitioner duly submitted to the office of Respondent No. 1 wherefrom 2 notices dated 10-9-86 and 22-9-86 (Annexure B B(1) were sent to the petitioner but no order was passed as to extension of the tenure of the petitioner as Mutawalli.

4. The petitioner carried on his duties as Mutawalli of the Estate and paid subscriptions to the office of Respondent No. 1 on different dates vide receipts (Annexure-C series). The petitioners elder brother (Respondent No. 2) Moulana A. Hai left the paternal house and settled in village Yarpur, permanently and joined at the Kabilpur Madrasha and have been working there, as Imam of Kabilpur Mosque. He was never interested to be Mutawalli of the Estate.

5. One Dana Miah earlier tried to be Mutawalli of the Estate but was unsuccessful, Subsequently his nephew namely Tayeb Ali in collusion with some local people including UP Chairman acted against the interest of the wakf Estate and tried to oust the petitioner from the office of Mutawalli. Over cutting of paddy from wakf property some criminal cases had to be filed by the petitioner against the local enemy group who made conspiracy in collusion with local MP and submitted a proposal of a new committee to the Respondent No. 1 proposing name of said Tayeb Ali as Mutawalli of the Estate, after obtaining an enquiry report (Annexure-J) from respondent No. 3 without notice and knowledge of the petitioner.

6. The petitioner suddenly received the memo dated 10-6-99 (Annexure-K) from the office of Respondent No. 1 and learnt that Respondent No. 2 has been appointed Mutawalli of the Estate for 3 years vide order dated 8-6-99 rejecting the petitioner's prayer vide petition dated 3-5-99 for extension of his tenure and directed the petitioner to hand over charge to the newly appointed Mutawalli within 10 days from the receipt of above order (Annexure-K) communicative to him vide memo 89 (3) Sa dated 10-6-99. Being aggrieved by the said order vide Annexure-K to the writ petition the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the Rule.

7. Respondent No. 2 namely appointed Mutawalli namely Moulana Abdul Hai appeared through engaged Advocate, filed Affidavit-in-opposition denying the claim and allegations of the petitioner and stating that he being elder brother of the petitioner is competent to be the Mutawalli as per terms of the Waqf deed and that he never was unwilling earlier to be the Mutawalli as alleged by the petitioner. That the petitioner was appointed Mutawalli for 3 years vide order dated 10-11-81 and on expiry of the said period the petitioner has no locus standi to field on the charge of Mutawalli. He stated further that the petitioner acted against interest of the "wakf Estate misappropriating income and fund of the Estate. The petitioner caused mismanagement to the Estate in different ways for which complaint was made to the Administrator, the allegations were found true and accordingly the petitioner was removed from the charge of Mutawalli and this respondent No. 2 being elder brother of petitioner and elder son of Maulana Md Sayed has been appointed as Mutwalli vide impugned order (Annexure-K) which having no legality is not likely to be set-aside. It has been stated that the writ petition will not lie as the petitioner has the relief under Section 32 (2) of the Ordinance.

8. At the hearing learned Advocate for the petitioner shows that in Annexure the appointment of petitioner as Mutawalli was "for period of 3 years or until further order." The said order was dated 10-11-81 and after its expiry `no further' order as passed by the Administrator and as a result the petitioner continued to carry on the duties as Mutawalli. He submits that after expiry of 3 years from 10-11-1981 the petitioner will not be without locus standi to hold an the charge as Mutawalli in the absence of any further order in the matter by the Administrator as disclosed in order dated 10-11-81 (Annexure-A).

9. Leaned advocate refers to the Proviso of Section 32(1) of Wakfs Ordinance 1982 which provides that "no such action for removal of a Mutawalli shall be made without giving him an opportunity of being heard". He refers to the impugned order dated 8-6-99 communicated to the petitioner vide Memo 89(3) Sa dated 10-6-99 as evidenced from Annexure-K that the petitioners prayer for extension of the tenure as Mutwalli vide petition dated 3-5-99 was rejected which in fact tantamount to his removal as the Mutawalli of the Estate for mismanagement of the Wakfs Estate and for misappropriation of Wakf fund and property and for other allegation about which enquiry (Annexure-J) was submitted after a holding enquiry in the locality under direction of the authority and in view of said enquiry report (Annexure-J) the impugned order of removal of petitioner was passed without serving any show cause notice as required on the petitioners to explain his position about the allegations. He submits that obviously the said order was passed without observing the mandatory provision of the Proviso to Section 32(1) of the Ordinance by not giving the petitioner on opportunity of being heard before passing the said and, as such, according to him the impugned order cannot be tenable in law. In this retard he relies on the decisions reported in 45 DLR 70 and 35 DLR 277 wherein it was held that removal of a Mutawalli without observing mandatory provisions of the Proviso to Section 32(1) will be illegal and untenable in law.

10. He submits that the Proviso of Section 32(2) of the Ordinance as regards filing appeal to the District Judge against order of removal contains non reliable precondition to hand over charge to the newly appointed Mutawalli before filing appeal and, as such, with petition will lie. In this regard he refers to decisions ported in 17 DLR 40 and 4 MLR(AD) 19 where in it was held that writ petition will lie instead of filing regular appeal to this District Judge under provisions of Section 32(2) when the ordinance is non-relaxable pre-condition to hand over charge before filing the appeal to the authority.

11. Learned Advocate refers to the provisions of Section 38 of the Ordinance and submits that the Administrator is empowered to take action against an existing Mutawalli after holding regular enquiry by himself under Section 38 of the Ordinance. He contends that in the instant case no such enquiry was held by the Administration before passing the impugned order as evidenced by Annexure-K. He therefore argues that the impugned order or removal being illegal cannot stand in law and according to him it is liable to be set-aside and the Rule should be made absolute.

12. Learned Advocate for the Respondent 0.2 argues that after expiry of 3 years from the date of appointment of petitioner as Mutawalli vide order dated 10-11-91 (Annexure-A) the petitioner will have no locus standi to hold on the charge and continue as Mutawalli. He further submits that during local enquiry about the allegations against the petitioner under direction of the authority it came to light that the petitioner was liable for mismanagement of the wakfs Estate, misappropriation of wakfs fund and property and some other allegations vide enquiry report as evidenced from Annexure-J and in view of such enquiry report (Annexure-J) the Administrator removed the petitioner vide impugned order (Annexure-K) and appointed this Respondent No. 2 (Moulana A Hai) as Mutwalli in view of fact the respondent No. 2 is elder son of Maulana Md. Sayeed and also elder brother of petitioner and, as such, respondent No.2 is more competent than the petitioner according to the terms of the wakfs deed for appointment as Mutawalli. He also argues that writ petition will not lie as the petitioner has the remedy under Section 32(2) in the manner of appeal to the District Judge. So according to him the Rule is liable to be discharged.

13. Order dated 10-11-81 of the Administrator of wakfs (Annexure-A) snows that appointment of the petitioner as Mutawalli of the Estate was "for a period of 3 years or until further order. Such fact was communicated to the petitioner vide Annexure Act (1) Subsequently after expiry of the said period of 3 years 'no further' order' in that regard was passed by the Administrator and in the absence of any "further order" as intended in Annexure-A the petitioner was allowed to hold on the charge as Mutawalli of the Estate and continued to have regular correspondence as Mutawalli with the office of the Administrator as evidenced by Annexure-B, B1, C series G and 1. Therefore the connection that after expiry of said 3 years the petitioner lost locus standi to hold on charge as Mutawalli of the Estate cannot be legality tenable.

14. From Annexure-J copy of inquiry report dated 16-5-99 by one Kamal Hossain during local enquiry held by him under direction of the authority about various allegations against the petitioner Md. Abdul Kalam as Mutawalli regarding mismanagement of wakfs Estate misappropriation of wakf found and property and other allegations the same were found true and it appears that in view of above allegations, against the petitioner as Mutawalli the Administrator removed the petitioner as Mutawalli and appointed in his place his elder brother respondent No. 2 Moulana A. Hai as new Mutawalli vide order dated 8-6-99 as evidenced by Annexure-K. It obviously appears that removal was made for various allegations like mismanagement .of the state and misappropriation of fund and property of wakfs Estate attracting the offence under provision of Section 32(1) (i) of the Ordinance 1982 and accordingly the proviso to Section 32(1) will be clearly applicable.

15. The proviso to Section 31(1) runs as follows:—

"Provided that no such order for removal of a Mutawalli Shall be made without giving him an opportunity of being heard."

16. Admittedly no show cause notice was served on the petitioner as officiating Mutawalli of the Estate at the time before passing the impugned order of removal dated 8-6-99 communicated vide memo No. 89 (3) Sa dated 10-6-99 as evidenced by Annexure-K and it is an obvious violation the mandatory provision of the above proviso to Section 31(1) of the Wakf Ordinance 1982.

17. In the case of Nadira Rahman vs Amir Hossain reported in 35 DLR 277 as cited on behalf of the petitioner it was held that section 32 of the Ordinance is of Penal nature as it punishes the Mutawalli by taking away the vested right. Because of this sense of penalty the law givers in their anxiety had made it incumbent upon the Administration of wakfs to hear the person who is an accused before him and hear him before he is punished and before he is found guilty of the allegations made. The Administrator of wakfs being a court while acting under section 32 of the ordinance needs to come to a finding as a court of law.

18. In the case of Tabarak Ali Sikder vs Administrator of Wakfs reported in 45 DLR 70 as cited on behalf of the petitioner 'it was held that. "The Mutawalli has a right to be heard and lot reply to the allegations made against him specially when the right has been given in the proviso of the section. It has always been considered a cardinal principle of interpretation of any deed or statute that a proviso to a section will have an overriding effect over the whole provision. By denying the Mutawalli his right to be heard, the Administration of wakf has committed a breach of the mandatory provision of the wakf ordinance."

19. On the same point reference was made by the petitioner to the decision in the case of Nuruzzaman vs Secretary Education Department Govt. of last Pakistan reported in 17 DLR 46 wherein it was held and observed. That Section 32 of the Ordinance is of a Civil nature and all enquiry by it must be conducted in a manner followed in a Civil Court which only means that the Administrator is to act judicially. On a point of procedure it is to be kept in mind that the essential duty of a Court is to secure fairness and fairness cannot be secured without giving a gearing to a person against whom some allegations have been made." It has been obviously clear that before passing impugned order of removal as Mutawalli as evidenced from Annexure-K no scope was offend to the petitioner through show cause notice to provide him with the opportunity of being heard and it was clear violation of the provision of the proviso to the section 32(1) of the Ordinance.

20. Regarding non, filing of appeal to the District Judge under provision of section 32(2) of the ordinance reference has also been made by the petitioner to some decision reported in 17 DLR 46 wherein it was held that." In our as the remedy of appeal in sub-section 2 of section 32 of the Ordinance in conditioned by the fact that the appellant has to make over possession before filing the appeal, it is not an adequate remedy within the meaning of Article 98".

21. On the same point reliance was put on the decision in the case of Tafijul Huq vs Bangladesh reported in 4 MLR (AD) 19 = 3 BLC (AD) 135 where in it was held and observed that alternative remedy of appeal under section 32(2) of the Wakfs Ordinance will not be a bar to writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution if there is non-relaxable precondition for bringing the appeal. Same view was taken in the decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 46 DLR (AD) 191.

<u>22. In view of above facts, circumstances and legal position we are clearly of the opinion that the impugned order of removal of the petitioner as Mutawalli of the Wakfs Estate vide Annexure-K was passed in obvious violation of the provision of the Proviso to the section 32(1) and provision of section 38 of the ordinance and, as such, the same cannot be sustainable in law. We see merit and substance in the Rule.</u>

<u>In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. Impugned order of removal of the petitioner Md. Abul Kalam as Mutawalli of the Wakfs Estate dated 3-6-99 communicated vide Memo No. 89 (3) Sa dated 10-6-99 (Annexure-K) in clear violation of the mandatory provision of the proviso to section 32 (1) and provisions of section 38 of the Wakfs Ordinance 1982 is declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effects. The Administrator of Wakfs will be always free to move in accordance with the provisions of the Wakf ordinance 1982 to deal with any matter relating to the Wakf Estate concerned if circumstances and necessity demand and call for.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Md Azizul Hoque, Advocate—For Petitioner.
Sheikh Atiar Rahman with Habibullah, Advocates—For Opposite Parties.
parties:
Anwara Khatun & others ------ Defendant-Respondent-Petitioners
vs
Tofjal Huq and others ------ Plaintiff Appellant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 31-1-2000 (decree signed on 7-2-2000) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Feni in Title Appeal No. 29 of 1992 allowing the appeal after reversing those dated 22-3-1992 (decree signed on 29-3-1992 ) passed by the learned subordinate Judge, Feni in Title Suit No. 51 of 1982 should not set aside.

2. Material facts of the case, as necessary for the disposal of the rule are that the opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted title suit No.51 of 1982 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Feni for specific performance of contract in respect of the suit land as described in the plaint alleging, inter alia, that the defendant No. 1, Anwara Khattm had agreed to sell the Suit land for Tk. 47,481 and accordingly defendant No. 1, executed a bainapatra on receipt of Taka 38,000 out of Taka 47,481 through her husband on 21-4-1980 corresponding to 8th Baishakh, 1387 BS and it was stipulated therein that on payment of the balance consideration the defendant No. 1, would execute and register the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff but subsequently, the defendant No. 1 denied to perform her part of the contract and hence the suit.

3. The defendant No. 1, Anwara Khatun contested the suit by filing Written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that she never made any such bainapatra for sale of her property nor she had received any money from the plaintiff through her husband. It is also asserted that the bainapatra in question is forged and created one. The plaintiff is a man of no means, the plaint case is all false and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. Upon the pleadings of the respective parties the trial Judge framed as many as 5(five) issues to decide the case namely:—

i. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form?

ii. Whether the suit is barred by limitation?

iii. Whether the bainapatra was properly executed?

iv. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree as prayed for?

v. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get any other relief?

5. At the trial both the parties led evidence both oral and documentary to prove their respective cases. The Trial Court by its judgment and decree dated 22-3-1992 (decree signed on 29-3-1992) dismissed the suit on con-test on the findings that the plaintiff side miser-ably failed to prove that on receiving cash money the defendant No. 1, Anwara Khatun executed the bainapatra.

6. On appeal, Title Appeal No. 29 of 1992, the learned Additional District Judge, Feni allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court dated 22-3-1992 (decree signed on 29-3-1992).

7. Being aggrieved thereby the present defendant-petitioners have come before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Md Azizul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-respondent-petitioners in the course of argument after placing the judgments of 2 (two) Courts below and deposition of witnesses submits that the trial Court rightly doubted the bainapatra in question on the grounds that the plaintiff claimed in his plaint total 0.57 acres of land but the schedule of bainapatra contained only 0.42 acres of land and PW 3, Abdur Rahman, who stated that only Taka 3,800 was paid as advance money which clearly contradicts the plaintiff's case that the defendant No. 1, executed a bainapatra on receipt of Taka 38,000 out of Taka 47,481 through her husband on 21-4-1980 but the lower appellate Court without adverting all these material findings of the trial Court abruptly reversed the decision of the trial Court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 31-1-2000 which is, in fact, not a proper judgment of reversal ,and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside.

9. Mr Azizul Hoque, next after placing the bainapatra in question submits that the defendant's husband Tobarak Ullah's signature in the bainapatra and in the deposition sheet as well as in the civil revisional application upon a compare it would found that the signature of Tobarak Ullah in bainapatra is totally different with his signatures as made in the deposition sheet and in the civil revisional application but the Court of appeal below most illegally ignoring such fatal inconstancies mechanically decreed the suit believing the plaintiff's case.

10. Referring to the evidence of PW 3 Mr Azizul Hoque submits that the trial Court rightly held that the plaintiff could not prove his possession over the suit land whatsoever. Mr Azizul Hoque, the learned Advocate finally relying on the decisions reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 195 = 50 DLR (AD) 52 and 7 BLD (AD) 124 submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract the primary question before the Court is whether the plaintiff has been able to prove the genuineness of the agreement/bainapatra by producing cogent, reliable and independent evidence but in this case the plaintiff failed to prove the genuineness of the bainapatra by adducing any cogent, reliable and independent evidence. In this connection he also adds that in a suit for specific performance of contract the opinion given by the expert whether a bainapatra is genuine or not is not at all a conclusive evidence whatsoever.

11. On the other hand, Mr Sheikh Atiar Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties supports the impugned judgment and decree which was, according to him just, correct and proper Mr Atiar, next in the course of argument after placing the plaint of the suit and the depositions of PWs and DWs submits that all the PWs including the PW 2, hand writing expert and PW 3, deed writer categorically stated that original defendant No. 1 Anwara Khatun executed the bainapatra by putting her thumb impression and thus, the appellate Court below committed no wrong in reversing the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff could not prove the genuineness of the bainapatra by adducing cogent and reliable evidence. Mr Atiar further submits that, in a suit for specific performance of contract the possession of the suit property is not at all an important issue but the trial Court below under misconception of law and fact most illegally gave emphasis in deciding the suit on the question of possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate further submits that it is now well settled that mere omission to assign reasons in the impugned judgment is not fatal if in law the judgment and order is sustainable.

12. Mr Atiar further submits that minor discrepancies as pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner are not fatal since there is sufficient evidence on record to show that the defendant No. 1, executed the bainapatra on receipt of Taka 38,000. Moreso, PW 2, hand writing expert after examination of the thumb impression of defendant No. 1 gave opinion that the thumb impression of defendant No. 1 as put in the disputed bainapatra is genuine and other evidence on record also corroborates the expert opinion. The learned Advocate finally submits that the Court of appeal below as last Court of fact on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record rightly reversed the judgment of the trial Court which should not be disturbed. Mr Atiar, the learned Advocate in support of his submission has relied on the decisions reported in 12 DLR 453, 9 MLR (AD) 201 = 56 DLR (AD) 41, 45 DLR 279, 56 DLR (AD) 42 and 3 BLC (AD) 85.

13. I have perused the Revisional application along with annexure including the judgments of 2(two) Courts below and considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the respective parties. The real question for consideration in this case whether the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 has been able to prove the genuineness of the bainapatra by producing cogent reliable and independent evidence.

14. At the trial the plaintiff examined as many as 4 witnesses and the defendant No. 1 examined 4 witnesses including herself as DW 1 to prove their respective cases. It is found that plaintiff-Tofjal himself was examined as PW 1 who stated that on receiving Tk. 38,000 the defendant No 1, Anowara Khatun executed bainapatra on putting her LTI on 21-4-1980. This witness denied the suggestion that the bainapatra is false, fabricated and prepared fraudulently. 15. PW 2, Md Mozahar Hossain, who as a hand writing expert submitted his opinion on 10-1-1985. This witness in his deposition stated that:

আমি উপরোক্ত বায়নাপত্র্রের তিনটি টিপের সহিত নমুনার টিপগুলির পরীক্ষা-তুলনা করি উহাতে দেখা যায় আরজি, বায়নার ক, ক(১), ক(২) চিহ্নিত। LTI এর সহিত Specimen এর খ চিহ্নিত LTI তুলনা করিয়া রিপোর্ট দাখিল করিয়াছি। উহাতে দেখা যায় উভয় প্রকার LTI হুবহু মিল আছে। আমার রিপোর্ট সত্য। এই সেই রিপোর্ট সই। PW3, Nurul Kabir stated in his deposition that: আমি দলিল লেখক। অত্র দলিল আমি লিখিয়াছি। ইহা ২১-৪-৮০ইং তারিখে লিখিয়াছি। ইহার দাতা আনোয়ারা এবং গ্রহীতা তফজল হক। ইহা একটি বায়নাপত্র। বায়না পত্রে উল্লেখিত টাকা লেনদেন হইয়াছে মর্মে পক্ষগণ আমাকে বলিয়াছে। This witness proved the bainapatra as Exhibit 1 and his signature thereon as Exhibit 1 (ka) and 1 (Kha). PW 4, Abdul Rahman as attesting witness of the bainapatra proved his signature as Exhibit 1 (Kha). This witness denied the suggestion that the bainapatra is false and prepared fraudulently.

16. From the above quoted evidence, it transpires that the defendant No. 1, Anowara Khatun executed bainapatra in question on putting her LTI in presence of the witnesses.

17. It is found that defendant No. 1 Anowara Khatun herself was examined as DW 1, who stated that she did not execute any bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of Taka 38,000 out of Taka 47,481 through her husband on 21-4-1980 DW 2, Tobarak Ullah is husband of defendant No. 1 who stated in his deposition that আমি ইকবাল মেমোরিয়াল কলেজের দারোয়ান এবং ১নং বিবাদীর স্বামী। আমার স্ত্রী বাদীর নি���ট কোন জমি বিক্রয় করে নাই বা তাহার নিকট হইতে কোন টাকা পয়সা নেই নাই, বা কোন বায়নাপত্র সম্পাদন করে নাই।

18. DW 3, Kamal Uddin stated in his deposition that plaintiff is his uncle and defendant No. 1 is his cousin. This witness also stated that the suit land is possessed by the defendant's husband. DW 4, Mominul Haque also stated that defendant's husband possessed the suit land.

19. On a careful scrutiny of the evidence of DWs, it appears that DW 3 and DW 4 deposed nothing with regard to genuineness of the bainapatra. So, it cannot be said the testimony DW 1 and DW 2 with regard to genuineness of bainapatra finds support from the evidence of DW 3 and DW 4.

20. It appears that the Court of appeal below, on consideration of the facts, circumstance of the case and the evidence on record came to a conclusion that the plaintiff by adducing sufficient corroborative and reliable evidence has been succeeded to prove the genuineness of the bainapatra (Exhibit 2).

21. The Court of appeal below also held that there was overwhelming evidence on record to show that the defendant No. 1, Anowara Khatun understood the contents of bainapatra and she executed the bainapatra by putting her thumb impression in presence of witnesses but the learned Assistant Judge has committed wrong in holding that the plaintiff failed to prove the genuineness of bainapatra in question which resulted in the failure of justice.

22. Now, let me examine the legal position in this regard.

23. In the case of Syed Munsif Ali vs Shashanka Mohan Chowdhury reported in 3 BLC (AD) 85, it has been held that:

"The material question for consideration in a suit for specific performance of contract is as to whether the agreement is genuine and whether consideration passed between the parties."

24. In the case of Serajuddin Ahmed vs AKM Saiful Alam reported in 56 DLR (AD) 41; it has been held that:

"Law permits the Court to compare signature of a person with his admitted signature, but still then superior Courts have sounded caution to avoid the course of comparing the signature thumb impression by the Court itself. Since by scientific process or method examination of signature, particularly thumb impression, has developed much and, as such, it is safe and sound to leave the matter of examination of signature including thumb impression as well as hand writing to the expert or to the person specialized in the examination of writing including thumb impression for avoiding possibility or probability of failing very much in error in arriving at an opinion by the Court upon resorting to comparison for ascertainment of similarity or dissimilarity of writing or thumb impression."

25. In the case of Jahanara Begum vs Md Aminul Islam Chowdhury reported in 17 BLD (AD) 195 = 50 DLR (AD) 52, it has been observed that in a suit for specific performance of contract the primary question before the Court is whether the plaintiff has been able to prove the genuineness of the agreement by producing cogent, reliable and independent evidence.

26. In the case of Eklas Khan vs Prajesh Chandra Das reported in 7 BLD (AD) 142, where it has been held as follows:

"Opinion of an expert, such as, a handwriting expert, is only a relevant fact under section 45 of the Evidence Act. The Court will certainly consider the expert's opinion but it is the Court which alone will come to its own conclusion regarding the matter on which the Expert gives opinion. That is why an expert's opinion, particularly of a hand-writing expert, is always received with great caution."

<u>27. On an analysis of the aforesaid decisions, it appears that in a suit for specific performance of contract the primary question before the Court is whether the plaintiff has been able to prove the genuineness of the agreement by producing cogent, reliable and independent evidence. It also appears that the expert's opinion is not conclusive evidence but expert's opinion enables the Court to come to a satisfactory conclusion, though the said opinion is not binding upon the Court.</u>

<u>28. In this connection it may be further mentioned that the Court itself can compare any signature of LTI of any concerned person himself under section 73 of the Evidence Act and come to a decision but it is better to have an expert's opinion also particularly in case of LTI. As already noticed earlier that in this case the opinion of the hand writing expert with regard to LTI of defendant No. 1 finds support from the evidence of PW 1, PW 3 and PW 4. Besides, it also appears that DW 3 and DW 4 stated nothing with regard to genuineness of the bainapatra.</u>

<u>29. It is found that the lower appellate Court after discussion of the evidence on record adverted all the material findings of the trial Court and came to the conclusion that the trial Court below committed wrong in disbelieving the bainapatra by merely looking at the irrelevant evidences on record. The learned Additional District Judge, Feni upon a proper consideration of the entire evidence on record including the bainapatra as well as expert's opinion found that case of the plaintiff to be acceptable. This being a finding of fact which, in fact, in my opinion, based on proper appreciation of the evidence and materials on record I, therefore find nothing to interfere with the findings and decision of the lower appellate Court.</u>

30. The grievance of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the Court of appeal below without considering the material omissions and inconsistencies of the plaintiff's case mechanically reversed the judgment of the trial Court appears to be without any substance.

31. Mr Azizul Hoque, the learned Advocate for fortify his submission has relied on 3 (three) decisions namely the decisions reported in 7 BLD (AD) 142, 17 BLD (AD) 195 = 50 DLR (AD) 52 and AIR 1961 (SC) 1728. I have studied the said decisions to the best of my ability and it appears that in the facts of the present case the principle enunciated in those decisions in no way help the defendant-petitioner rather it supports the plaintiff's case.

33. In view of any discussion made in the foregoing paragraphs vis-a-vis the cited decisions by now it is clear that the instant Rule must fail.

34. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Let a copy of the judgment along with lower Court's record be sent down at once.

End.
